This third National Risk Assessment of Money Laundering provides an updated understanding of the threats and vulnerabilities facing the Isle of Man between 2020 and 2025 . As a mature international finance centre serving predominantly non-resident customers, the Island remains inherently exposed to cross-border financial crime, increasingly complex global structures, and evolving digital payment channels.

The overall Money Laundering Risk remains Medium High, unchanged since 2020. While threats have intensified, national controls have strengthened accordingly, resulting in a stable but increasingly sophisticated risk landscape.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), Ministerial Introduction - 737dae74eb339ad5
body:
I am pleased to present the Isle of Man's third National Risk Assessment of Money Laundering. This report represents the culmination of extensive work by government authorities, regulators, law enforcement, and crucially, the Island's financial services industry and wider private sector. It builds on the foundations laid by the previous NRAs published in 2015 and 2020 and reflects our ongoing commitment to maintaining the Highest standards in the fight against financial crime.
This Money Laundering NRA is an overarching assessment for the Isle of Man, providing a comprehensive analysis of the key money laundering risks facing our jurisdiction. It is important to note that this report should be read in conjunction with a suite of other risk assessments, including those on terrorist financing, proliferation financing, non-profit organisations, and the detailed sectoral money laundering reports. The report on legal persons and arrangements offers insights into the risks that can be associated with complex structures and beneficial ownership. Together, these documents provide a holistic view of the threats and vulnerabilities we face and the measures in place to mitigate them.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), Ministerial Introduction - 857ca5001a2811ee
body:
The Isle of Man is a well-established international finance centre, and as such, we are acutely aware of the evolving nature of money laundering threats, both globally and domestically. The period covered by this assessment has seen significant geopolitical and technological change and the Island has responded proactively to both emerging and existing challenges. We have strengthened our legal and regulatory frameworks, enhanced our supervisory and enforcement capabilities, and invested in new technologies and training. Our approach is risk-based, dynamic, and informed by the latest international standards and best practice.
Minister for Justice and Home Affairs Hon Jane Poole-Wilson MHK
This NRA would not have been possible without the invaluable contributions of industry. I would like to extend my sincere thanks to all those in the private sector who have engaged so constructively with government and the regulators throughout this process. Your expertise and commitment to upholding the Island's reputation as a responsible and well-regulated jurisdiction are deeply appreciated.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 2. Executive Summary, Introduction - 0584f9bd546cc708
body:
The Isle of Man's third National Risk Assessment (NRA) of Money Laundering (ML) is a central pillar of its ongoing commitment to global anti-financial crime standards. Recommendation 1 of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) requires countries to identify, assess, and understand their money laundering, terrorist financing (TF), and proliferation financing (PF) risks, forming the foundation for the effective design and implementation of a risk-based regime for combatting ML and countering TF and PF.
As an established international finance centre (IFC), the Isle of Man (IOM) is inherently exposed to cross-border activity, diverse customer bases, and complex financial structures. These features bring economic opportunity but also increase exposure to international financial crime risks. The 2026 ML NRA serves as a detailed, standalone assessment that reflects both the Island's maturing risk framework and the evolving nature of threats impacting the jurisdiction.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 2. Executive Summary, Introduction - 10a300c14abfd3f4
body:
This assessment builds on the previous 2015 and 2020 NRAs but is considerably more comprehensive, benefitting from improved data, enhanced supervisory capability, expanded inter-agency cooperation, and deeper sectoral engagement. It is complemented by NRAs on Terrorist Financing, Proliferation Financing, Non-Profit Organisations (NPOs) (specifically, their vulnerabilty to TF), Virtual Assets (VAs) and Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs), and Legal Persons and Arrangements (LPAs), as well as standalone sectoral reports on Banking, Insurance, Trust and Corporate Service Providers (TCSPs), and Gambling, creating a comprehensive suite of national risk products. Taken together, these form a holistic understanding of the Island's financial crime exposure.
The ML NRA is intended to guide government agencies, regulators, law enforcement, and industry in assessing their own risk landscapes and to inform a jurisdictional risk appetite statement. It must also be clearly reflected in Business Risk Assessments (BRAs), Customer Risk Assessments (CRAs), and Technology Risk Assessments (TRAs), ensuring alignment across the national system.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 2. Executive Summary, Country Risk Context, 2020-2025 - ea5e54bfd2cf8deb
body:
The period since the last NRA has seen significant global turbulence, including the COVID-19 pandemic, fuelling an increase in cybercrime and cyber-enabled fraud, and human trafficking and exploitation.
The geopolitical landscape has altered significantly since 2020, notably as a result of the Russian Federation's invasion of Ukraine and the conflict between Israel and Hamas in Gaza. In response to international sanctions, the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU) led multi-agency reviews of exposure to the Russian Federation, Belarus, and Kazakhstan, with additional actions taken by other agencies to de-register aircraft owned by sanctioned persons and to strengthen the legal framework for sanctions compliance.
Throughout evolving geopolitical concerns, the Island demonstrated the ability to respond at short notice, including through the imposition of financial and trade sanctions in line with international and UK measures. This includes a legal framework enabling efficient introduction of new sanctions and improved communication of updates to sanctions lists.
The rapid growth of transnational organised crime in Southeast Asia, particularly related to scam operations involving cyberenabled fraud and money laundering, was identified as a significant threat by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC). Their reporting highlights a concentration of Asian-facing organised crime groups (OCGs) in casino and online-gambling-related businesses.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 2. Executive Summary, Country Risk Context, 2020-2025 - f198fde02b3fc1dc
body:
As this threat emerged, impacting the Isle of Man and numerous other jurisdictions, the Island took specific mitigating action: improved inter-agency cooperation, targeted inspections from the Gambling Supervision Commission (GSC), FIU typology publications, enforcement actions, joint intelligence gathering, outreach, legislative reforms, and expanded information-sharing powers. An urgent review was undertaken on the exposure of the online gambling market, including development of a National Risk Appetite Statement accompanied by Ministerial Statements.
The global growth in alternate payment methods, including the use of virtual assets, has also been a feature since the last NRA. Although only a small number of VASPs operate in the Isle of Man, use of VAs is recognised as increasing globally. There is a separate VA and VASP Risk Assessment covering ML, TF, and PF risks, also to be published in spring 2026.
Domestic crime rates remain the lowest in the British Isles, with the most prevalent proceeds-generating crime being the supply of illegal drugs. United Kingdom (UK)-based organised crime groups continue to target the Island due to higher drug prices. Law enforcement has made considerable progress disrupting this activity, arresting offenders and seizing drugs and criminal cash. The success of operations has resulted in the prison population nearing capacity, with 33% of inmates linked to organised crime.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 2. Executive Summary, Country Risk Context, 2020-2025 - 77c745f59db69fdd
body:
Ports security has been an area of focus, with improvements made through better coordination of resources. Vulnerabilities identified during and after the COVID-19 pandemic included exposure to drug trafficking, ML, and more recently, organised immigration crime exploiting the free movement of people and goods between the Isle of Man, UK, and Ireland.
A 2025 independent report ("Isle of Man and UK Immigration Gap Analysis") highlighted significant immigration system abuse by organised criminality, including fraud, illegal entry, modern slavery, salary underpayments, forgery, illegal recruitment fees, public benefit fraud, and creation of sham jobs or synthetic businesses. Two visa routes were closed due to concerns.
Since the 2021 census, the Isle of Man has seen increasing numbers of visa applications from South Africa, the Philippines, China, and India. Nationality on visa applications does not always reflect original citizenship due to dual nationalities or earlier acquired citizenships. Demand for golden passports and visas has risen sharply globally. While investment-based citizenship and residency schemes can be legitimate tools for economic development, they also present risks by enabling concealment of identity, sources of funds, and evasion of sanctions.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 2. Executive Summary, Geographic Exposure and Higher-Risk Jurisdictions - 844091ed5d9664d6
body:
The Isle of Man's geographic exposure reflects its position as an international financial centre that serves predominantly nonresident customers. Financial flows are heavily concentrated around major advanced economies, principally the UK, United States (US), and Germany, which together account for the majority of inbound and outbound activity. This profile has remained broadly stable since the 2020 NRA, although growth in certain emerging markets has shifted specific sectoral risk dynamics. Notably, increased activity linked to South America, particularly Argentina, has been driven primarily by money or value transfer service (MVTS) expansion and greater use of international payment platforms, requiring strengthened monitoring of flow patterns and source jurisdictions.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 2. Executive Summary, Geographic Exposure and Higher-Risk Jurisdictions - 0c37e4766224f3f7
body:
In parallel, the Island maintains a robust approach to assessing exposure to higher-risk jurisdictions. While South Africa previously featured as the only List B country within the top 10 jurisdictions by financial flow, its removal from the FATF's list of "Jurisidictions Under Increased Monitoring" (the "grey list") in October 2025 resulted in a reduction in overall customer exposure linked to higher-risk jurisdictions, from approximately 5.5% to around 3%. Nonetheless, the underlying composition of the higher-risk jurisdictions customer base continues to require careful attention. Risk indicators that have been used for this NRA include residency origins, use of non-natural persons, politically exposed persons (PEPs), use of introducers, and complex beneficial ownership (BO) structures. The Isle of Man's published lists of higher-risk jurisdictions support industry-wide risk assessment and help guide enhanced due diligence (EDD) where exposure is elevated.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 2. Executive Summary, Overall National ML Risk - 12a073ddf7145eb0
body:
National ML Risk = Medium High (unchanged since 2020) The national ML risk remains Medium High, unchanged from 2020, reflecting a stable yet increasingly complex risk environment. While the Island has strengthened its supervisory, intelligence, and enforcement capabilities since the previous assessment, the nature of ML threats has also evolved, with a growing emphasis on cross-border criminality, cyber-enabled offending, and the misuse of international financial services. These developments mean that, while controls have improved, the overall level of threat pressure remains significant and continues to challenge national resources and risk mitigation frameworks.
The Medium High threat rating reflects the prominence of transnational organised crime, cyber-enabled fraud, foreign predicate offending, and exploitation of cross-border financial channels. The Island's profile as an international financial centre with large non-resident flows means that exposure to global criminal networks is unavoidable. At the same time, domestic threats, including drug trafficking, immigration crime, and exploitation of ports and travel routes, add to the aggregate threat picture. The assessment concludes that, compared with 2020, threats have become more sophisticated and globally integrated, requiring enhanced intelligence-sharing, improved financial flow analysis, and continued investment in multi-agency capability.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 2. Executive Summary, Overall National ML Risk - 00c655bffbf7203e
body:
The Medium vulnerability rating recognises that, while the Island's controls have strengthened, certain structural vulnerabilities persist. These include the scale and complexity of cross-border activity, challenges associated with complex structures and beneficial ownership verification, and the resource demands of supervising diverse sectors. In addition, rapid technological developments, including virtual assets, alternative payment methods, and AI-enabled obfuscation, are creating emerging areas where controls and understanding are still developing. Improvements in FIU capability, risk-based supervision, and enforcement have helped constrain vulnerabilities, but the overall national ML risk remains Medium High due to the combined effect of threat intensity and residual weaknesses.

These sectors combine materiality, international customer bases, and exposure to complex structures or transactional activity.
The Banking sector remains central to the Island's financial system and its ML risk profile. Banks serve a predominantly non-resident customer base, with cross-border flows linked to major economies including the UK, US, and Germany, and exposure to emerging markets via MVTS and corporate structures. Elevated risks arise from high-value international transactions, complex ownership arrangements, and introduced business. Nonetheless, the sector demonstrates strong overall compliance, with robust systems and controls supported by risk-based governance. Enhanced monitoring expectations apply to higher-risk jurisdictions, politically exposed persons, and non-natural persons, consistent with the sectoral ML assessment.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 2. Executive Summary, Sectoral ML Risk - c1c0ee0358458612
body:
Insurance, particularly long-term life insurance, constitutes the Island's largest financial services subsector. While funds under management are substantial, the ML risks are generally understood as inherent rather than residual, given that products typically have clear premium-payment structures and redemption constraints. However, vulnerabilities include the global distribution model, varying intermediary standards, and the potential for misuse of surrender or early-withdrawal features in higher-risk cases. The sector has strengthened oversight frameworks, distribution-chain management, and customer-risk assessment processes.
Online gambling is one of the largest contributors to national income and presents a unique risk profile due to its global customer base and fast-moving payment flows. Although most operators provide business-to-business (B2B) technical services rather than direct player-facing activities, higher-risk factors include exposure to Asia-facing organised crime, misuse of gaming platforms to facilitate fraud proceeds, and vulnerabilities in source-of-funds verification. Multi-agency action, including GSC thematic reviews, FIU typologies, and strengthened information-sharing powers, has helped mitigate these risks, though continued vigilance is required.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 2. Executive Summary, Sectoral ML Risk - 6e350d7a2497c4fd
body:
TCSPs remain a core part of the Island's international business model, facilitating company, foundation, and trust structures for global clients. Inherent ML risks stem from complex beneficial ownership, introduced business, cross-border customers/services, and potential misuse of corporate vehicles. Supervisory reforms, market consolidation, and improved BO verification processes have strengthened sectoral resilience. Nonetheless, TCSPs continue to require enhanced scrutiny given their centrality to structure formation and the Island's exposure to higher-risk jurisdictions.
Professional service sectors, including legal, accountancy, and estate agency services, show varied risk profiles. While they are not uniformly high-risk, vulnerabilities emerge from occasional involvement in complex transactions, client-fund flows, real-estate purchases, or cross-border structuring. Estate agents face exposure to foreign purchasers and opaque ownership structures, though risks are mitigated by relatively low transaction volumes and non-cash handling. Legal and accountancy professionals contribute to risk mitigation through gatekeeper responsibilities, yet ongoing thematic monitoring remains essential.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 2. Executive Summary, Sectoral ML Risk - 94111177340d6b2c
body: Other Sectors, including high-value goods dealers (HVGDs), NPOs, MVTS/e-money providers, and VASPs, present more targeted or emerging risks. MVTS and e-money providers have expanded their international reach, necessitating enhanced oversight. NPOs generally present low ML risk, though TF vulnerabilities require monitoring (a separate report on NPO vulnerability to TF has been published). Although the number of active VASPs is small, VASPs contribute to exposure to global VA trends; this is addressed through a dedicated VA/VASP Risk Assessment. Together, these sectors form part of a diverse risk landscape requiring coordinated supervision and consistent application of the risk-based approach.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 2. Executive Summary, Recommended Actions - c965d49fdd52e462
body:
The NRA identifies a programme of national, sectoral, and thematic actions.
Recommended actions focus on strengthening the Island's overall AML/CFT system by improving the quality, consistency, and accessibility of data across authorities; enhancing analysis of cross-border financial flows through better datasets, intelligence exchange, and analytical tools; reinforcing risk-based supervision through expanded thematic work, sector-specific guidance, and more proactive oversight; improving the accuracy, verification, and ongoing maintenance of beneficial ownership information; and expanding both domestic and international intelligencesharing mechanisms to support faster detection of complex ML typologies and more effective joint operational outcomes. The recommendations outlined below represent national priorities. While the NRA highlights a broad spectrum of actions, including numerous regulatory initiatives, this executive summary focuses on the most impactful measures at the national level.
Strategic Aim: Public sector and industry work together to achieve a common goal of meeting international standards.
Review new AML/CFT/CPF governance arrangements by April 2026 to ensure their effectiveness. Introduce outstanding memoranda of understanding (MOUs) and Codes of Practice, (in particular, in relation to effective information-sharing among border and law enforcement agencies).

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 2. Executive Summary, Recommended Actions - d411469f9634776d
body:
Implement outstanding legislative provisions aimed at strengthening the AML framework, including the review and updating of provisions in the Proceeds of Crime Act 2008 to ensure that the framework is appropriate for the IOM.
Deliver further changes to enhance the effectiveness of the Beneficial Ownership regime, as per recommendations within the Legal Persons and Arrangements NRA.
Maintain ongoing engagement with industry to strengthen AML resilience. Embed the IOM Financial Crime Partnership and expand its remit, including the online gambling strategic working group.
Continue to progress Government-wide initiatives in respect of conducting CDD among Isle of Man Government agencies.
Strategic Aim: Actions are informed and driven by best practice and standards, both domestically and internationally.
To further enhance the understanding of complex structures, any future data outreach requests to the TCSP sector should look at seeking further detail on these structures so that a deeper understanding of all jurisdictions and asset types and locations is captured in the national data.
Enhance financial flow information and data to enable further analysis of risk, including from non-banking sources - in particular, VASPs, money transmission services (MTS), EMIs, and overseas ATMs.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 2. Executive Summary, Recommended Actions - 36d0eaa54162a694
body:
The FSA should continue to develop a formal approach with the FIU (and other relevant stakeholders) to document the analysis process for financial inflows and outflows, including for higher-risk countries and IFCs.
Formalise cross-agency intelligence-sharing arrangements, including centralised border/route intelligence and appropriate visa information-sharing, to strengthen detection and disruption.

Develop and disseminate relevant typologies informed by current trends and emerging threats identified in each sector and regularly update in consultation with industry stakeholders. A structured approach to sharing these typologies, both domestically and with international partners, should be embedded within supervisory and outreach frameworks.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 2. Executive Summary, How Industry Should Use This NRA - 1d783573415872ff
headers: How Industry Should Use This NRA
body:
Businesses in the regulated sector are obliged to undertake and maintain a Business Risk Assessment (BRA) which must have regard to any relevant findings of the most recent NRA relating to the Island. Therefore, industry must be able to show how they have considered and mitigated the relevant risks identified in this NRA, Given a number of NRAs are being published in sucession, it is acceptable to consider each NRA as it is published, but update the overall BRA at its next formal review date. Consideration should also be given to the Customer Risk Assessment (CRA) and the Technology Risk Assessment (TRA) and if these require updating.
Businesses in the regulated sector are obliged by the AML/CFT Code 2019 to undertake and update the BRA which 'assists relevant persons' to understand where, when, how and to what extent they are exposed to ML/TF risk and which areas of their business they should prioritise in combatting ML/TF. The Code state that a BRA must have regard to any relevant findings of the most recent NRA relating to the Island. Therefore, industry must be able to show they have considered and mitigated the relevant risks identified in this NRA.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 2. Executive Summary, How Industry Should Use This NRA - 37be9fab8c4dccb4
headers: How Industry Should Use This NRA
body:
One of the key inputs to the Island's NRAs is the risk data provided via STRIX AML. Where published NRAs and sector reports include aggregated industry data, each firm should consider how their own data compares with the published data. This will assist them to better understand their own risk profile compared to the national metrics, threats and vulnerabilities.
There are requirements under the Gambling (AML/CFT) Code 2019 Part 3 - Risk Based Approach (paragraph 7) for licence holders to carry out and record business risk assessments of ML/TF and review and update the business risk assessment at appropriate intervals and where there is a "material change in the business or in the risk of money laundering or financing of terrorism".
Given that the NRA is being published in sections in close succession, it is acceptable to consider each NRA as it is published but update the overall business risk assessments at the next formal review date.
Businesses must be able to demonstrate clear, practical application of this NRA and also consider integrating the findings into the CRA and TRA if these require updating and into policies governing onboarding, monitoring, screening, outsourcing, and governance. ■

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 3. Introduction, National Money Laundering Risk Assessment - 0664901009e4080a
body:
This is the third National Risk Assessment of Money Laundering from the Isle of Man Government. The Risk Assessments published in 2015 and 2020 both covered money laundering and terrorist financing together in a single document. The NRA has been developed throught a series of sectoral and topical reports into this overarching ML NRA to enable a detailed consideration of the key areas of risk for the Isle of Man. There are several other risk assessments including Terrorist Financing, Proliferation Financing, and Non-Profit Organisations. For a full list of sections which make up the 2025/6 NRA, please see page 10.
The Isle of Man has undertaken a comprehensive NRA to meet the Recommendation 1 of the Financial Action Task Force, which requires countries to identify, assess, and understand their money laundering, terrorist financing, and proliferation financing risks and to applying a risk-based approach to mitigate these risks effectively. (This includes designating an authority or mechanism to coordinate further actions in assessing risks and deploying resources.)
As FATF Recommendation 1 provides the essential foundation upon which an effective and efficient framework for identifying and addressing ML risk is built, it is important that a robust methodology is used. The ML NRA uses the World Bank methodology; the WB methodology was used in 2015 and 2020, allowing the findings of this NRA to be effectively benchmarked against those previous risk assessments.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 3. Introduction, National Money Laundering Risk Assessment - f2d8346d0e39494e
Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 3. Introduction, National Money Laundering Risk Assessment - 4efd2fa7ef695288
body:
Regulated businesses' respective AML/CFT Codes (the AML/ CFT Code 2019 and the Gambling AML/CFT Code 2019) both require that "... the business risk assessment must have regard to all relevant risk factors including [...] any relevant findings of the most recent National Risk Assessment relating to the Island."
Regard has also been given to the Risk Assessments of several other countries, mainly those which have certain economic similarities and similar risk profiles to the Isle of Man, notably Jersey, Guernsey, and Gibraltar. Given the close economic and legal/cultural relationship, particular attention has also been given to the recent Risk Assessment of the UK.
The IOM has a National Financial Crime Strategy which incorporates mission, aims, strategic objectives, and actions, and clearly demonstrates publicly the very strong goal of tackling all forms of financial crime. In Appendix 4 of the National Financial Crime Strategy document, a timeline is provided for the key activities in the development and maintenance of the Island's AML/CFT/CPF regime in line with international standards.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 3. Introduction, National Money Laundering Risk Assessment, METHODOLOGY - cd3fb339368e4389
body:
The National Financial Crime Strategy states its Strategic Objective 2 to be: to "use a risk-based approach to identify risk, coordinate appropriate actions, and apply resources to ensure identified risk is addressed and mitigated." The AML/CFT Policy Office team within the Government's Department for Home Affairs co-ordinates the NRA work. WB methodology was used for the 2015 and 2020 ML/TF NRAs. It has been used to provide consistency with previously published NRAs. The World Bank approach is consistent with FATF guidance published in 2025.[2.]
In the WB methodology for risk assessment, the tool treats ML risk as a product of two main components: threat and vulnerability. The consequences are integrated into those two components through weights, preconditions, and network structure and are not assessed separately. This approach is adopted at both national and sectoral levels for the IOM.
ML threat considers predicate offences such as fraud, tax crimes, drug trafficking, cybercrime, sanctions evasion, and crossborder risks. ML vulnerabilities evaluate the legal and regulatory frameworks and any weaknesses or gaps, sectoral controls such as customer due diligence and beneficial ownership, and institutional capacity including he resources and expertise of regulators, law enforcement, and the Financial Intelligence Unit.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 3. Introduction, National Money Laundering Risk Assessment, METHODOLOGY - bb72abeddc36acad
Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 3. Introduction, National Money Laundering Risk Assessment, METHODOLOGY - 93671b37f399a9bc
body: The National ML Risk Assessment of the IOM has been conducted as a self-assessment by the IOM authorities using the National ML Risk Assessment Tool that has been developed and provided by the World Bank Group. Data, statistics, and information used for completing the National ML Risk Assessment Tool modules, as well as findings, interpretation, and judgement under the scope of the National ML Risk Assessment, completely belong to the IOM authorities and do not reflect the views of the World Bank Group. ■

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 4. Country Risk Context 2020-25 - ff46fe7421d982b9
body:
The period since the last NRA has seen significant global turbulence, including the COVID-19 pandemic, leading to an increase in cybercrime and cyber-enabled fraud, and human trafficking and exploitation; the Isle of Man FIU published a risk assessment on COVID-19 in January 2021, focusing on the threats from cybercrime, fraud, counterfeit goods, and related activities. The report concluded that the risk of ML and financial crime relating to COVID-19 on the Isle of Man was low, provided typologies, and highlighted that the need for continued vigilance.
The geopolitical landscape has altered significantly since 2020, notably as a result of the Russian Federation's invasion of Ukraine and the conflict between Israel and Hamas in Gaza. In response to the conflict between the Russian Federation and Ukraine and the introduction of international sanctions, the Isle of Man has taken steps to assess and mitigate the risks of sanctions breaches relating to financial and non-financial exposure to the Russian Federation and its allies, including Belarus and Kazakhstan. These measures have determined that the risk of sanctions breaches is considered Medium Low.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 4. Country Risk Context 2020-25 - 11d63a33898f4059
body:
At the same time, the Isle of Man Aircraft Registry was directed by the Department for Enterprise (DfE) to exit all Russian Federation and Belarusian business. The Aircraft Registry was able to successfully act upon all sanctioned individuals' aircraft using a public interest article in the Air Navigation Order, ahead of UK sanctions being published. In response to international sanctions, the FIU led multi-agency reviews of exposure to the Russian Federation, Belarus, and Kazakhstan, with additional actions taken by other agencies to deregister aircraft owned by sanctioned persons and to strengthen the legal framework for sanctions compliance. The Financial Services Authority issued a letter reminding all regulated and registered persons of their obligations under AML/CFT legislation and emphasising that sanctions obligations applied to all persons and businesses in the Isle of Man.
Throughout the rapidly evolving worldwide events and geopolitical concerns, the Island has demonstrated the ability to respond at short notice, including through the imposition of financial and trade sanctions in line with international and UK measures. This includes a legal framework that enables the introduction of new sanctions in a more effective and efficient manner, and improved communication of updates to sanctions lists.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 4. Country Risk Context 2020-25 - 9bf12c331a0acf61
body:
The rapid growth of transnational organised crime in Southeast Asia, particularly related to scam operations involving cyberenabled fraud, money laundering, and other illicit activities, has been identified as a significant threat by the UN Office on Drugs and Crime. The report identifies that there has been a significant concentration of Asian-facing organised crime groups on casinoand online gambling-related businesses.
As this threat emerged, impacting the Isle of Man and countries across the world, the Island took specific action to mitigate the risks from this threat. This involved improved inter-agency cooperation, targeted GSC inspections, FIU publication of typologies, enforcement actions, joint intelligence-gathering, outreach, updated guidance, legislative reforms, and expanded information-sharing powers. An urgent review was initiated regarding the exposure of the online gambling market to this activity and a National Risk Appetite Statement for the Online Gambling sector was developed, accompanied by Ministerial Statements. The Isle of Man authorities are under no illusion that transnational crimes of this nature have not had a direct impact upon the jurisdiction, and the Island continues to take action to mitigate those risks.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 4. Country Risk Context 2020-25 - 28fa83622d8b4d53
body:
The global growth in alternative banking and use of virtual assets has been a further feature since the last NRA. However, there are only a very small number of active virtual asset service providers in the Isle of Man which are supervised in respect of AML/CFT by the FSA. Despite this, it is recognised that the use of VAs generally has increased. To fully understand the level of use of VAs, a separate assessment has been conducted that will consider VA and VASP risk in relation to ML, TF, and PF. This will be published in 2026.
Domestic crime rates overall have continued to be the lowest in the British Isles, with the most prevalent proceeds-generating crime to date being the supply of illegal drugs. UK-based OCGs continue to target the Isle of Man, seeking to produce, import, and supply Class A and B drugs with higher prices, making the Isle of Man a particularly attractive market. Law enforcement agencies, working closely with the UK, have made considerable progress in disrupting this activity, seizing drugs and criminal cash and arresting offenders at various levels in the supply chain, as attempts are made to integrate proceeds of crime and/or remove the same from the Isle of Man.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 4. Country Risk Context 2020-25 - 695c15165b1a513e
body:
The Chief Constable's Annual Report 2023/24 outlines the work taking place to deter, pursue, and prevent organised crime in the Island. It notes that immigration crime is beginning to emerge as a significant threat, alongside drug trafficking and ML. The success of the Constabulary in tackling organised criminality has resulted in the prison population being almost at capacity, with 33% of inmates linked to organised crime.
The security of the Island's ports has been an area of focus during this period, with improvements being made through effective co-ordination of existing resources. The vulnerability of the ports to criminal activity, notably drug trafficking and associated ML, was exposed during and in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic. More recently organised immigration crime has also attempted to exploit the existing arrangements on the relative free movement of people and goods to/from the UK and Ireland.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 4. Country Risk Context 2020-25 - af5e5bb206753b1e
body:
A 2025 independent report prepared for the Cabinet Office, "Isle of Man and UK Immigration Gap Analysis," has highlighted the abuse that the immigration system has experienced in recent years including from organised criminality, citing "fraud; illegal entry; modern slavery and exploitation; salary underpayments; forgery; charging illegal recruitment fees to migrants; public benefit claims; and the creation of "sham jobs or synthetic businesses" to facilitate immigration." The "IOM Worker Migrant (Seasonal)" and "IOM Representative of Overseas Business" routes were consequently closed to new applicants because of concerns.
Since the 2021 census, the Isle of Man has seen increasing numbers of immigration (visa) applications from South Africa and the Philippines, with China and India also showing increases. These trends partly reflect the Island's established economic connections, existing diaspora communities, and government strategies aimed at fostering economic growth and attracting investment. The nationality listed on visa applications may not always reflect an applicant's original citizenship, as many individuals hold dual nationalities or have acquired new citizenships prior to applying.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 4. Country Risk Context 2020-25 - 2cf5d3a07c92220a
body: This pattern is part of a broader global trend whereby demand for "golden passports" and "golden visas," citizenship or residency acquired through investment, has risen sharply in recent years. Such schemes can be a legitimate tool for economic development, but they can also present risks, with individuals able to obtain multiple citizenships and, by extension, multiple identities. This enables individuals to conceal their true identity and the source of their funds/wealth, making it easier for those facing international sanctions to transfer illicit funds, facilitate ML, evade tax and, ultimately, pose a threat to national and global security. The Isle of Man mitigates these risks using powers available to the authorities, including, for example, Section 15 reports, competent authority (including law enforcement) access to ultimate beneficial owner (UBO) information via the Isle of Man Database of Beneficial Ownership, oversight inspections, and Central Registry powers to check the accuracy of, and request further information regarding, UBOs, etc. ■

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 5. Jurisdictional Profile, BACKGROUND - c5f74160564f6610
body:
The Isle of Man is a self-governing British Crown Dependency located in the Irish Sea. It has a resident population of c. 84,500 and, in 2023/24, a GDP of £5.84 billion. The Isle of Man has its own directly-elected parliament (Tynwald), legal and financial systems, and independent courts. The legal system is based on common law principles and underpinned by a well-developed statutory framework. Political leadership is led by the Chief Minister. The representative of the King is the Lieutenant Governor, who is a formal point of contact between the Isle of Man and the Crown.
The UK Government is responsible for certain international matters, such as defence and international relations; however, the Isle of Man retains autonomy over domestic matters. The UK does not act internationally on behalf of the Isle of Man without prior consultation.
The Isle of Man is not a member of the UN, but it implements sanctions measures imposed by Security Council Resolutions due to inclusion as a party to the UK's membership of the UN. Isle of Man policy is to implement all UK and UN international sanctions measures without delay.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 5. Jurisdictional Profile, BACKGROUND - ea98c968d6a3e2e5
body:
There is a formal Customs and Excise Agreement with the UK , providing an overarching policy for customs administration on the Isle of Man. Under the Agreement, the Isle of Man and the UK are part of the same customs and value-added tax (VAT) territory; the movement of goods between the two countries are not usually subject to customs checks. Certain goods are prohibited or restricted, including restrictions on cash, with declarations required to be made by individuals travelling with, or transporting via postal packets, cash across the border, including between the Isle of Man and the UK.
There is freedom of travel within the Common Travel Area (comprising the UK, Ireland, Guernsey, Jersey, and the Isle of Man). Holders of UK visas may travel to the Isle of Man using their UK visa without needing to hold a separate visa (and vice versa). Individuals from outside the UK or Ireland wishing to relocate and work must hold a valid visa with permission to work on the Isle of Man.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 5. Jurisdictional Profile, BACKGROUND - 3e0f9d6858b7cbe6
body: The 2021 census shows that 49.6% of the population was born in the Isle of Man and 38.2% in the UK. The figures for the UK reflect the proximity and economic ties. The next highest country of birth was the Republic of Ireland, at 1.9%. The Isle of Man, with its capital Douglas and several smaller towns, is overall a homogenous society. Since 2020/21, there has been an increase in residents from South Africa, the Philippines, China, and India. The Isle of Man hosts several South African banks and has established communities of South Africans and Filipinos.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 5. Jurisdictional Profile, BUSINESS MODEL - 3c772c1bbd8f5a6d
body:
The IOM attracts a broad spectrum of international customers, owing to a combination of its strategic location, regulatory robustness, and commercial appeal. Its geographical proximity to both the UK and the Republic of Ireland positions the Island as a natural hub for cross-border business activity, particularly for enterprises with operations or assets spanning multiple jurisdictions. This advantage is further strengthened by longstanding cultural and economic ties especially with the North West of England, which enhance connectivity and foster trust.
Government policy has been instrumental in cultivating a business-friendly environment. The Island offers a robust legislative framework, efficient company registration processes, and a well-established legal system. Its tax regime, featuring a 0% corporate tax rate for most businesses and a 10% rate for Banking and Retail sectors, remains a key incentive for crossborder investors.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 5. Jurisdictional Profile, BUSINESS MODEL - 8eae613ccfe0041e
body: The Isle of Man has a diversity of sectors, and its business model provides global enterprises with political and economic stability, competitive taxation rates, and a dependable IT infrastructure. There is a well-developed and comprehensive regulatory and statutory framework, high levels of compliance with international standards (evidenced by strong Technical Compliance against FATF standards), and access to an efficient legal system. The IOM benefits from a highly-skilled workforce, and the Island's reputation for reliability has made it a preferred jurisdiction for customers engaging relocation services, particularly those seeking to preserve wealth in a stable and secure environment. The Island's competitive cost base reflects both its scale and pragmatic policy approach.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 5. Jurisdictional Profile, BUSINESS MODEL - a355c8443bd13803
body:
The Life Insurance sector continues to be the predominant financial services sector by National Income, with an international customer base, while Online Gambling represents the largest sector outside of finance. The most significant economic contribution is derived from the Life Insurance, Banking, and Trust and Corporate Service Provider sectors The Isle of Man also has internationally recognised ship and aircraft registries. The Ship Registry, established in 1984, consistently retains a position on the Paris MOU "White List" of top performing flag states and has a diverse fleet of merchant ships, yachts, and fishing vessels. The Aircraft Registry, established in 2007, registers private and corporate jets and helicopters.
The Isle of Man's direct and indirect taxation systems, together with its National Insurance system, fund a range of services for Island residents similar to those provided in the UK, such as the National Health Service, a State Pension, social Care services, etc. The Isle of Man operates a responsible tax system and has a long-standing policy of compliance with international standards as they are promulgated by bodies such as the FATF and the OECD. The Isle of Man is recognised by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the OECD for meeting international transparency obligations.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 5. Jurisdictional Profile, BUSINESS MODEL - 55e871d541c7da0b
body:
There are very close historical, geographical, cultural, and economic ties between the Isle of Man and the UK. It is unsurprising, therefore, that trade with the UK dominates the Isle of Man's business model. Data from the UK Office of National Statistics (ONS) and HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) shows that, for the 12 months up to the end of June 2025, total trade in goods and services, including financial services, between the Isle of Man and the UK was valued at £1.9 billion.
Data highlights that a significant proportion of the Isle of Man's business is regional in nature - i.e., it is substantially conducted with the UK and to a lesser extent with the Channel Islands.
As an international finance centre, the Isle of Man has commonalities with other smaller jurisdictions with economies based significantly on international finance and business, notably Jersey and Guernsey. All three islands are also Crown Dependencies with strong links to the UK (as outlined above). Nevertheless, IFCs differ with regard to their international profiles and the services they provide. For example, the economies of Jersey and Guernsey have particularly significant International Banking and Funds sectors.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 5. Jurisdictional Profile, BUSINESS MODEL - 75e9fd0e3324ae37
body:
The Isle of Man is significantly UK-centric, with the UK involved in over 45% of banking flows and, as identified in this report, a significant number of customer relationships directly linked to the UK. Analysis of Jersey's investor and funding profile - informed by the Centre for Economics and Business Research (Cebr) report "Jersey's Contribution to Global Value Chains" (commissioned by Jersey Finance, 2021) - shows that a substantial majority of capital administered through Jersey is sourced from non-UK jurisdictions. Available information indicates that Guernsey's financial services sector is overwhelmingly internationally-sourced, with most managed assets attributable to non-UK investors (although there is still substantial investment into UK assets).
International banking is important for the IOM; it is also significant for other smaller IFCs, for example Monaco, while Gibraltar and Malta have developed sectors in Online Gambling and Virtual Assets, amongst other services. For further information regarding the geographic exposure of the Isle of Man to other countries, including IFCs, see Chapter 8.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 5. Jurisdictional Profile, ECONOMIC STRATEGY - f888dd00bebe34ca
body:
In November 2022, Tynwald approved an Economic Strategy, a wide-ranging 10-15 year strategy. The Economic Strategy identified that, while the economy was diversified to some extent, there was sectoral concentration, with reliance on a small number of established sectors (Insurance, Online Gambling, Banking, and TCSPs), which created vulnerabilities and limited resilience. Three priority outcomes were identified for business:

(1) an increase in business productivity, (2) an increase in business innovation and investment, and (3) an improvement in the quality and growth in the size of the workforce.

Skills shortages were highlighted as the main business concern, with difficulties in recruiting and retaining skilled workers. This is a theme that was repeated in the NRA sectoral workshops, with many sectors experiencing challenges in recruiting and retaining experienced staff - in particular, compliance staff. Digitisation, changing taxation regimes, and global competition were also identified. Artificial intelligence was not identified as a key enabler/challenge in the Strategy, but in September 2025 the Chief Minister announced the creation of a National AI Office.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 5. Jurisdictional Profile, SIGNIFICANT ECONOMIC SECTORS - d8d5a3636d69e6da
body: The largest/materially most significant sectors in the Isle of Man are Banking, Insurance, Online Gambling, and Trust and Corporate Service Providers; a brief overview of each is provided below. For further, detailed information, see the individual sectoral reports in Chapter 12.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 5. Jurisdictional Profile, SIGNIFICANT ECONOMIC SECTORS, Banking - d25a26a647c7c3aa
body:
The Isle of Man Banking sector is a mature sector which is fully regulated and supervised by the FSA. The sector has seen consolidation over time, resulting in there now being a smaller number of banks which are mainly branches or subsidiaries of larger UK and international banking groups. Banking revenues are 9% of national income. This compares to Insurance, the largest sector of the economy at 17%, and Gambling, which contributes 14% The Banking sector held over £46 billion in assets as of December 2024. There are 11 banks operating in the IOM (and one bank representative office). The countries of origin (ultimate parent bank/group) for the current 11 banks are:

Figure 3: Countries of origin for banks in the IOM
- UK: 4; Spain: 1; South Africa: 3; Trinidad and Tobago: 1; Isle of Man: 2

Domestic banking is mainly delivered through UK banking groups. Banks also serve non-resident personal customers and, to a lesser extent, international businesses, including cross-border activity. There is a wide geographical spread of non-resident banking customers by residency and nationality. The largest number of non-resident customers are from the UK, reflecting the close geographical and economic ties between the UK and the IOM. There is also a significant number of South Africanresident banking customers, reflecting the Banking sector's longstanding links to that country.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 5. Jurisdictional Profile, SIGNIFICANT ECONOMIC SECTORS, Insurance - d2a3c648d9dd09ab
body: The Insurance sector is the largest financial sector in the Isle of Man, representing 17% of national income. As a politically and economically stable jurisdiction with a strong regulatory framework, the Isle of Man has become an international centre for establishing and managing insurance structures. The Insurance sector is fully regulated and supervised by the FSA. The sector encompasses Life, Captive, and General insurance, with Life being the largest part of the sector. As of 31 March 2025, there were 12 authorised long-term (Life) insurers, 94 authorised general (non-Life) insurers, 30 General Insurance Intermediaries, and 11 permitted insurers, with £88.1 billion of funds under management in the Life sector and £4.8 billion in the non-Life sector as of 31 December 2024.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 5. Jurisdictional Profile, SIGNIFICANT ECONOMIC SECTORS, Gambling - 6f978ec32ab22bef
body:
The Online Gambling sector in the Isle of Man has been in existence since 2001; licences are issued by the GSC, which regulates and supervises all forms of gambling carried out in the Isle of Man. The GSC also maintains an elective software supply licensing regime that allows licence-holders to list pre-approved games. Although they are not casino operators and therefore fall outside the scope of international AML/CFT standards, they are subject to entry controls and proportionate AML/CFT supervision as part of the Isle of Man licensing regime.

The concentration of businesses lies in online operations, with most licence-holders being online casino operators and software suppliers. Terrestrial (land-based) gambling remains smaller, with one land-based casino, three licensed bookmakers, and five machine suppliers servicing 87 premises (as of 30 November 2025). The Online Gambling sector is significant and, while it has reduced in size somewhat in recent years, remains the largest nonfinancial sector, contributing 14% of national income in 2023/2024.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 5. Jurisdictional Profile, SIGNIFICANT ECONOMIC SECTORS, Trust and Corporate Service Providers - 1efa16b669a04191
body:
Trust and Corporate Service Providers are regulated and supervised in the Isle of Man by the FSA. CSPs have been regulated since 2000, and licencing was extended to include providers of Trusts in 2005. TCSPs represent 3% of national income (according to the Isle of Man National Income Report

2023/24). The number of TCSPs has steadily reduced between 2017 and 2023, mostly due to consolidation of the market. Several of the TCSPs in the Isle of Man are part of wider Groups. Just over 40% of TCSPs are small (fewer than 10 employees) and around 50% have 10-100 employees.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 5. Jurisdictional Profile, MATERIALITY - 4ad837669f2f9592
body:
The Isle of Man is a small international finance centre, ranked 55th in the 2025 Global Financial Centres Index. In common with other IFCs, the majority of the customer base is nonresident by number and by value of the business transacted.

The economy is diverse; financial services make up a significant proportion, with Insurance representing the largest individual sector at 17%. Company income is the primary economic driver, accounting for c. 60% of GDP in 2023/24. Personal incomes contribute c. 33% to the economy. Figures in 2025 show that the Island has a workforce of over 36,000 and an unemployment rate of c. 0.7%. There are no restrictions on property ownership for residents or non-residents.

Figure 4: National Income 2023-24

Banking, Insurance, and Corporate Services are the largest employers in the financial and non-financial sectors. Employment numbers in these sectors have remained stable.

Figure 5: Employment by Sector in the Isle of Man

The Isle of Man's Economic Strategy aims to strengthen resilience with four key shifts, including increasing GDP and creating 5,000 new jobs by 2032.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 5. Jurisdictional Profile, TAXATION AND TRANSPARENCY - 09fcc719589cdd93
body:
The Isle of Man operates a responsible tax system and has a long-standing policy of compliance with international standards as they are promulgated by bodies such as the OECD and the FATF. The Isle of Man has a wide network of international tax agreements that provide for various forms of exchange of information for tax purposes, and the Island has been a party to the OECD/Council of Europe Convention on Mutual Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters since March 2014.
The Isle of Man is an active participant in the OECD's Global Forum on Transparency and Exchange of Information for Tax Purposes ("the Global Forum").
Source: Statistics Isle of Man, Cabinet Office to more than 70 jurisdictions annually. The Isle of Man has been providing similar detailed financial account and ownership information to the UK (HMRC) since 2016 and to the US (Internal Revenue Service) since 2015.
Under the international standard for the exchange of information on request (EOIR), the Isle of Man's Income Tax Division processes requests for information from other jurisdiction's tax administrations, including UK HMRC, in respect of both criminal and civil tax investigations. Details of these requests are confidential, in accordance with the tax agreements under which the data is exchanged.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 5. Jurisdictional Profile, TAXATION AND TRANSPARENCY - 36dc3b4ecc83c26a
body:
The Island's second OECD Peer Review Report for EOIR, published in November 2017, concluded that the Island continued to be compliant (the highest possible rating) with the international standard on transparency and exchange of information upon request.
The Isle of Man made an early commitment to the Common Reporting Standard (CRS) and in 2014 signed the CRS Multilateral Competent Authority Agreement (MCAA). Under the CRS, the Isle of Man provides over 35 million lines of data Source: Statistics Isle of Man, Cabinet Office
The 2022 Global Forum peer review of Automatic Exchange of Information (AEOI), which looks at jurisdictions' implementation of the CRS, assessed the Isle of Man as being 'on track,' the highest possible rating for that form of review at this time.
A new AEOI standard has also been developed to address the tax risks associated with crypto assets (the Crypto Asset Reporting Framework, "CARF"). The Isle of Man was in the first group of signatories to the applicable MCAA for the CARF that was signed in November 2024. At the same time, the Isle of Man committed to implementing a series of changes to the CRS (commonly referred to as the "Amended CRS"), which will be applicable from 2026.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 5. Jurisdictional Profile, TAXATION AND TRANSPARENCY - 36106df13d0e9204
body:
In terms of other international taxation standards, Countryby-Country Reporting (CbCR) has been introduced, and the Isle of Man also spontaneously exchanges potentially relevant information, including any in respect of certain tax rulings (ETR), and takes measures to ensure that treaty-related disputes are resolved in a timely, effective, and efficient manner, and in line with the best practices.
In October 2017, the Isle of Man became the second jurisdiction (after Austria) to ratify the OECD's Multilateral Convention to Implement Tax Treaty-Related Measures to Prevent Base Erosion and Profit Shifting, preventing multinationals from avoiding tax by shifting profits to other countries.
In October 2021, the OECD's Inclusive Framework, including the Isle of Man, agreed on a two-pillar plan to address the tax challenges of the digital economy and base erosion and profit shifting (BEPS). Pillar Two establishes a global minimum tax rate of 15% for multinational enterprises with turnovers above €750 million, affecting about 800 businesses on the Island. In May 2023, the Crown Dependencies announced their intention to tax profits within their islands from 2025 and the Isle of Man introduced a Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-Up Tax (QDMTT), with legislation approved in November 2024 that has been effective since 1 January 2025.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 5. Jurisdictional Profile, TAXATION AND TRANSPARENCY - 23949e5c3be00be5
body:
The Isle of Man has a history of working constructively with the EU Code of Conduct Group on Business Taxation (CoCG). In response to concerns identified by the CoCG, in December 2018, the Isle of Man introduced an economic substance test for certain Isle of Man tax resident companies within relevant business sectors to ensure that profits registered in the Isle of Man are linked to commensurate economic activity.
The measures were assessed by EU finance ministers, as well as the OECD's Forum on Harmful Tax Practices (FHTP); both groups concluded that the Isle of Man's domestic legal framework is in line with the standards and, as a result, in March 2019, the EU listed the Isle of Man as a cooperative jurisdiction for tax purposes.
Legislative amendments approved by Tynwald in June 2021 brought partnerships into the scope of substance. There are now annual joint reviews of the Isle of Man's implementation of substance conducted by the FHTP and COCG which, to date, have always concluded with no issues identified.
Positive engagement on tax matters takes place with the UK on a continued basis. Most recently, the Isle of Man Treasury Minister and the UK Exchequer Secretary to the Treasury issued a joint statement on 27 May 2025 concerning Isle of Man promoters of UK tax avoidance schemes, committing to enhanced information flows, joint working, and other measures.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 5. Jurisdictional Profile, BENEFICIAL OWNERSHIP - 8aa5896670014fe7
body:
The Island has a central Database of Beneficial Ownership which collects and maintains detailed information about the registrable beneficial owners of legal entities created in the IOM. Under Section 26 of the Beneficial Ownership Act 2017 (BOA), the Database is directly accessible to relevant competent authorities, including law enforcement and regulators. Foreign counterparts can access information through established international cooperation channels.
In December 2024, secondary legislation was introduced to allow obliged entities (those persons obliged to conduct customer due diligence in line with the AML/CFT Code 2019 or the Gambling (AML/CFT) Code 2019) access to the Database to assist in performing customer due diligence checks. Additionally, from January 2023, the Central Registry commenced Identification and Verification (ID&V) checks on all submissions from natural persons and a sample (25%) of submissions from a regulated corporate service provider of beneficial ownership information onto the database.

Each Isle of Man legal entity to which the BOA applies must have a Nominated Officer whose duties include receiving beneficial ownership information from the legal owner of each interest in a legal entity, preservation of required details, and, from the information received, ascertaining which beneficial owners may be registrable and subsequently submitting the required details in respect of any registrable beneficial owner to the Database. A Nominated Officer is also responsible for ensuring the accuracy of information submitted to the Database. The Nominated Officer must ensure that the required details which they obtain are accompanied by information from a reliable and independent source, which acts to verify the adequacy and accuracy of the beneficial ownership in line with FATF requirements. body:
The IOM's AML/CFT framework includes a robust suite of legislation and guidance, a risk-based approach to supervision, and a dissuasive array of enforcement tools. This framework:

- a) is established to minimise the abuse of the international and IOM financial system by actors wishing to conduct ML;

- b) is based on the FATF Recommendations and is continually updated in line with the FATF changes; and

- c) implements the requirements of the international conventions extended to the IOM (see section 6)

The Island achieved a high level of compliance with the FATF's 40 Recommendations at the time of the last MONEYVAL follow-up assessment, with 39 out of the 40 Recommendations being scored Compliant or Largely Compliant (see Appendix III for further details).

The key piece of IOM legislation relating to ML is the Proceeds of Crime Act 2008 (POCA). chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 6. The Legal, Supervisory, and Law Enforcement Framework for Addressing Financial Crime in the IOM, DOMESTIC, Criminalising ML - f5e54003cf6dc180
headers: 6. The Legal, Supervisory, and Law Enforcement Framework for Addressing Financial Crime in the IOM
body:
The IOM has maintained a robust legal framework for criminalising ML. ML is criminalised under POCA 2008: Section 158(11) provides a definition that is aligned with international standards, including FATF Recommendations. Tax crimes and self-laundering are included as predicate offences and a conviction for the underlying offence is not required for an ML conviction. Penalties range from fines to up to fourteen years' imprisonment, and all parties, including those who fail to disclose, can be prosecuted.

Scope of FATF Standards: Financial institutions/Designated Non-Financial Businesses and Professions and Exemptions and Simplified Measures

Schedule 4 to the POCA 2008 sets out which sectors are in scope of the Island's AML/CFT legislation Framework. The financial institutions (FIs) and designated businesses included in the FATF Standards are included in the Isle of Man framework and therefore must apply the requirements in the preventative measures and AML/CFT Codes. The Isle of Man has not disapplied any of the FATF standards to the cohort of financial institutions and designated businesses.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 6. The Legal, Supervisory, and Law Enforcement Framework for Addressing Financial Crime in the IOM, EXEMPTIONS FROM FINANCIAL SERVICES LICENSING - e4c37f40cd332444
headers: 6. The Legal, Supervisory, and Law Enforcement Framework for Addressing Financial Crime in the IOM
body:
The Financial Services (Exemptions) Regulations 2011 identify certain activities and entities that are exempt from holding a financial services licence with the FSA. These exemptions, however, remain subject to the AML/CFT legislative framework, including the requirements of the AML/CFT Code, but are not subject to routine supervisory oversight for compliance with the Code (although the FSA retains supervision and enforcement powers over this cohort of persons where appropriate).

An internal risk assessment has recently been undertaken by the FSA to determine whether these persons should be covered by the AML/CFT Code, whether the AML/CFT Code should apply, or whether these persons are suitable to remain exempt from routine supervision for Code compliance.

This risk assessment considered:

- the nature and scale of the exempt activities;

- the inherent ML/TF risk profile of the activity; and

- whether the activity falls within the scope of FATF Recommendations.

Following this review, the FSA concluded that, while some exemptions relate to activities not captured by FATF standards or present a particularly low ML/TF risk, the current approach and scope remains appropriate and proportionate.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 6. The Legal, Supervisory, and Law Enforcement Framework for Addressing Financial Crime in the IOM, SIMPLIFIED MEASURES - b5fd98ecb6e88f27
headers: 6. The Legal, Supervisory, and Law Enforcement Framework for Addressing Financial Crime in the IOM
body:
The AML/CFT Code 2019 includes numerous simplified customer due diligence measures and exemptions (Part 6 of the AML/CFT Code) which may be utilised where lower risks are identified. The AML/CFT Handbook provides guidance on the implementation of said exemptions and simplified measures, with sector-specific AML/CFT guidance providing further detailed guidance where simplified measures or exemptions relate to certain sectors.
The purpose of these simplified measures is to ensure that compliance obligations are proportionate to risk so that resources can be allocated in the most effective way. These measures are subject to periodic review to ensure they remain justified and aligned with evolving risks and international standards. They are also reviewed at trigger events such as legislative changes or emerging typologies. Where any simplified measures are permitted by the AML/CFT Code 2019, they must not be utilised wherever a matter poses a higher risk or where there is a suspicion of ML/TF.
Relevant persons (or, in the case of the "acting on behalf of" concession, receiving regulated persons) are expected to make a reasoned, proportionate, and documented risk-based determination as to whether they are going to apply these measures. Such determinations must:

- be informed by the relevant person's Business and Customer Risk Assessments;

- remain sensitive to the ML/TF/PF risks; and

- ensure that the relevant person can manage and mitigate the risks effectively.

The FSA will normally supervise a licence-holder on both a solo and consolidated basis. Where the licence-holder is part of a group, the FSA may want to assess the whole group. body:
Restraint: The Attorney General can apply to the High Court for a restraint order (in criminal cases) or a property freezing order (in civil recovery cases) to secure assets for potential recovery. Provided that the conditions in the Proceeds of Crime Act 2008 are met, restraint and property freezing orders may be made even at an early stage in the investigation.
Confiscation: POCA 2008 and related legislation allows for the investigation, tracing, and seizing of property suspected of being derived from criminal activity, including direct proceeds and property of corresponding value. Criminal and civil (nonconviction -based) confiscation are covered and foreign nonconviction-based confiscation orders can also be enforced. Civil Forfeiture: This allows for the confiscation of assets without a criminal conviction, provided the court is satisfied that the property is the proceeds of crime. Use of Proceeds: Confiscated assets are placed into a Seized Assets Fund managed by the Treasury and used to support law enforcement and crime prevention initiatives.

body: The legal framework for cash controls is set out in the Customs and Excise Management Act 1986. Anyone importing or exporting cash exceeding £10,000 must declare it to a Customs officer, whether or not the cash is carried as freight or on a person. This includes movements between the IOM and the UK. The definition of 'cash' is broad and includes notes, coins, cheques, bearer bonds, and certain monetary instruments. Customs officers have powers to search, detain, and seize undeclared or suspicious cash, and failure to declare is a criminal offence which can result in up to two years' imprisonment and/ or fines.

The Island is also a member of the Camden Asset Recovery Interagency Network (CARIN) since September 2004 and has been a core donor to the Basel Institute's International Centre for Asset Recovery since January 2017. The Island holds associate membership in the International Anti-Corruption Coordination Centre (since July 2020) for intelligence-sharing on grand corruption, is part of the UN GlobE Network with the UK (since 2021), and participates in the AntiMoney Laundering Operational Network (AMON). ■

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 7. Progress on 2020 NRA Actions and Significant Agency Developments, SIGNIFICANT AGENCY DEVELOPMENTS SINCE 2020, FSA and GSC - 802f4767807a6557
headers: 7. Progress on 2020 NRA Actions and Significant Agency Developments
body: In 2021, the FSA created a standalone AML/CFT Division which supervised designated businesses in respect of AML/CFT. During 2023/24, the FSA consolidated all AML/CFT supervision (for designated businesses and financial institutions) into this division, increasing staff and adopting an enhanced, risk-based supervisory approach. The AML/CFT Division supervises according to the financial crime risk of a firm. In respect of non-AML supervision, this is split over three further divisions, and supervision is undertaken according to firm risk. Collaboration with the GSC led to significant upgrades in technology infrastructure, including the launch of the Atlas back office supervisory system and new data tools such as the STRIX AML risk analysis tool to improve risk-based supervisory engagement, risk assessment, and reporting. The FSA also updated its AML/CFT Handbook and published a revised supervisory methodology framework to reinforce risk-based supervision and internal governance processes.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 7. Progress on 2020 NRA Actions and Significant Agency Developments, SIGNIFICANT AGENCY DEVELOPMENTS SINCE 2020, FSA and GSC - 77993f888b203df2
headers: 7. Progress on 2020 NRA Actions and Significant Agency Developments
body: From 2023 to 2024, the GSC significantly enhanced its AML/ CFT framework by establishing a dedicated division, expanding staff with AML/CFT roles, and improving data collection and analytics systems to better inform supervision and risk assessments. Key developments included implementing enhanced quarterly returns, introducing a new enforcement framework for consistent application of sanctions, updating sector-specific guidance, and enacting the Permitted Disclosure Order 2025 to facilitate broader intelligence-sharing, alongside ongoing legislative reforms to further strengthen the supervisory regime.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 7. Progress on 2020 NRA Actions and Significant Agency Developments, SIGNIFICANT AGENCY DEVELOPMENTS SINCE 2020, Law Enforcement Agencies - 018833b6192d3325
headers: 7. Progress on 2020 NRA Actions and Significant Agency Developments
body:
Between 2022 and 2025, the FIU enhanced capacity and capability by increasing staff numbers, investing in professional training, introducing initiatives such as standardised feedback for Money Laundering Reporting Officers (MLROs), and updating guidance for disclosures. The FIU supported the pilot project, introducing public-private partnerships initially with the Banking sector, although the scope has now widened. The FIU Act 2016 was amended to capture bribery, corruption, and sanctions breaches. In 2025, the FIU hosted an Advanced Strategic Analysis Course on virtual assets on behalf of Egmont Region II.
In September 2022, the Isle of Man Constabulary established PIMLIT to focus specifically on complex international money laundering, separating this responsibility from the Economic Crime Unit (ECU). PIMLIT, comprising police officers and civilian financial investigators (including secondments from the Banking and Corporate sectors) was created to advance international money laundering investigations, convert FIU intelligence into evidence, and pursue prosecutions under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2008. While the ECU continues to handle domestic money laundering and complex fraud, it coordinates with PIMLIT during periods of high demand. PIMLIT collaborates closely with the FSA, GSC,
Customs and Excise, the Financial Crime Asset Recovery Unit, and ICART, and has officers co-located within the FIU.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 7. Progress on 2020 NRA Actions and Significant Agency Developments, SIGNIFICANT AGENCY DEVELOPMENTS SINCE 2020, Law Enforcement Agencies - bba79ff9725c86ca
headers: 7. Progress on 2020 NRA Actions and Significant Agency Developments
body:
In autumn 2024, the Isle of Man Constabulary assumed responsibility for port security, integrating the existing security team under police management to improve information-sharing and foster a multi-agency approach. Customs officers' broad search and entry powers, combined with specialised police skills and cross-agency intelligence, have increased operational effectiveness at the border. This has already resulted in notable achievements, such as the seizure of criminal proceeds, the arrest of offenders, and the impounding of crime-related assets. Additionally, law enforcement agencies are evaluating new technologies to further strengthen the identification of serious criminal and security threats.
In January 2024, the Customs and Immigration Division was created by merging the Customs and Excise Division with Passport, Immigration, and Nationality services to streamline operations at the Island's border. The Law Enforcement section has more than doubled in size since 2020, expanding from 7 to 15 personnel to better address border threats. The Division has also enhanced its focus on sanctions, with a dedicated Sanctions Officer overseeing financial and trade sanctions and an Investigation Officer appointed to handle potential breaches.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 7. Progress on 2020 NRA Actions and Significant Agency Developments, SIGNIFICANT AGENCY DEVELOPMENTS SINCE 2020, Law Enforcement Agencies - c9addecbc06b62c9
headers: 7. Progress on 2020 NRA Actions and Significant Agency Developments
body:
Immigration resources have significantly increased, with the number of Immigration Officers rising from 3 in 2023 to 8 in 2025 and the formation of a dedicated Immigration Compliance Team. Recent policy and legislative changes have tightened immigration rules. The closure of the "Seasonal Worker" and "Representative of Overseas Business" routes and a comprehensive review of the "Worker Migrant" route reflect a robust response to identified system abuse. A detailed review has been conducted and actions are continuing to be implemented as a result.
ICART has been strengthened by the addition of new legal and support staff, enhancing its capacity in civil asset recovery and MLA. All domestic civil asset recovery has now been merged into Prosecutions with a newly formed Financial Crime and Asset Recovery Unit, who work with the AML Group, FIU, PIMLIT, and other domestic partners to identify cases for prosecution and civil recovery providing assistance in disrupting criminal activity.
ICART has used a number of previously untested methods to deprive criminals of their illicit gains and disrupt multi-national organised crime.

Within the Prosecutions Division, which advises the Isle of Man Constabulary and public authorities on criminal charges, a dedicated FCARU has been established as a specialised, ringfenced resource, with automatic referrals from PIMLIT and the ECU.
