The FSA receives and analyses the volume and total value of transactions made by each underlying bank, as well as the source and destination of the aggregate values. The FSA is developing a formal approach with the FIU to review inflows and outflows involving higher-risk jurisdictions, along with any other relevant intelligence the FIU holds. Payments, countries, and trends of interest will then be discussed by the FSA with the respective bank to ensure there is a good understanding of the potential threat. The TF NRA recommends documenting the analysis process for incoming and outgoing financial flows to/from higherrisk countries to understand how the data is used by the FSA and the FIU, and for the FIU and FSA to consider the flows from the Island to IFCs in a similar way to the analysis with financial flows to higher-risk jurisdictions. body:
Although the majority of the Isle of Man's trade and finance is regional (i.e., with the UK), the Isle of Man also conducts transactions with personal and corporate customers in other jurisdictions worldwide. Evaluations of the controls available in these countries are publicly available via a number of sources, including the FATF (and its regional bodies), the Corruption Perceptions Index, and the OECD amongst others. Consideration is also given to the effectiveness of AML measures of countries where there are significant inward or outward flows to the IOM, or where the IOM has a significant customer base. The DHA maintains a list of jurisdictions that pose or may pose a higher risk. Lists are kept updated and published regularly. Industry is well accustomed to updating their own systems and relevant procedures and controls using these Lists. Countries are categorised by the risk they pose, using the FATF-published lists and an additional list of jurisdictions that the IOM Government has identified as potentially presenting a higher risk of ML or TF using data gathered from various commercial intelligence sources.
Appendix IV provides an analysis of countries characterised by: (a) the largest financial flows; (b) a resident customer base exceeding 5%; and/or (c) significant numbers of non-natural persons, utilising information from the latest Mutual Evaluation Report for each country.

Southern African connections are rooted in longstanding commercial and personal ties, particularly with South Africa, which has maintained robust links through trade, investment, and financial services and signifies a continuing trend of Southern African enterprises using the Isle of Man as a gateway to global markets and a hub for cross-border wealth and estate management. As noted earlier, South Africa was removed from the FATF 'grey list' in October 2025, and its removal is acknowledged at appropriate points within the following narrative.

A recent development in the business profile of the IOM is the substantial increase in customers from South America (predominantly Argentina), which in 2024 comprised nearly 47% of the total customer base. This increase, which is driven by the MVTS sector, was in line with projected growth.

Although over half of the 1.9 million new customers are classified as 'inactive', these figures nevertheless indicate a significant expansion of the IOM's customer base, increasing from approximately 1.58 million to 3.51 million. Whilst there are good controls in place within the sector, with customer numbers anticipated to increase still further, this is an area that is currently under active review.

Annual data collected by the FSA and GSC provides an overview of jurisdictional and sectoral exposure, including by natural and non-natural persons, PEPs, UBOs, and introduced business. This data has been mapped against the 2024 DHA lists (specifically, the lists for ML deficiencies) providing information regarding jurisdictional and sectoral activity with countries identified on the lists.
Residency of customers (natural persons and non-natural persons): An analysis of customer residency data over several years indicates consistent patterns, with the highest volumes reported from the same higher-risk countries. This trend is primarily associated with specific, established licence-holders within the Banking and Insurance sectors. As of December 2024, of the total number of customers in the Banking and Insurance sectors 0.10% were from List A countries, 2.35% were from List B(i) countries, and 12.78% were from List B(ii) countries. Most customers in the B(i) and B(ii) lists are from South Africa and Kenya; this trend has been stable for a number of years. Most South African customers are linked to Banking and Insurance. More recently numbers, relating to Tanzania, Cameroon, and Nigeria have increased; this relates to increases in customer numbers within the MTS sector.

Customers (natural and non-natural persons) located in higher-risk jurisdictions therefore constitute a very small percentage of the overall customer base (see Figure 18). It is also important to note that, with South Africa being delisted by the FATF in October 2025, this percentage of the customer base resident in higher-risk countries has decreased to 3%.

Introduced business: "Introduced business" refers to a customer being introduced to a relevant person by a third party, known as the "introducer", who has already carried out some of the required CDD checks and provides the CDD to the relevant person taking on the customer. In this scenario, no reliance is placed on the third party as they are providing any elements of CDD they have collected; the relevant person must still complete their own CDD on the customer.
Between 2023 and 2024, numbers of customers being introduced under Paragraph 9 of the Code fell significantly. This is attributed partly to improvements in data quality, with the 2024 figures being more accurate. In December 2023, the FSA published an updated AML/CFT Handbook which included further regulatory clarification around 'introduced business' to assist business with applying this requirement and may have prompted changes. An accompanying webinar was also published to assist with industry understanding in this area.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 8. Geographical Exposure, ONLINE GAMBLING AND JURISDICTION -RELATED VULNERABILITIES - 9e931fd0e0f01b07
body: In terms of money flows into and out of the Isle of Man, online gambling tends to operate differently to traditional banking. Typically, money is deposited into a gambling account through a payment service provider (PSP) which may or may not be established in the IOM. The PSP then pools together deposits from various individuals and, after a period, sends only the total net amount to the gambling operator. As a result, the IOM financial flows of gambling companies are more aligned with total net flows, rather than on each individual deposit/withdrawal.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 8. Geographical Exposure, ONLINE GAMBLING AND JURISDICTION -RELATED VULNERABILITIES - ed22791758172504
body: In conclusion, exposure to higher-risk jurisdictions is limited, well-monitored through supervisory controls, and actively mitigated, contributing to ongoing risk assessment. More recent supervisory activity has had an impact on that risk understanding, with a demonstratable reduction in higher-risk customers. Higher jurisdictional risk accounted for approximately 7% of transacting customers and is not systemic, being concentrated over a small number of operators which are easier to monitor. Supervisory action does, therefore, have a material and instant impact on the sector's overall risk profile. Exposure to List A jurisdictions has been identified by operators through their own compliance controls and rapidly dealt with, even with the use of obfuscating technology such as VPNs. The small number of PEPs and lack of PEP exposure to higher-risk jurisdictions indicates that operators have a low onboarding risk appetite. The risk is well-understood, monitored, subject to supervisory scrutiny and actions, and responsive to changes in national risk appetites. ■

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 9. ML Risks, BACKGROUND - 7c2a0837a65b52f9
body:
The WB model looks at national threat and national vulnerability as the two main factors impacting the risk of ML at the national level. Consideration of National Threat is addressed in Chapter 11 and National Vulnerability in Chapter 12.
The overall ML risk for the IOM in this 2026 NRA is assessed as Medium High, unchanged from the 2020 assessment. This outcome reflects the continued balance between a Medium High threat level and a medium level of national vulnerability.
While the headline risk rating remains the same, the underlying risk profile has evolved materially since 2020, as identified throughout this report. The period covered by this assessment has been characterised by a measurable increase in the scale, complexity, and internationalisation of ML threats, including a greater prevalence of cyber-enabled fraud, transnational organised crime, sanctions evasion, and the exploitation of cross-border financial systems and LPA structures. These developments have increased both the sophistication and the speed of laundering methodologies affecting the IOM.
At the same time, the Island has strengthened key elements of its preventative, supervisory, and enforcement framework, including enhanced data collection and analysis, improved inter-agency coordination, increased use of financial intelligence, and risk-based supervisory engagements. These measures have acted to contain the growth in vulnerability, notwithstanding the widening threat environment.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 9. ML Risks, BACKGROUND - 9da9246900c6eebb

As a result, the overall ML risk remains Medium High but is assessed as being closer to the upper end of that category than in 2020, with a greater concentration of risk in specific sectors, typologies, and cross-border exposure. The stability of the rating should therefore be understood as reflecting dynamic risk management in the face of increasing external threat, rather than an absence of change in the Island's ML risk landscape.

- Year: 2026; National ML Risk: Medium High; National Threat: Medium High; National Vulnerability: Medium
- Year: 2020; National ML Risk: Medium High; National Threat: Medium High; National Vulnerability: Medium
The 2026 National Risk Assessment for the Isle of Man considers risks in respect of ML/TF/PF. ML continues to present the highest risk to the Isle of Man. As an IFC, the bulk of the Isle of Man's customer base consists of non-residents, both in terms of the number of customers as well as value of transactions. As a result, most activities leading to funds being held in the jurisdiction occur outside of the Isle of Man. Therefore, if funds are linked to criminal activity, the underlying predicate offence is most likely to have occurred outside of the Island. The Isle of Man's primary ML risk lies in the placement and layering of criminal proceeds.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 9. ML Risks, BACKGROUND - 8bd495013fe3c286
body: Global reports from FATF, Europol, and the Basel Institute on Governance highlight the changing nature of ML, with red flags such as large cash deposits becoming less relevant. Rapid electronic money transfers, including cryptocurrency, digital banking, and increasingly sophisticated techniques for obscuring transactions, have significantly evolved the traditional ML stages. Technologies and online payment platforms enable swift, cross-border movement of illicit funds, as detailed in the Illict Financial Flows From Cyber-Enabled Fraud, with criminals exploiting instant payment systems, smurfing, and layering funds across multiple jurisdictions. The use of money service businesses (MSBs) both domestically and internationally is seeing significant growth; together with the use of virtual assets and the increasing uptake of artificial intelligence, this will present ongoing challenges for LEAs to trace and recover illicit proceeds. This surge in digital payment methods, including digital wallets and challenger banks (some of which have directly marketed to Isle of Man residents) creates vulnerabilities for regulatory oversight.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 9. ML Risks, BACKGROUND - 2572ebfe41bfc5dd
body:
The adoption of AI provides enhanced security but also introduces tools that can assist criminals in obscuring the origins of illicit funds. The World Economic Forum's Global Risks Report 2025 notes that, while adverse outcomes of AI technologies is low in the risk ranking on a two-year outlook, "complacency around the risk of such technologies should be avoided given the fast-paced change in the field of AI and its increasing ubiquity." It is possible that fast-developing AI-driven tactics could outpace the ability of authorities to detect and prevent financial crime.
As noted by Transparency International and the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, the rise of financial hubs including the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Hong Kong, China, has shifted the axis of criminal money movement. Additionally, geopolitical uncertainty, highlighted by increased deregulation in significant markets such as the US, further complicates the global response to these challenges. This emphasises the importance of international cooperation and collaboration and the development and adoption of technologies that can help address these evolving threats.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 9. ML Risks, BACKGROUND - e7163aaf1ec03581
body: In the IOM, rapid growth in the Gaming-Related Software sector occurred alongside a backdrop of a changing global financial crime landscape which accelerated significantly following the COVID-19 pandemic. Criminality is characterised by complex fraud typologies and transnational laundering networks. At the time, controls were not aligned to identify the scale and complexity of these emerging risks, and the expansion indirectly impacted other elements of the Island's control framework, including immigration processes. While the IOM had already introduced a precautionary Software Supply Licensing (SSL) regime in 2019 and introduced new AML supervision measures in 2020 to mitigate risks, the scale, complexity, and transnational nature evolved rapidly and extensively.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 9. ML Risks, BACKGROUND - 8d32d8c43d941014
body:
This rapid evolution, identified through cross-agency work, is being used to inform further considerations regarding risk understanding of activities outside of online casinos and, where appropriate, mitigation measures that may be required. Strengthening of the framework and enforcement for compliance failings have contributed to a number of businesses surrendering their licences, although surrenders have also resulted from closing markets and for multiple other reasons. The industry is collaborating with government agencies to identify and manage risks, including the creation of an Online Gambling Strategic Working Group under the Isle of Man's Financial Crime Partnership. Measures to improve cooperation and informationsharing between agencies, including Immigration, Customs, and the Police, have been introduced, with further developments planned.
The 'National Risk Appetite Statement on eGaming and Financial Crime: Activities, Risk Appetite and Mitigation' and the FIU document 'Online Gambling: Red Flags and Typologies for Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing, and Proliferation Financing,' both published in May 2025, clearly set out the threats and the actions that industry should take.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 9. ML Risks, BACKGROUND - 20e8733574b0e60c
body:
The evolving complexity of ML can be seen with crossborder interconnected predicate offending; cases now frequently encompass a web of foreign, cross-border, and domestic predicate offences, complicating both detection and enforcement. In March 2025, further to actions taken by law enforcement authorities in the Isle of Man, the Minister for Home Affairs made a statement regarding the threats facing the Island and the response to those threats:
"The Isle of Man Government and the Island's authorities take the illicit actions by transnational organised criminals to exploit the island's business environment and immigration security extremely seriously. Significant and wide-reaching actions are being taken by agencies, with investment in law enforcement and investigation capability. This includes strengthening the Island's immigration systems and processes."

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 9. ML Risks, PERCEPTIONS FROM OPEN-SOURCE MATERIALS - 2d4edfb222518a74
body: Development of the NRA has also included an analysis of perceptions of adverse media from open-source materials relating to the IOM and an evaluation of their implications for the Island's ML and wider financial crime risk profile, forming part of the NRA's consideration of the risks posed by external perceptions, which in some instances can create a reputational risk. The analysis was based on an extensive review of Englishlanguage media reporting, with articles categorised into several areas to enable comparison across different strands of narrative risk using a standardised framework. This is part of a broader programme of risk work within the IOM to continue to monitor the threat of ML/TF, including from information available through open-source media.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 9. ML Risks, HIGHER-RISK THEMES - d313e51439308208
body:
Organised crime groups and the Online Gambling industry Media reporting, United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime analysis, and domestic law enforcement operations indicate that transnational organised crime groups, primarily from East and Southeast Asia, have attempted to exploit online gambling businesses registered in the IOM. Enforcement actions taken against several operators are widely reported as demonstrating the effectiveness of the IOM supervisory framework in identifying and disrupting these threats.

Human trafficking, visa fraud, and migrant worker exploitation Large-scale trafficking networks have not been identified to date; however, a small number of confirmed cases (alongside further allegations) have suggested that the IOM's migration controls were vulnerable to exploitation by transnational organised crime networks who seek to exploit migrants to carry out financial crimes and illicit operations. The IOM Government has already undertaken a review of historic visa applications, and there is heightened scrutiny of the risks associated with the threat of labour exploitation, with potential trafficking being of concern.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 9. ML Risks, MEDIUM-RISK THEMES - b806771f597bce71
body: Online gambling compliance and AML enforcement Media reporting highlights enforcement actions taken by the GSC against licensed firms. While these cases reflect compliance deficiencies, the enforcement actions themselves are evidence of strong regulatory functioning within the IOM. The perceived risk arises from external misinterpretation: continued, transparent enforcement mitigates, though does not fully neutralise, reputational exposure.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 9. ML Risks, MEDIUM-RISK THEMES, Fraud schemes - 4a7fda8ee7db0696
body: Several fraud cases, including cross-border investment and 'pig-butchering' frauds, have featured IOM entities and premises. The connection between fraud schemes and online gambling entities creates adjacency with the transnational organised crime infiltration theme and compounds reputational risk. However, the effectiveness of the IOM regulatory network in identifying and shutting down criminal operations limits exposure and demonstrates systemic vulnerability does not exist.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 9. ML Risks, MEDIUM-RISK THEMES, Tax evasion (cross-border) - b15b851b31d34e75
body: Perceptions surrounding the Island's status as an IFC and an offshore jurisdiction can create a narrative which frames the IOM as providing vehicles that could enable transnational taxevasion schemes. Despite strong cooperation with international authorities and tightened regulation and transparency, this is a narrative which does continue in international media.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 9. ML Risks, LOWER-RISK THEMES - 5fc3d41bbe37990e
body: Prevailing narratives often stem from misunderstandings and misconceptions regarding the IOM's regulatory environment, frequently conflating it with other offshore jurisdictions. Despite claims relating to beneficial ownership, tax avoidance schemes, and the use of corporate vehicles, the IOM maintains robust compliance frameworks, a strong Beneficial Ownership framework, and effective information-sharing mechanisms. Issues around the Aircraft Registry and VAT refunds have been independently reviewed and resolved, although media attention persists due to associations with high-profile individuals.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 9. ML Risks, CONCLUSIONS - b9fa88fcb7c6c1e3
body:
- Criminal exploitation by transnational organised crime is the primary driver of the high-risk narratives. The most serious cases involve foreign criminal networks attempting to use the IOM, with the IOM authorities subsequently detecting and disrupting the illegal activity. These observations relate to a genuine threat and risk, as outlined throughout the NRA.

- Transparency and enforcement visibility increase perceived risk but reduce actual risk.

- the underlying structural vulnerabilities identified within historic data or investigative journalism have been resolved; however, it is the case that when the narrative involves high-profile public figures, this drives disproportionate media attention and increases the risk of misinterpretation and misrepresentation.

The highest-risk themes recently reported all intersect either directly or indirectly with the Online Gambling sector, causing an aggregation of reputational risk. This observation is in line with other threats and risks identified over the course of this NRA, with the Online Gambling sector being an area for convergence of risk factors. It is a risk which has been the subject of further mitigating measures, as described elsewhere in the NRA. ■

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat, METHODOLOGY - fc3f24c0577e759d
headers: 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat
body:
The Module on threat involves identifying the main predicate offences, origins, and flows of criminal proceeds and sectors, ML techniques, and trends. The process involves the systematic collection of data to assess ML threats and the analyses of cross-border threats from foreign jurisdictions.

The overall ML Threat Level for the IOM is assessed as Medium High. This rating takes into account the threat assessment conducted by experts from agencies including the FIU, law enforcement, and regulators, and considers the crossborder threat (discussed above) and the foreign and domestic ML threats (discussed below). The level of domestic ML threat is assessed as Medium Low.

- Domestic threat level: Medium Low; Cross-border threat level: Medium High; Foreign threat level: Medium High

The threat assessment analysed data obtained from MLA, SARs, and intelligence requests on amounts of assets seized (including at the border), frozen, and confiscated. It also considered cases currently under active investigation as well as cases that have been prosecuted, and the outcomes. The suspected predicate offences, location of the suspected offending, and the location of the subject of interest have also informed this assessment.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat, UK NATIONAL RISK ASSESSMENT 2025 - 240b95f8e4e6049b
headers: 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat
body:
As the UK is the Island's largest market for trade and financial services, the UK NRA 2025 and the FATF Mutual Evaluation Report (MER) on the UK from 2018 have been given particular consideration. The MER notes the risk of the UK being used as a destination or transit location for criminal proceeds. It identifies the main ML risks being high-end ML, cash-based ML, and the laundering of proceeds from fraud and tax offences, drug offending and human trafficking, and organised crime. Significant risks were identified as arising from laundering the proceeds of foreign predicate crimes, including transnational organised crime and overseas corruption.

The 2025 NRA also highlights cybercrime (including cyberenabled fraud), human trafficking, sanctions evasion, and overseas corruption as significant predicate offences. Crypto assets and AI are identified as emerging tools for laundering and fraud, with fraud being the largest predicate offence, accounting for over 43% of all recorded crime. Vulnerabilities that are relevant to the Isle of Man include high-end ML involving complex ownership structures and the use of international intermediaries.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat, IOM NRA 2020 - 7384de2d25b7f55f
headers: 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat
body:
The 2020 NRA for the Isle of Man identified the threat from ML as Medium High. Cybercrime (including cyber-enabled fraud) and human trafficking/modern slavery were seen as emerging risks. Tax evasion remained a key risk, with the need for international cooperation prioritised. Domestic threats such as fraud and the illegal drug supply were growing concerns, to be addressed by dedicated strategies and ongoing monitoring. The report concluded that gatekeeper institutions played a crucial role in combatting financial crime. Controls such as SAR reporting and continued regulatory oversight were vital. It also noted that exposure to higher-risk jurisdictions was low but that further collection and analysis of financial data was required.

The main predicate offences generating criminal proceeds remain fraud (including theft), tax evasion, drug-related offences, corruption, and bribery. There is an increase in cyber-enabled fraud and human trafficking, as anticipated in the 2020 National Risk Assessment, along with heightened involvement of OCGs. The expanding activities of sophisticated OCGs from the UK and from Asian-organised crime has been a notable development since the last NRA. The combination of the Island seeking to grow the economy, as OCGs also grow, creates a risk of importing new cross-border threats requiring controls to be continually monitored and updated.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat, CROSS-BORDER THREAT, Summary of current imported and exported threats - 3dee36bbb104caf6
headers: 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat
Summary of current imported and exported threats
body: The cross-border threat assessment for the Isle of Man considered several key factors, identifying the main corridors, countries, or regions involved in cross-border activities and assessing the nature of the threats, specifically whether these threats are imported into or exported from the IOM. The assessment also examined future trends that might affect these threats and determined which regulated and unregulated sectors are most impacted. The main corridors considered were those between the IOM and the UK, and between the IOM and the other countries.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat, CROSS-BORDER THREAT, IOM - UK - 55a40f96c1c59b7f
headers: 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat
body:
The assessment identified several key threats affecting the IOM in its cross-border activities with the UK. A significant threat arises from the layering of criminal proceeds. This process was found to pose both an imported and exported risk, as illicit funds can flow into and out of the jurisdiction through complex financial transactions. Banks, TCSPs, MSBs, and virtual assets are particularly vulnerable to the risks associated with the layering of proceeds, given their central role in handling

and moving funds.

Another major threat comes from ML linked to drug-related activities. In this context, drugs themselves are considered an imported threat to the IOM, with proceeds from drug sales subsequently exported to the UK. The cash generated from these drug sales is often used to finance further criminal operations, perpetuating a cycle of illicit activity.

Banks, VASPs, and high-value goods dealers are exposed to the dangers posed by the illicit trade in drugs. This threat is further compounded by a growing trend towards the use of alternative methods for transferring value, such as MSBs and virtual assets, which can make detection and prevention more challenging.

Threat level: Stable

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat, CROSS-BORDER THREAT, IOM - Other countries - 53f580296b939d38
headers: 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat
body:
Organised immigration crime and people trafficking

The UK and other countries present an imported and exported risk from organised immigration crime. This reflects the evolving nature of cross-border criminal enterprises, often facilitated through UK micro-companies but also from further afield. This is a relatively recent emerging threat for the IOM, which has recently seen three people charged with 17 counts of people trafficking. Banks are particularly vulnerable due to their role in processing transactions that may be linked to these activities. However, the threat extends across a wide array of economic sectors. Industries such as healthcare, agriculture, retail, and food services are especially at risk as they frequently depend on imported labour, creating opportunities for criminal networks to exploit vulnerabilities in recruitment and employment practices. Threat level: Increasing

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat, CROSS-BORDER THREAT, Financial sanctions evasion - 7665ccd4a17a614a
headers: 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat
body:
Imported cross-border threats were identified in relation to the evasion and circumvention of financial sanctions, particularly through countries such as Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Kazakhstan. Criminal actors exploit these jurisdictions as channels to transfer illicit funds; these processes frequently employ ML activities.

This threat is further exacerbated by an apparent substantial shift in the global epicentre of illicit finance, with regions such as the UAE and Hong Kong, China, emerging as major hubs. Funds originating from or passing through these centres may be routed to the Isle of Man as part of sophisticated layering processes, designed to obscure the origins of the proceeds.

A range of sectors within the Isle of Man are exposed to these risks. Banks, Life Insurance providers, TCSPs, and Collective Investment Schemes (CIS) are all vulnerable to exploitation by criminal networks utilising these cross-border methods. Threat level for financial sanctions evasion: Stable Threat level for the shift in illicit finance: Increasing

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat, CROSS-BORDER THREAT, Transnational organised crime - 1ca901e7c245d7bc
headers: 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat
body:
There has been a notable increase in transnational organised crime, particularly involving sophisticated fraud schemes such as investment scams and romance scams. These criminal activities primarily emanate from China and Southeast Asia and present a significant imported cross-border threat to the IOM.

The Online Gambling industry has been identified as a particular target for these groups. In addition, financial institutions such as TCSPs and virtual asset service providers, and other professional services such as law firms and accountancy practices, are also considered to be at risk. Banks have also been used to launder the proceeds of organised crime from, for example, romance frauds and cloning frauds. In addition to fraudulent activities, these organised groups are known to offer professional money laundering services to other criminal organisations, facilitating the movement and concealment of illicit funds on a global scale.

A further concern is the presence and operation of Chinese underground banking systems, which represents another avenue for the laundering and transfer of criminal proceeds. This is an area currently under review. Threat level: Increasing

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat, CROSS-BORDER THREAT, Threats from higher-risk jurisdictions and business expansion - 6e356cdc01fa3b9b
headers: 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat
Threats from higher-risk jurisdictions and business expansion
body:
Nationals from countries assessed as higher-risk may present threats to the IOM's financial services sector. Individuals may attempt to exploit vulnerabilities to facilitate illicit activity, including ML and sanctions evasion. The risks are particularly pronounced where existing controls may be circumvented through complex international business structures or opaque ownership arrangements.

Additional risks arise from activities aimed at opening or extending business channels with new markets, especially where these jurisdictions are associated with heightened financial crime risks. Such expansion can inadvertently introduce new and emerging threats by increasing exposure to unknown or insufficiently understood actors and/or practices The Department for Enterprise plays a crucial role in overseeing the development of key business activities. However, business expansion also places increased responsibility on both Government and the regulated sector, who can be targeted for exploitation by cross-border criminal networks. Regulated businesses must remain vigilant and enhance their due diligence measures to mitigate potential threats originating from higher-risk countries and emerging/ extending business relationships. Threat level: Emerging

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat, CROSS-BORDER THREAT, Professional intermediaries - 4cb457328008c5b0
headers: 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat
body:
Professional intermediaries within the IOM face significant risks of either inadvertently or intentionally facilitating overseas criminals in concealing the proceeds of crime. This may involve hiding or enabling the transfer of funds or other assets, which can lend a sense of legitimacy to unlawful activities. This risk is recognised as both an imported and exported threat.

The sectors considered to be most vulnerable include Accountants, Lawyers, TCSPs, MTSs, Investment Business, Estate Agents, CIS, VASPs, and NPOs. Threat level: Stable

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat, TRANSNATIONAL CRIME - 9852af7e49bfe72e
headers: 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat
body:
The FATF explicitly aligns its understanding of 'transnational crime' with the UN Convention against Transnational Organised Crime (UNTOC), which provides the formal international definition. Isle of Man entities are less likely to receive criminal proceeds directly from foreign predicates; it is more likely that proceeds will be disguised via complex international routes and arrangements. The most significant risk arises from multijurisdictional structuring to layer and integrate criminal funds, leveraging the products and services available. These services include the use of shell companies and other financial products to obscure the origin of criminal proceeds via investments and high-value assets, including real estate.
The Chief Constable's Annual Report 2024-25 highlights the threats arising from international ML, in particular, transnational organised crime syndicates originating from South East Asian regions "using existing immigration policy, labour exploitation and our Central Registry to base and promote regulated and unregulated business here in the Isle of Man." The report goes on to note that large amounts of proceeds of crime are suspected of being laundered through legitimate businesses.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat, TRANSNATIONAL CRIME - 49db77b50663cfd8
headers: 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat
body:
PIMLIT is collaborating with partner agencies on three major investigations linking directly to criminal typologies outlined in recent UNDOC publications. Additionally, ten other investigations are underway where the predicate criminal activity occurred outside the Isle of Man, but large-scale proceeds of around £340 million have been restrained. Parallel restraint and forfeiture investigations are conducted by PIMLIT and FCARU to identify assets for recovery from predicate criminality. Virtual assets, in particular Tether (USDT) (a cryptocurrency), are increasingly being used to move illicit funds; during 2024, $1.2 million USDT was recovered as part of ongoing investigative work.
PIMLIT has undertaken a comprehensive assessment of threats posed by Chinese transnational organised crime. Strategic risks and vulnerabilities have been identified across the Online Gaming regulated sector, immigration controls, exploitation of the Companies Registry, and elements of the Island's policies and procedures for attracting new businesses from particular regions. This assessment is being utilised to address both present and emerging risks.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat, INTELLIGENCE EXCHANGE - b7c5d702411f02ed
headers: 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat

SARs linked to foreign predicate offences generate cross-border intelligence exchange. The number of international disseminations fluctuates but has stayed stable since 2020.

Figure 24. FIU Intelligence Exchange

From 2020 to 2024, the FIU made a total of 3,765 international disseminations, of which 43% were made to UK, 6% were made to the US, and the remainder were made to international partners in over 70 jurisdictions worldwide. Over the period, international offences overall accounted for 13% of all recorded ML crimes; these relate to a wide variety of predicate offences, but most commonly fraud (30%). body: Fraud is rising worldwide, especially cyber-enabled and investment fraud. According to Interpol's Global Financial Fraud Assessment 2024, financial fraud has not only increased but also diversified substantially - both in terms of volume and the methods used to perpetrate it. PIMLIT investigates complex, multi-jurisdictional cases of money laundering in which fraud is frequently the primary motive, though other offences are also involved. A main typology is romance fraud, which involves developing a relationship, sometimes purporting to be romantic, over varying periods of time. The victim is encouraged to invest in fraudulent investment schemes via a VA wallet which is controlled by criminals. Funds are stolen when the investment is substantial enough, moved around and across blockchains (chain-hopping), and sent to VASPs in different global locations, sometimes then exchanged into fiat currency. Individuals involved in committing these scams may also be victims of human trafficking, with criminal networks adopting various means to capture and compel people to conduct industrial-level scams (see also Human Trafficking and Modern Slavery below.)

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat, FOREIGN PREDICATE OFFENDING, Tax evasion - 7ad9ed4f38c2ebb6
headers: 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat
body:
The FATF identifies 'tax crime' as a category of predicate offences; it is for each country to specify what is criminal in their legislation. Tax evasion is described as typically involving deliberate acts to avoid paying taxes, such as hiding income, falsifying records, or using complex structures to conceal assets in order to reduce tax liabilities. The money owed to the relevant tax authority becomes the proceeds of crime and efforts to conceal those proceeds can constitute ML.
The Isle of Man actively participates in international treaties aimed at tackling tax evasion and has frequently been an early adopter of such initiatives. Nevertheless, the features which attract legitimate business to IFCs are also attractive to those persons wishing to evade tax in their own country (usually direct tax such as income or corporation tax). This makes the Isle of Man inherently vulnerable to ML involving tax crimes. Methods of tax evasion often involve concealment of funds held in bank accounts, investments in assets such as real estate, the creation of legal structures such as trusts or shell companies, or the transferring of profits to subsidiaries via artificial transactions. Jurisdictions with lower tax rates may also attract those seeking to conceal and maximise illicit proceeds - for example, OCGs, by investing in assets and legitimate businesses, taking advantage of sophisticated business environments that provide access to a range of professional intermediaries.

There are very low numbers of international requests for information in relation to indirect taxes. .

In 2023 a Douglas businessman was sentenced to three years and seven months in prison for orchestrating a series of VAT frauds amounting to more than £1.1 million. The offences, which began in 2015, involved deliberated manipulation of company finances and abuse of his position of authority. The individual operated several companies under an umbrella organisation. Over a prolonged period, he created false invoices, shifted funds between company accounts, and actively avoided routine VAT inspections. The fraudulent activity expanded to fund personal lifestyle expenses including family holidays and university fees for his children. The conduct was described as 'planned' and 'sophisticated,' involving an abuse of authority, with the sustained and deliberate nature of the frauds supporting a 'lavish lifestyle' at the expense of public revenue. The individual was also disqualified as a director.

Human trafficking and modern slavery were identified in the 2020 NRA as emerging risks. Global increases in illegal immigration, human trafficking, and modern slavery have seen the Isle of Man targeted, connected partly to other criminality and partly to opportunism, taking advantage of the disparity between the immigration rules of the Isle of Man and the UK and the accessibility afforded by the Common Travel Area. Evidence has shown that vulnerabilities in the Isle of Man's immigration system have been targeted for abuse over recent years, including fraudulent visa applications, exploitation of migrant workers, and the potential use of the Isle of Man as a backdoor into the UK. Some of the immigration matters concern suspected offences related to the Online Gambling sector (see also Exploitation of Labour and Immigration Crime, page 87).

The principal legislation that covers bribery and corruption in the Isle of Man is the Bribery Act 2013. The Bribery Act establishes that it is an offence to give or receive a bribe, bribe a foreign public official, or fail to prevent bribery. There is also a duty under the Bribery Act for certain individuals to report bribery. The FIU has had associate membership of the IACCC since July 2020; this organisation is specifically aimed at exchanging intelligence in respect of 'grand corruption' cases. List B(ii), which specifies jurisdictions that have been identified by the IOM Government as potentially posing a higher risk of ML or TF, covers transparency and bribery/corruption risk in addition to ML and TF.
Between 2020 and 25, 308 POCA SARs were submitted identifying bribery and corruption, predominantly by the Banking, Life Insurance, Gambling, and TCSP sectors. 11 cases investigated or under investigation since 2020 have a suspected bribery/corruption element. In a recent court case, an Isle of Man-based defendant was acquitted of his involvement in the bribery of a Ugandan official. It is probable that cases of international foreign bribery and corruption are not always identified, with submitted SARs relying predominantly on identification of adverse media as the grounds for forming a suspicion. The IOM remains vigilant to the risks of the Island being used for laundering from these activities.

body: Financial services offered in the Isle of Man may be used by foreign PEPs (albeit overall numbers are low), including those from higherrisk countries, although their activity is concentrated within Banks, TCSPs, and Life Insurance. Due to their position, foreign PEPs might be targeted for corruption and bribery attempts, and ultimately for money laundering or terrorism financing activities. Being a foreign PEP does not automatically mean someone is involved in criminal activities. However, their status enhances the threat that is posed, and therefore enhanced due diligence and monitoring measures must be implemented by the supervised entity to manage the risks posed by the relationship.

body: In response to the threat of the international financial system being used for hiding the proceeds of corruption, in 2023, the FSA began requesting firms provide data on commerciallyexposed persons (CEPs) in their Annual AML/CFT return in addition to the existing PEP data. CEPs are defined by the FSA (in the AML/CFT Handbook) as senior executives associated with a specific industry or activity which typically has increased vulnerability to bribery and corruption and ML. CEPs are connected to customers who are employed in or associated with occupational activities such as arms/weapons trading; casinos/ gambling; construction/development; adult entertainment; oil and gas; pharmaceuticals; mining and trading in precious metals and stones; shipping and transport; etc. The sectors with the highest concentration as a percentage of the total Island exposure are Life Insurance (36.12%), TCSPs (19.40%), and Banking (18.38%). The occupational activities with the largest share are construction and development (30.85%); oil and gas (21.45%); and casinos, gambling, and betting (13.78%). The collection of this data commenced in 2023; since its introduction, the FSA has made clarifications to the supporting guidance to aid interpretation. Therefore, the data may not be fully accurate, but it does provide an indicative CEP profile overview. It is expected that the accuracy of the data will increase with each submission cycle.

While robust legislation and increased regulatory oversight exist to combat bribery and corruption in the Isle of Man, the complexity of financial crime and the involvement of high-risk sectors and individuals mean that continued vigilance and proactive measures are essential.

The most common types of financial sanctions are targeted asset freezes, which apply to named individuals, entities, and bodies, restricting access to funds and economic resources; these restrictions apply to a wide variety of financial markets and services and direct them to cease all business. As Highlighted earlier in this report, in response to the Russian Federation-Ukraine conflict and the introduction of international sanctions, the FIU led multi-agency reviews of exposure to the Russian Federation, Belarus, and Kazakhstan, with additional actions taken by other agencies to strengthen the legal framework for sanctions compliance. The number of individuals and entities that currently fall under the Isle of Man's sanctions regime has significantly increased. In October 2025, the IOM took part in the sanctioning of targets linked to the Prince Group of companies, instituted by the US and UK Governments. The group, described by the US Office of Foreign Assets Control as 'a transnational criminal empire through online investment scams targeting Americans and others worldwide,' is linked to ongoing ML investigations in the IOM.

The Isle of Man is consistently considered one of the safest places to live. The Chief Constable's Annual Report 2024/5 shows a 10% reduction in recorded crime (following a 5% reduction the previous year) and an increased detection rate to 56%. Drug importation generates high-profile cases concerning proceeds of crime on the Island. Other threats include labour exploitation, fraud, and theft, with convicted fraud and theft cases typically involving self-laundering. For example, in September 2021 an individual pleaded guilty to a £50,000 benefits fraud which ran for more than 5 years; and in December 2024, an individual previously found guilty of benefits fraud and theft related to a charity had their appeal against a prison sentence refused and has also been disqualified as a director.

The ECU has responsibility for investigating complex domestic financial crime (other than international ML). In 2024-5, the ECU adopted 15 new domestic ML cases, with 23 active investigations underway. The majority of recorded ML cases originate from domestic offences linked to drug importation and cash confiscations at the Island's borders, which have seen a significant increase in seized cash as a result of enhanced proactivity at the ports.

Since July 2024, IOM authorities have seized drugs valued over £880,000 (mainly cannabis and cocaine) and over £154,000 in cash suspected to be criminal proceeds (including drug trafficking, fraud, and theft).

The importation of illicit narcotics by OCGs from countries surrounding the Isle of Man and from Europe is a clear and present threat. The Island's proximity to the North West of England's drug markets in particular provides an attractive proposition as the price drugs command is Higher; this creates all of the associated criminality, including increases in cuckooing, money mules, child exploitation, and violence as OCGs seek to import drugs and extract the proceeds of crime. The Chief Constable's Annual Report 2024-5 refers to proactive operations targeting OCGs, with 37 local and 22 UK-based individuals having been arrested for various offences, including drug importation, money laundering, and serious fraud. Cocaine with an approximate street value of £464,000 was seized, as was 14.5 kilograms of cannabis, valued at £250,000; 1.5 kilograms of ketamine, valued at £75,000; and criminal property amounting to approximately £127,000. As a result of these operations, a number of lengthy prison sentences were imposed by the IOM Courts, including:

- 20 years for a leading OCG member in the IOM, for a number of importations of drugs even after being incarcerated in the IOM Prison;

- 15 years for a leading UK member of an OCG, for importing drugs to the IOM, including whilst incarcerated in a UK Prison; and

- 21 years 9 months for an OCG member responsible for importing Class A drugs to the IOM and conspiring to remove over £1 million of illicit proceeds.

In almost all cases, drug seizures were "inbound" and proceeds of crime "outbound". Increased success by police and customs at the ports of entry is contributing to a move away from attempts to physically remove criminal cash or to insert it into the banking system via for example, mule accounts utilising young and/or vulnerable people. The exploitation of labour in the Isle of Man is linked to immigration crime and people trafficking. Intermediaries, advisors, and unregulated immigration agents in the UK, Middle East, and locally promote immigration scams and offer services which facilitate immigration abuse, such as creating fictitious jobs and businesses and charging unlawful fees. OCGs and other actors have exploited vulnerabilities following changes to immigration policy since 2018, resulting in the closure of two immigration routes. Authorities report cases involving migrants who have been made vulnerable to exploitation due to employer and agent practices, encountering substandard living and working conditions. According to the Isle of Man and UK Gap Analysis Report (May 2025), "exploitation of migrant workers is an international concern. Addressing this issue is challenging because of power differences between employers and workers, as well as the presence of a 'migration industry' of intermediaries profiting from migrant labour."

The Isle of Man has an Anti-Bribery and Corruption Framework and Strategy (2022-2027) which is led by the AML/CFT Policy Office. The website provides information and guidance, resources, details of relevant legislation, and an online reporting channel for concerns regarding bribery and/or corruption (domestic and foreign). Reports are made to the FIU and actioned appropriately. Mandatory biannual training is provided to all Isle of Man Government staff via the eLearn Vannin electronic learning platform. An Anti-Bribery Policy is in place for all staff. The AML/CFT Policy Office provides annual face-to-face training to Members of Tynwald, which is arranged by the Clerk of Tynwald's Office. This covers the Bribery Act, delivery against the AntiBribery and Corruption Strategy, and how to raise concerns.

In January 2026, the IOM Government reported, in response to a written Parliamentary question, that three allegations of bribery had been made regarding Government staff over the previous financial year. One allegation of bribery had been made the previous year. Figures are reported to the Audit Advisory Division of Treasury, while allegations will be referred to the Police.

Many entities incorporated in the IOM have foreign beneficial owners and hold assets overseas. This complexity increases oversight challenges and demands robust due diligence by TCSPs and other regulated entities. The analysis for the LPA NRA also Highlights vulnerabilities associated with limited-service offerings, such as registered office or registered agent services, which inherently carry Higher risk.
Professional intermediaries, including TCSPs, lawyers, and accountants, play a critical role in mitigating these risks. However, weaknesses in controls, insufficient questioning of customers, and varying risk appetites across firms can create vulnerabilities. The misuse of LPAs by OCGs and transnational networks remains a significant threat, particularly where structures are designed to evade sanctions or exploit gaps in beneficial ownership transparency.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat, MONEY LAUNDERING MODALITIES, Citizenship By Investment - 98ccbaed5c5dca92
headers: 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat
body: The IOM does not offer a Citizenship by Investment (CBI) programme. Instead, there are residency pathways such as the "Business Innovator" route which provide investment-linked residency visas. While these pathways may eventually lead to settlement, eligibility for citizenship requires individuals to comply with naturalisation regulations, including a requisite period of lawful residence, obtaining indefinite leave to remain, fulfilling language proficiency requirements, and passing character assessments. Authorities are aware of various third-party websites purporting to offer IOM citizenship by investment; however, such offers are not genuine. IOM entities face risks from individuals with criminal backgrounds who obtain citizenship by investment elsewhere and use new identities to gain credibility, secure visas, and conduct business. Authorities have noted that CBI recipients are frequently ultimate beneficial owners or initial investors in structures relevant to ongoing criminal investigations. Individuals who appear to have been complicit in criminal activities have also used the CBI route to obtain residency and banking services. While CBI can be legitimate, its use is common in such schemes and requires close scrutiny. As part of the amended tax CRS, from January 2026, financial institutions have to carry out enhanced due diligence on CBI/Residency by Investment (RBI) jurisdictions identified by the OECD, which may assist in mitigating some of this risk.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat, MONEY LAUNDERING MODALITIES, Cross border cash - d7b9f5dcf9585bcf
headers: 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat
body:
The enhanced security arrangements at the ports have generated more than 60 separate significant seizures of illicit goods and money suspected to be proceeds of crime at the Island's points of entry in the financial year 2024-25. Seized goods included significant quantities of cannabis, cocaine, ketamine. and anabolic steroids to a value of approximately £1 million, with cash seizures just under £100,000. In almost all cases, drug seizures were "inbound" and proceeds of crime "outbound". Multiple arrests have been made in connection with the seizures described, for offences including production of Class A drugs and money laundering. Most cash seizures have taken place either following the search of a premises or at the main port (Sea Terminal).

The IOM Post Office (IOMPO) was identified as a frequent location for cash seizures, amounting to over 14.4% (over £270,000) in the period 2020‐24. Efforts to move criminal cash off-Island have moved towards transferring value into HVGs in recent years. The police have noted that the purchase of jewellery and watches, vehicles, art, and luxury clothing have all been used to avoid detection, with the amounts carefully structured to avoid triggering automatic registration and reporting requirements relating HVGDs. The FSA has been undertaking outreach to the local businesses that may deal in HVGs to alert them to the threat of ML and remind them of potential registration requirements where certain parameters are met.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat, MONEY LAUNDERING MODALITIES, Trade Based ML - 1530bfc5d60d61de
headers: 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat
body: Trade-based money laundering (TBML) is the process of disguising the proceeds of crime and moving value using trade transactions, rather than financial transactions, to legitimise their illicit origins. In practice, this can be achieved through the misrepresentation of the price, quantity, or quality of imports or exports. TBML techniques vary in complexity and are frequently used in combination with other money laundering techniques to further obscure the money trail. Real or fictitious services could just as easily be involved. A complex laundering system may involve both real and purported movements of goods and real or imaginary 'services' (such as consultancy, inspection, insurance, etc). TBML may be relevant to the IOM, but there are no evidenced cases at this time.

headers: 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat
body: The Isle of Man faces a growing threat from the use of VAs in money laundering activities, evidenced by an increase in international cases under investigation. These cases are marked by their complexity, often involving multi-jurisdictional structuring, shell companies, and a range of financial products to conceal criminal proceeds. There has been a notable rise in the use of VAs, particularly stablecoins such as USDT, to transfer illicit funds as part of money laundering processes. The main domestic threat relates to drug trafficking and supply. The use of IOM banknotes paid into third-party accounts and subsequently transferred to the UK (as a virtual asset) remains a common laundering method. That said, with effect from 1 January 2026, VASPs that are Reporting Crypto-Asset Service Providers (RCASPs) have to identify and report information, including beneficial ownership information, to the Income Tax Division, with respect to Reportable Users on an annual basis that will be exchanged with the jurisdictions in which the Reportable Users are tax resident.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat, MONEY LAUNDERING MODALITIES, Artificial Intelligence - 2879314747eec23d
headers: 10. National ML Cross-border, Foreign, and Domestic Threat
body:
Artificial intelligence is reshaping the financial crime landscape. For jurisdictions with a large cross-border customer base and a sophisticated TCSP sector, AI represents both an opportunity to strengthen detection and a set of new and fast-moving threats. International bodies, including the FATF, the Egmont Group, and Europol, note that data-driven analytics, machine learning, and collaborative analysis can materially improve the effectiveness of AML/CFT, while simultaneously recognising that criminals are using generative AI (GenAI) and synthetic media (deepfakes) to defeat onboarding, identity verification, and ongoing monitoring controls. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has published papers Highlighting that generative AI and deepfakes pose significant cyber- and financial crime risks, including identity spoofing, synthetic document creation, and impersonation attacks that can undermine CDD and remote onboarding processes.

AI-enabled obfuscation therefore compounds risks already identified in this NRA, particularly where structures are complex and span several jurisdictions. ■

Ratings for each of the 22 control variables are inserted into the Excel file of the NRA tool. Once the ML vulnerability ratings for each sector are inserted into the tool (see Figure 32 in Chapter 11) combining sectoral vulnerability and into account taking any deficiencies in national combatting ability, a score for National
Vulnerability is produced. The score ranges from 0.0 to 1.0 and corresponds to one of five levels ranging from Low to High. The assessments for each control variable below are summarised from the detailed worksheets created as part of the process with further information in Appendix VI.
The IOM Government has strengthened its antimoney laundering (AML) system with new resources, a revised structure, and strategies aligned with global standards. Approved plans guide policy, resource allocation, and cross-government collaboration.
Authorities and regulated entities are updating their practices. Legislative measures to align the AML framework with FCSB objectives have seen some delays and a number will require prioritisation following the 2026 General Election.
Module 2 Effectiveness of ML Crime Definition 1.0 Excellent
Money laundering is criminalised under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2008, in line with international standards. There are no specific sentencing guidelines within the Manx courts, the judiciary refer to the UK sentencing guidelines for ML. Penalties for ML range from fines to up to fourteen years' imprisonment.

The Prosecutions Division established a dedicated Financial Crime Unit in 2024, providing specialist expertise for financial crime cases. A senior legal officer is seconded to the police to support PIMLIT and ECU. The Prosecutions Division works closely with ICART to identify where parallel civil investigations may be appropriate. While ML prosecutions show success in convictions and confiscations, these primarily relate to drug trafficking; international ML convictions are still developing.

The Isle of Man is a separate legal jurisdiction, with a legal system based on English common law and Acts of Tynwald. Manx courts are guided by English precedents unless local law applies. Deemsters (judges) lead the judiciary. Serious criminal cases are dealt with by the Court of General Gaol Delivery, while appeals go to the Staff of Government Division and, ultimately, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London. Specialist judges handle financial crime, and recent reforms allow judge-only trials for complex fraud. Legal training and digital capacity have improved; planned legislative updates aim to address some practical matters regarding modernising court facilities.
Module 10 Independence and Integrity of Judges 1.0 Excellent
Judicial appointments in the Isle of Man are independent and transparent, with senior judges chosen by the King on expert recommendation. Judges are not politically appointed and must retire at 75, upholding impartiality and integrity. Trials proceed without interference or corruption, with all judgments published and complaints handled through a set process. Judicial conduct is governed by a strict code and supported by anti-corruption measures; ongoing legal service reforms stem from Lord Garnier KC's 2023 independent review, addressing advocate training, Law Society roles, and disciplinary procedures.
Module 11 Quality of Border Controls 0.4 Medium Low

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 11. National Controls and Residual Vulnerabilities, CONTROLS FOR AML - 26a7caace371272d

The Isle of Man, as part of the Common Travel Area, permits free movement for British and Irish citizens, with entry typically via major ports. Post-pandemic border reopening saw targeted operations against organised crime, leading to significant seizures. A 2021 review Highlighted intelligence gaps around human trafficking and forced labour. Border security has been bolstered through enhanced policing, monitoring, and technology upgrades. In 2024,
Immigration and Customs merged under Treasury oversight to improve efficiency. While policies are closely aligned with the UK, differences have created some exploitation risks, as reflected in recent convictions. The 'Securing our Island' strategy focuses on reducing risks through improved information sharing, digital system alignment, and additional enforcement resources.
Module 12 Comprehensiveness of the Customs regime on cash and similar instruments 0.9 Close to Excellent
Customs controls in the Isle of Man are overseen by the Treasury's Customs and Immigration Division. Goods generally move freely with the UK, but some are restricted. Cash over £10,000 must be declared at the border, and officers have powers to enforce compliance. The regime is based on the Customs and Excise Management Act 1986 and is regularly updated to match port security and policy changes.
Module 13 Effectiveness of the Customs Regime on Cash and Similar Instruments 0.6 Medium High

Most traffic enters the Isle of Man through one airport and ferry terminal, aiding enforcement. While the coastline is vulnerable to illegal entry, robust controls and improved agency cooperation have led to effective cash and ML enforcement at ports. The non-cashbased economy limits large-scale cash generation, with most smuggled cash tied to drug trafficking from UKbased OCGs; authorities have documented attempts to import and remove such cash. Tracking locally issued notes leaving the island remains a challenge. Ongoing efforts focus on enhanced training and intelligence-sharing among agencies.
Module 14 Effectiveness of Domestic Cooperation 0.7 High
Domestic cooperation in the Isle of Man is underpinned by a robust governance framework focused on risk management and inter-agency collaboration. Key groups meet regularly and share information efficiently, supported by statutory provisions and ongoing development of MOUs. Coordination by the AML/
CFT Policy Office ensures streamlined national and international engagement. Recommendations include enhancing risk awareness in less-involved Government departments. While law enforcement has legislative powers to share border security information, a formal Code of Practice is required.
Module 15 Effectiveness of international cooperation 0.7 High

The Isle of Man has a robust legal framework enabling international cooperation on money laundering and terrorist financing, with mutual legal assistance coordinated by the AGC and supported by effective participation in global networks supporting asset recovery, extradition, and information sharing. Module 16 Availability of Independent Audit 0.8 Very High
Audit laws remain unchanged; audits follow UK and Ireland international standards, with oversight by the UK's Financial Reporting Council for market-traded companies. Most 2006 Act firms are exempt; 1931 Act firms require audits unless exempted based on size and staffing criteria. FSA- and GSC-regulated entities must submit annual audited accounts, except for certain DNFBPs, and license-holders or those handling client money need independent auditor assurance. Specific rules apply for insurers and Retirement Benefit Scheme administrators.

Criminal and civil proceedings involving professionals are publicly reported, with enforcement notices and judgments accessible online. The Isle of Man Treasury oversees both direct and indirect tax functions, with the Income Tax Division (ITD) responsible for income tax and National Insurance, and the Customs and Immigration Division handling indirect taxes. The Income Tax Division (ITD) operates under strict confidentiality and statutory rules, but can share confidential information with other authorities, including law enforcement and the regulators, where appropriate to do so. The Division has strong powers to address non-compliance, including penalties and public proceedings for serious cases. Tax compliance is generally strong. Consideration is being given to developing a specific AML Tax strategy to support the overall approach of the Division to addressing financial crime. The Collector leads indirect tax overseeing administration, compliance, and enforcement. Regular audits are conducted by the UK NAO, and HMRC provides training and policy coordination. The audit team sets its own risk-based targets for trader audits. Legal powers allow broad information sharing and data collection for assigned matters. Most court cases center on VAT fraud, with recent convictions and fines Highlighting enforcement activity.
Module 19 Formalisation of the Economy 0.9 Close to Excellent

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 11. National Controls and Residual Vulnerabilities, CONTROLS FOR AML - ea9ba65443c1bc57
body:
The Isle of Man's economy is predominantly servicesbased, with minimal informal activity accounting for less than 10% of GDP. Residents must participate in the financial system to access utilities and government services, with strict regulations and VAT registration required for most business activities.
High employment, and declining cash usage underpin robust law enforcement, although recent rises in drug and cash seizures, immigration crime, and labour exploitation indicate the need for ongoing vigilance against shadow economy risks.
Module 20 Availability of Reliable Identification Infrastructure 0.7 High
The IOM Government issues various photographic identification documents, including passports and driving licences; there is no requirement to carry identity cards. The Island acts as an issuing authority for British Passports; driving licences are issued by IOM Post. The Island keeps an Electoral Register. There are no formal border controls within the CTA and therefore no mandatory ID checks; this can allow some to avoid identification. Enhanced data collection and sharing between police, customs, and immigration is being developed. Closer working between the DoI Highway Services, the police, immigration and potentially other agencies is recommended. Staff at businesses are trained to identify fraudulent documents, and extra precautions are taken for non face-to-face transactions.
Module 21 Availability of Independent Information Sources 0.7 High

Government and industry rely on internationally recognised credit and identification services, using robust screening tools and independent data sources for due diligence. External databases and agencies are widely used for customer and transaction checks, and although there is no local credit bureau, international providers fill this role. Regulatory and public information is easily accessible online for verification purposes.
Module 22 Availability & Access to Beneficial Ownership Information 0.7 High
Beneficial ownership information is readily accessible to law enforcement through several channels, including the central Beneficial Ownership database managed by the Companies Registry. The Beneficial Ownership Act 2017 requires legal entities to record beneficial ownership details and appoint a Nominated Officer, with TCSPs acting in this role for most companies. The central database is supported by verification processes, penalties for non-compliance, and access for multiple agencies. Ongoing improvements focus on strengthening accuracy, coverage, and regulatory scope in line with international standards.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, INTRODUCTION AND METHODOLOGY - 492f7f6de9879d01
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
Modules 3-7 of the WB tool seek to assess the risk of sectors in the jurisdiction to help fully understand the national ML risk. Not only may the features of a sector lend themselves to being exploited by money launderers, but weaknesses in the AML controls in different sectors may also contribute to ML vulnerability. However, not all sectors are equally at risk from ML. The level of materiality, types and features of products, and geographic reach of a sector have an impact on the level of risk that a sector may face.
The depth of the ML assessment will also depend upon the level of data available for that sector. For sectors that are smaller and primarily domestic in nature, there is sometimes insufficient data to input into the WB model. Nevertheless, all sectors have been assessed using the full WB model where possible, including an analysis of the products and services using the data that is available. For those sectors where there was not sufficient data held to put through the model (usually due to sector size), the risk assessment has considered any threats and vulnerabilities identified, the data available, the controls in place, and the expert judgement of the regulators.
For each sector, the WB methodology undertakes a review of:

- ML threat factors;

- inherent vulnerability factors (including materiality); and

- AML controls.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, INTRODUCTION AND METHODOLOGY - cac8c0ac5a1ceb8d
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
In line with the Isle of Man's AML/CFT Framework, for the purposes of this NRA, TCSPs have been treated as a financial institution, as they are fully regulated in the IOM (although deemed a DNFBP by the FATF). Conversely, Moneylenders have been included in the Designated Business section of this report as they are treated as such under the IOM Framework (however, the FATF defines Moneylenders as financial institutions).
The WB Tool recommends that industry representatives participate in the Risk Assessment process, providing their perspectives and the opportunity to raise awareness of the NRA amongst a key audience. Industry working groups were convened for several sectors as part of this process and approximately 35 meetings were held with about 40 firms to discuss the various sectors and the risks posed. The authorities also engaged directly with professional and industry bodies, via the Financial Crime Partnership and the AML/CFT Advisory Group, and via surveys designed to inform specific parts of the process. Feedback from the private sector into this process has been positive and constructive.
Further information regarding the process can be found at Appendix VII.

SECTORAL THREAT, VULNERABILITY AND MATERIALITY FACTORS
body: For each sector, relevant vulnerabilities were considered. This took the form of industry meetings, including meetings of the sectoral Financial Crime Partnership (where established) to gather information and insights as to what factors made their sectors (or products) vulnerable to ML. This information was considered and factored into the Risk Assessment. In addition, the WB model prescribes a number of different inherent vulnerabilities for each sector, which are set out in the model and the associated guidance. The agencies were able to rate each inherent vulnerability accordingly using information held by both agencies and industry, and also using the comprehensive data that is submitted to the regulators. An inherent vulnerability score was then determined, and this data, together with the AML controls scores, provided a residual vulnerability score/rating (i.e, after considering mitigating controls).

SECTORAL THREAT, VULNERABILITY AND MATERIALITY FACTORS
body: In order to assess the overall ML risk, the WB model requires that the relative importance of each sector and/or its share of the economy, as well as assets under management/administration (where relevant), is considered. Each sector is then 'weighted' according to its size/importance within the jurisdiction to determine the overall ML vulnerability. For the purposes of this assessment, a number of metrics were used: National Income (where available), size of sector (e.g. staff numbers/assets under management or administration), and interconnectedness with other sectors.

body: A detailed assessment of AML control factors forms part of the WB model. Explanations of controls in respect of Banking, Insurance, Gambling, VASPS, and TCSPs can be found in the stand-alone NRAs for these sectors. Individual sectoral control assessments were undertaken across agencies for all sectors, which included input from sector representatives at a series of workshops. The AML controls in relation to gambling are summarised under Gambling in 12.5 (Sectoral Reports). A summary of findings for the sectors that fall under the FSA is included below. The control scores for each sector were used to determine the residual vulnerability which feeds into the overall sectoral risk rating.
