- Focus on AML/CFT risk, including risk identified in the NRA, has improved since the previous NRA.
- The technical and human resources of the FSA for AML/CFT supervision have increased significantly. There is a dedicated AML/CFT Supervisory Division and staff receive regular training to enable them to undertake robust supervisory activities, including inspections.

- A comprehensive range of sanctions is available to the regulators, including use of directions, licence conditions, utilisation of third-party reporting professionals, civil penalties, and suspension or revocation of a licence. In the relevant circumstances, these are applied alongside a full remediation plan agreed with the firm and monitored accordingly. Publicity is always given to the application of civil penalties. In practice, greatest use is made of conditions and directions.
- Decisions on the application of discretionary civil penalties follow established internal governance processes, including the published FSA Enforcement Decision Making Process (August 2025). A guidance note has been published explaining the discretionary civil penalty framework.
- According to an Island Global Research survey of industry participants, 91% of respondents indicated they were aware or very aware of these enforcement actions.
- Civil penalties may not currently be applied to directors or key persons, and work is in progress to strengthen this framework. This was reflected in the scores assigned, but overall, this area of control was scored as Very Hgh across most sectors. - A comprehensive range of criminal sanctions is available and may be applied to Financial Institutions under the Proceeds of Crime Act and the AML/CFT Code, at levels intended to serve as a suitable deterrent. Offences under POCA include failure to report a suspicion as well "tipping off".
- A process is in place for the formal adoption and progression of potential ML/TF/PF investigations through the Anti-Money Laundering Group and PIMLIT's Case Development Unit.
- The framework governing criminal sanctions is robust and thorough, and appropriate specialist resources are available; however, as civil powers have been to date considered the most appropriate method of penalty, accordingly, this control has been assessed as Medium High across all sectors rather than High/Very High, as criminal sanctions have not been applied during this period.
5. Availability and Effectiveness of entry controls
- There is a well-established "fit and proper" registration regime in place (including a full criminality check for both local and foreign staff). However, the FSA is considering extending its access to additional databases and other tools to further pick up additional adverse media, connections to criminals, or reputational issues on an ongoing basis.

- Robust compliance requirements are in place in respect of financial institutions, including (i) the appointment of a Head of Compliance at a senior level with direct access to the board; (ii) requirement for monitoring plans to be commensurate to risk; and (iii) the FSA's Training and Competence Framework, which sets requirements in respect of ongoing training and competence (for all staff and key persons).

- In respect of all those supervised by the FSA, the Code requires entities to monitor compliance with the AML/CFT Code and to have a person at senior management level who is responsible for monitoring compliance. This would typically be reviewed on a supervisory inspection.

- Comprehensiveness of compliance systems can vary between sectors and firms. Findings from inspections were also taken into account when determining the sectoral scores for this area; therefore, again, there was some variation in scores, from Medium (in some of the smaller designated businesses) through to High (in regulated sectors).

9. Effectiveness of Suspicious Activity Monitoring and Reporting
body:
- Comprehensiveness of transaction and relationship monitoring can vary between sectors and firms depending on systems and procedures used. Findings from inspections that examined this area were taken into account when determining the sectoral scores for this area.

- In relation to SAR reporting, it is an offence if relevant persons do not report suspicious activity, actual or attempted, regardless of the amount. This includes AML/CFT/CPF suspicions under POCA and the Anti-Terrorism and Crime Act 2003 (ATCA). Section 24 of the FIU Act 2016 allows entities to report matters that may assist the FIU in its functions where a suspicion of ML/TF is not held. There is a wellestablished reporting framework in place and a requirement for ongoing monitoring of customers and transactions in order to identify suspicious activity and circumstances, and to keep records of the same.

- Input from the FIU was also considered in relation to this control, specifically regarding both the quality and quantity of SARs across the sectors.

- Based on the above considerations and the differences across sectors, there was some variation in scores from Medium Low (in some of the smaller designated businesses) through to Higher scores (in more mature regulated sectors).

10. Availability and Access to Beneficial Ownership Information
body:
- The AML/CFT/CPF regulatory framework requires entities to collect details of the beneficial ownership of their customers and verify this information.

- Access to beneficial ownership information contained in company registers varies by country, as does the quality of the information. In December 2024, the IOM made its register accessible to obliged entities. The FSA monitors compliance with the Beneficial Ownership Act 2017 and evaluates whether relevant persons fulfil their BOA obligations.

- FSA supervision has not typically found specific shortcomings in how entities identify and verify customers. Entities usually require a Government-issued passport or Isle of Man driving licence, plus supporting documents, as local photo ID for onboarding. There are procedures to accommodate those without these documents, such as the elderly or students. The Handbook offers detailed guidance on customer due diligence.
- Some entities may use electronic ID verification tools - mainly for UK residents, where data is more reliable. Technology can also remove the need for certified document copies during onboarding. The Handbook provides detailed customer due diligence guidance, including advice on the use of electronic tools.
12. Availability of Independent Information Sources
- The sources remain unchanged since the last NRA, with limited IOM-specific independent information available.
- Some sectors utilise external data sources to provide independent information on non-resident customers, particularly those customers resident in the UK. World-Check and other international databases are widely used to screen customers for PEP and sanctions connections and adverse press, and are accessible globally. Entities may also use UK resources such as credit bureaus, government lists, Companies House, PEP information, and regulator registers.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, BANKING, Background to the Sector - 4bfcadfb28f13127
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body: The IOM's Banking sector serves both domestic and international customers, with Banking forming a critical component of the IOM's financial system and economy. The sector is largely comprised of branches or subsidiaries of major UK and International Banks and is fully regulated by the FSA. As an IFC, most business, by value and number of customers, is international in nature, especially with strong connections to the UK and South Africa. This international profile increases the sector's exposure to cross-border ML threats, particularly the risk of foreign proceeds of crime entering the financial system. The IOM maintains a comprehensive legal and supervisory structure, and recent regulatory enhancements have targeted areas such as business introducers, PEPs, and targeted financial sanctions risk management. Ongoing risk-based supervision, thematic reviews and enforcement actions continue to strengthen AML/CFT/CPF systems and controls.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, BANKING, Background to the Sector - d75c6fa970a991dc
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body: Since the 2020 NRA was published, Banks have been required to prepare and submit more data to the FSA. This data is used to help assess ML risks and can also be useful to Banks to aid their own business understanding and risk assessment. To support this process, the FSA requested Banks' internal audit functions to conduct reviews in 2025. The findings to date have identified areas for improvement but did not affect the overall sector assessment. These findings Highlight the importance of ongoing data quality efforts particularly in areas such as financial flows where the consideration of continuous improvement should be embedded.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, BANKING, Size and Materiality - 78c04c6998331dae
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
This sector employs approximately 2,000 people and holds over GBP£40 billion in deposits, processing nearly GBP£80 billion in annual payments. Banking represents 8.6% of the IOM's national income (2023/24). As of 31 December 2024, there were 11 banks operating in the IOM (and one representative office). This is displayed below in Figure 33:
Figure 33: Countries of Origin for Banks in the IOM
- UK: 4; Spain: 1; South Afica: 3; Trinidad & Tobago: 1; Isle of Man: 2
Banks in the IOM provide traditional deposit taking and credit services to the domestic market, covering both individuals and businesses, as well as providing services to TCSPs, their customer structures, and other corporate sectors including regulated firms. Domestic banking is mainly delivered through UK banking groups operating on the IOM. Banks also serve non-resident personal customers and, to a lesser extent, international businesses; this includes cross-border activity. The transactional activity of banks in the IOM remains substantially traditional in nature, with the most usual payment methods being bank transfers, debit cards, cash, and cheques. The IOM's Banking sector offers a broad range of financial products and services, including savings and current accounts, private and premier banking (tailored to highincome customers with enhanced service offerings), investment services, various types of lending such as mortgages, treasury services, and foreign currency accounts, and exchange services.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, BANKING, Size and Materiality - 2c7888117dc96a8f
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
Many banking customers are non-residents, with a wide geographical spread by residency and nationality. The largest number of non-resident customers are from the UK, reflecting the close geographical and economic ties between the UK and the IOM. There is also a significant number of South Africanresident banking customers, reflecting the Banking sector's longstanding links to that country.
Over half of total bank deposits are from individuals (retail), and deposits overall continue to be used as a source of funding for the wider benefit of some banks' broader group operations (outside of the Island). The overall trend has been one of stable growth, with deposits increasing by c. 33% between 2020 and 2024 (an average annual rise of c. 7.5%). Refer to the Banking sectoral report for further details on Banking sector balances from 2020 to 2024.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, BANKING, Size and Materiality - f3ffd2a2702dd22b
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body: All Banks supply the FSA with quarterly transactional data of inflows and outflows (including within the IOM). The largest inflows and outflows to and from the IOM (2021 to 2024) were with the UK, which is in line with expectations given the close geographical and constitutional ties. There is a High concentration of customers in respect of three core countries: the IOM, UK, and South Africa. Around 15% of the sector's customers reside in Higher-risk jurisdictions, noting however that South Africa was removed from the FATF grey list in November 2025. Non-natural customer numbers are mainly driven by BVI incorporations, most of which will be customers introduced through TCSPs.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, BANKING, Threats - 15be08a1bb8c3a6c
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
The overall ML threat to Banks has been assessed as being Medium High, consistent with the overarching national threat assessment, noting that there is a medium domestic threat but a Medium High international (cross-border) threat.
The Banking sector has seen an increase in SARs from 2021 to 2024, largely driven by international threats such as fraud, tax evasion, organised crime, and the use of virtual assets, as well as increasing awareness in the sector of the requirement for SAR reporting. There is also a rising threat from Asian and UK-based organised crime groups and the increasing pace and complexity in financial flows. This is reflected in ongoing investigations, including those in relation to online gambling and cyber-enabled crime.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, BANKING, Threats - 8bf4e2bc21ca6f49
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
SARs have been steadily increasing over the period, most notably pertaining to fraud, which has almost tripled since 2020. Banks have consistently been the second-largest reporter after the iGaming sector; however, many of the reports by the latter constitute dual reports to the IOM as well as other jurisdictions. Of the most frequently reported criminalities, SARs relating to drug trafficking were generally domestic in nature, whereas SARs relating to tax crimes and organised criminal activity were more international. Fraud SARs relate to both domestic and international predicate offending; this is partially due to the victims' accounts often being held on the IOM, whilst the perpetrators of the fraud may be located off-Island. Suspected criminality occurring outside of the IOM largely relates to fraud and tax crimes, bribery, and corruption.
Between 2020 and 2024, the UK accounted for 49.2% of incoming MLAs relating to the Banking sector. The IOM is frequently used for company incorporations, trusts, and tax planning structures, some of which are routed through UK. The majority of incoming tax-related requests received were from the UK/Europe.

Although this threat is longstanding, the combination of fast-evolving markets and increasingly sophisticated criminal typologies creates enhanced opportunities to move and obscure illicit funds.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, RETAIL & PRIVATE BANKING (DOMESTIC & INTERNATIONAL), International Deposit Services - 246536d823246b77
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
Core products and services include current accounts, notice and fixed-term accounts, savings and investments, payment and FX services. Additional vulnerabilities arise from non-face-to-face business or use of third parties, Higher levels of international transactions, and some foreign PEP or High-net-worth business (with challenges to establish source of wealth). The international personal deposit book is the largest segment by value. There are strong customer take-on procedures, robust ongoing monitoring and screening, sufficient resourcing and investment in systems and controls; dedicated relationship contacts assist in understanding activity.

Products and services include current accounts, notice and fixedterm accounts, savings accounts, payment and FX services. The customer book is of relatively low value and low numbers. Some vulnerabilities exist in relation to the use of cash or local PEP connections, but Banks report domestic charities as not posing a Higher risk. Banks have encouraged a move away from cash.

International Credit Services - Medium Low Vulnerability Credit services (including some "buy to let" mortgages) are either lower-value or longer-term, less transactional, and not cash-based, reducing their vulnerabilities.

While the IOM Banking sector has made progress in strengthening its controls and mitigating many of the inherent vulnerabilities associated with its international and domestic activities, vigilance remains crucial. Ongoing global trends - such as the evolution of new payment technologies, growth in crossborder business, and the expansion of organised crime typologies require the sector and Authorities to continually adapt their risk management strategies and operational resilience.

Overall, the Banking sector continues to present one of the Highest levels of ML risks in the IOM's financial services sector. chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, CREDIT UNIONS, Background to the sector - 447a2214983c667f
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
Credit Unions are member-owned, not-for-profit financial cooperatives that provide savings, lending services, and other financial products exclusively to their members. In the IOM, the sector is very small, comprising a single institution registered under the Credit Unions Act 1993 which places restrictions on membership, shareholdings, and borrowing. A Credit Union operating from the IOM must also hold a Class 9 (Credit Union) licence under the FSA08, this brings the sector into the regulatory regime and the requirements of the AML/CFT Code.

Services provided by Credit Unions are limited to IOM residents. Membership is limited by legislation to 5,000 members, with the current sole Credit Union established locally having approximately 1600 members.

Credit Unions can only hold up to GBP£15,000 in total for an individual member. Whilst no interest is paid on Credit Union share accounts, an annual dividend may be paid. This is paid to members from profits earned during the financial year. Dividends are calculated after deducting from profits the expenses of running the Credit Union and contribution to reserves which a Credit Union is legally obliged to provide for. Lending activity is governed by rules, with lending limits set at GBP£5,000 (or such other sum as may from time to time be prescribed) in excess of the total paid-up shareholding per member in the Credit Union at that time.

The services offered by a Credit Union usually involve the acceptance of cash and sometimes a prepaid card may be offered, albeit this is currently not a service offered locally. These services could provide opportunities for placing illicit funds through small, repeated deposits. Any Credit Union on the IOM is subject to the requirements of the AML/CFT Code which sets out the required preventative measures and controls that must be implemented.

body:
FAs in the IOM generally undertake business on a face-toface basis (82%), providing advice predominantly to IOMresident clients (97%), the majority of whom (95%) are natural persons. FAs service a wide range of customers and provide advice relating to a range of products and services, such as protection, investment, or personal advice to prospective or existing customers.

Generally, FAs treat individual customers as retail clients, unless the FA undertakes an adequate assessment of the customer's relevant expertise, experience, and knowledge which gives a reasonable assurance that the customer is capable of understanding the risks involved in making their own investment decisions. In any case, whichever type of customer the FA deems the individual to be, this should be made clear in any written recommendations supplied to the customer.

FAs do not hold or manage client money in respect of investment business. Money being settled into an investment product recommended by an FA will pass from one regulated business to another, not to or from the FA. As part of their responsibilities to provide suitable advice, FAs must fully understand their clients and their needs, and their wealth, and assess the ML/TF risk.

Within the sector, there is very limited reliance on third parties for CDD collection or the use of introducers. Strong entry due diligence controls are in place.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, INVESTMENT BUSINESS - STOCKBROKING / ASSET MANAGERS / INVESTMENT MANAGERS, Background to the sector - 067525931ab81d2c
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
INVESTMENT BUSINESS - STOCKBROKING / ASSET MANAGERS / INVESTMENT MANAGERS
body:
The business undertaken in this sector includes asset and investment management services for individuals (including HNWIs), corporations, funds, and other financial institutions. These businesses control and manage their customers' funds/ assets, including on a discretionary basis. They may also act as or arrange for a firm to hold/safeguard the assets where required.
Services under a discretionary mandate mean that the firm is trusted by customers to make appropriate investment decisions on behalf of them. An initial assessment is completed with the customer to understand the investment objectives and the risk appetite of the customer, and then a strategy is planned to fit their profile and needs. The manager will then take charge of all investment decisions and ensure the appropriate documents are in place. This process will not require consent for transactions. Minimum investment levels tend to be Higher than those for FAs.
Advisory investment management is more intensive and often offered by larger firms and possibly by certain banks. The firm will advise on strategies for investment, but the customer makes the final decision and/or approvals. "Execution-only" means the customer instructs the firm and no advice is provided by an investment manager or FA.
Execution-only is best suited to experienced or knowledgeable investors, predominantly non-retail customers, but can also include well-informed retail customers.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, INVESTMENT BUSINESS - STOCKBROKING / ASSET MANAGERS / INVESTMENT MANAGERS, Background to the sector - 82d599c09b463115
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
INVESTMENT BUSINESS - STOCKBROKING / ASSET MANAGERS / INVESTMENT MANAGERS
body:
Stockbrokers may, on behalf of customers, buy and sell stocks, bonds, and other securities, either on an executiononly basis or via an advisory or discretionary offering. Stockbrokers are required to abide by stock market rules, which require them to prevent churning, market abuse, and treat customers fairly, such as ensuring best execution in performing deals. "Best execution" means achieving the best possible result for customers when executing their orders by considering the price, costs, speed, likelihood of execution and settlement, size, nature, or any other consideration relevant to the execution of the order.
Overall, this sector may involve larger and more complex transactions and customers that are considered to be HNWIs (including PEPs). The sector also handles customer money as part of the services provided. A key point to consider is the speed of transactions in this sector due to the nature of some of the services provided. This has also resulted in some parts of the sector increasingly using technology in the delivery of these services. However, in terms of mitigations, the sector is mature, with good-quality systems in place and a strong AML control environment.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, INVESTMENT BUSINESS - STOCKBROKING / ASSET MANAGERS / INVESTMENT MANAGERS, Vulnerabilities - 4e28e6667e21de35
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
INVESTMENT BUSINESS - STOCKBROKING / ASSET MANAGERS / INVESTMENT MANAGERS
body:
The main vulnerability relating to this sector is that a firm can handle customer money, potentially exposing the firm to handling and moving the proceeds of crime. This vulnerability is increased if the products have increased liquidity and transaction velocity and are utilised in a manner which is not in line with the expected activity of the customer. A key typology involves the early sale or encashment of an investment product or asset designed to deliver value over a longer holding period, where such activity is inconsistent with the customer's profile or lacks a clear commercial rationale.
The risks associated with the misuse of investment products, particularly those permitting early encashment or early exit, are mitigated through a clear understanding of how liquidity features can increase transaction velocity and facilitate ML where the activity is inconsistent with expected customer behaviour. These risks are addressed through product governance, proportionate CDD aligned to investment objectives, and ongoing monitoring to identify early sale or encashment activity that lacks an apparent commercial rationale. Additional mitigation is added by virtue of the predominant payment method in the sector being bank transfers. Cash is very occasionally accepted and never issued by the sector. Monitoring of such customer and account activity is also a key control.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, INVESTMENT BUSINESS - STOCKBROKING / ASSET MANAGERS / INVESTMENT MANAGERS, Vulnerabilities - 86159e457825f0f6
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
INVESTMENT BUSINESS - STOCKBROKING / ASSET MANAGERS / INVESTMENT MANAGERS
body:
The use of pooling client monies and investments is a feature of the sector which can pose additional risk; however, the AML/CFT/CPF requirements are robust in this area as to when any AML/CFT/CPF concessions relating to pooling (such as Paragraph 17 of the AML/CFT Code) can be utilised by firms and what controls must be in place to utilise such concessions.
The sector may be exposed to more complex transactions which can disguise the true origin of the funds and wealth. Particular care is needed in this area, especially where income incentives for the firm may be Higher. There may also be transactions that need to take place very quickly due to the nature of the services provided. In terms of mitigations, the AML/CFT/CPF framework requires the source of funds of all customers to be established at customer onboarding, and also that the sector displays strong controls around customer monitoring.
In certain parts of the sector, time-sensitive pressures to place trades due to market movements put particular pressure on the industry to have risk mitigation processes in place which don't hamper normal operating procedures, but nonetheless are in keeping with the AML/CFT/CPF framework that is in place.

body:
The Insurance industry is the largest financial sector in the IOM, accounting for 16.9% of national income in 2023/24. As such, Insurance plays a critical role in the overall economy. The sector is mature, well-established, and primarily international in nature, with a particular emphasis on Life insurance. Oversight and regulation of the industry is provided by the FSA.
In line with other sectors, recent regulatory enhancements have targeted areas such as introducers, PEPs, and targeted financial sanctions risk management. Ongoing risk-based supervision, thematic reviews, and enforcement actions continue to strengthen AML/CFT/CPF systems and controls.
The profile of the IOM's Insurance market remains broadly in line with the 2020 NRA. The Life Insurance sector continues to be focused on cross-border distribution of predominantly unit-linked insurance products to expatriates and non-resident customers in jurisdictions outside the IOM; the domestic market remains insignificant.
The Life Insurance sector continues to be made up largely of authorised insurers with ultimate ownership in developed, regulated markets, including the IOM or UK, in addition to other countries considered equivalent under prudential "Solvency II" standards (Bermuda, Switzerland, and Canada). Life permit holders show a similar spread of geographical ownership. chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, INSURANCE: LIFE AND NON-LIFE, Threats - 090aa0b9cc099d77
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
The overall ML threat to the Insurance sector has been assessed as medium. This rating is fundamentally derived from the threat assessment of the Life Insurance sector, noting that this is primarily of an international (cross-border) nature and given its relative size to the whole Insurance sector. The ML threat to the Life sector is assessed as medium. The ML threat to the Non-Life sector is assessed as Medium Low.
SARs made by the Insurance sector have remained broadly stable over a five-year period; disclosures predominantly arise from the Life Insurance sector, consistent with that sector's size and inherent risk profile. Disclosures from the Insurance Intermediary sector are very low. SARs submitted by the sector show an increase in the amount and proportion of suspected fraud cases, consistent with other sectors, and a reduction in disclosures where the predicate offence is not known. There have been no incoming MLA requests in recent years and no active criminal investigations. The Insurance sector would benefit from recent, relevant typologies and case studies.
Source: FSA

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, INSURANCE: LIFE AND NON-LIFE, Threats - 7370117bc27a836f
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
IOM insurers, notably in the Life sector, have some exposure to Higher-risk clients, including CEPs and PEPs from Higherrisk countries, as indicated in data submitted to the FSA by insurers. This increases the inherent risk of life insurers receiving proceeds of bribery and corruption. The threat is not new and control measures are well-established; however, emerging, fastpaced markets and a shift away from historic centres of illicit financial flows towards newer geographical markets identified in published reports as the 'Dubai-Hong Kong' axis is particularly relevant to the IOM's Life insurance sector as locations where a number of insurers have established branches. The Life Insurance sector also has a relatively High percentage of customers - and correspondingly, PEPs - who reside in Argentina. This is commensurate with larger firms having branch operations in Argentina, where the licensing regimes allow branches of foreign insurers to distribute to domestic markets.
Within the Life sector, the geographical spread of non-natural customers is strongly biased to the UK, reflecting the use of life assurance products held in trust and corporate structures for recognised estate and tax planning purposes. The Life Insurance sector has a c. 4.5% exposure to customers resident in Higherrisk countries, predominantly natural customers, with this level relatively stable over the reporting period.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, INSURANCE: LIFE AND NON-LIFE, Threats - 9c9a0c4862f4ab9e
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
For the Non-Life sector, the profile for commercial insurers is shown to be very Highly concentrated on a narrow range of markets, principally the UK, IOM, and the other Crown Dependencies of Jersey and Guernsey. There are no customers from Higher-risk countries. For captive insurers, there is a more diverse customer residence profile. The concentration of captive business customers reported in Liberia and the Marshall Islands relates to the insurance of merchant ships.
The General Insurance Intermediary sector is Highly focused on the IOM market, both for natural and non-natural customers, and correspondingly, the exposure to Higher-risk countries is negligible. The residency profile for PEPs is slightly wider than for natural and non-natural persons, with c. 20% foreign PEPs (a relatively low number in absolute terms).

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, INSURANCE: LIFE AND NON-LIFE, Vulnerabilities - 9891a4654688b3b5
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
The consolidated Insurance sector has a medium ML level of vulnerability, reflecting some inherent vulnerabilities prevalent in the products and services identified below, partly mitigated by a Medium High AML control framework. The Life Insurance sector has products with Higher vulnerability; Non-Life sector products and services have lower inherent vulnerabilities.

The international scope of the Life Insurance sector in particular, use of legal persons and arrangements, product flexibility, and exposure to PEPs (although relatively limited) present areas of vulnerability. Approximately 5% of PEPs (by residency) within the Life Insurance sector originate from Higher-risk jurisdictions. The use of corporate structures can further increase these vulnerabilities, making it more difficult to identify the true source or ownership of funds. As noted, the industry operates in several Higher-risk jurisdictions; however, it benefits from substantial levels of expertise and experience, with many firms having maintained a presence in these markets for several years.

The sectoral ML vulnerability assessment, which considers a range of factors including market size, concludes that the most vulnerable product/service segments are in the Life Insurance sector (single and regular premium products/services). Summary details of the product assessment across the sector are as follows:

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, A. LIFE INSURANCE, A1 Single premium investments (including unit-linked protection) - a9272f71d95d8046
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
A1 Single premium investments (including unit-linked protection)
body: These products are lump sum life investment contracts linked to limited internal or mirror funds. Though they are intended for medium-to-long-term investment, they can be surrendered at any time, making them more vulnerable than other life insurance options. Typically sold and managed remotely, their inherent vulnerability is rated Medium High, and after controls, medium.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, A. LIFE INSURANCE, A2 Single premium portfolio bonds - 87ba0dcc0b9179f2
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body: These lump sum investments, linked to external funds or even private company shares, expose policy benefits to market fluctuations. Surrender values and remote distribution increase vulnerability, which is rated Medium High before controls and medium after mitigation.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, A. LIFE INSURANCE, A3 Single premium capital redemption bonds - 9970383ce51a81bf
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
A3 Single premium capital redemption bonds
body: These products are single-payment, long-term investments with a set redemption date and no life assured, making them available to entities such as companies. They usually offer unit-linked options with early surrenders and are mostly sold remotely. Their inherent vulnerability is rated Medium High, which reduces to medium after controls are applied.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, A. LIFE INSURANCE, A4 Pure protection products - 26274889ca44dfcd
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
These non-linked protection products are usually structured as regular premium contracts and have no investment element, which means there is no surrender or maturity value. This absence of an investment element reduces the inherent vulnerability to ML when compared with other life insurance products. The inherent vulnerability for pure protection products is assessed as medium, with the final vulnerability after control mitigation assessed as Medium Low.

A5 Regular premium savings (including unit-linked protection) Long-term insurance products require ongoing premium payments and often have an initial lock-in period with High charges, slightly lowering vulnerability. Surrender value later becomes important, and policy values are tied to a narrow range of funds. For unit-linked contracts, death benefits may depend on policy value or include fixed amounts as riders, with options for critical illness and hospitalisation benefits. These protections help reduce vulnerability. Overall, regular premium savings are considered Medium High in inherent vulnerability, reduced to medium after controls.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, A. LIFE INSURANCE, A6 Regular premium capital redemption bonds - 481499c1545ab985
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
A6 Regular premium capital redemption bonds
body: These contracts have a set redemption date and value, typically span 99 years, require recurring premiums, and are not linked to insured lives. Policy values track internal funds and surrender value affects vulnerability, which is rated Medium High before controls and medium after mitigation.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, B. NON-LIFE INSURANCE, B1 Captive insurance (self‑insured) - f069656b42b3355f

body: Captive insurers typically re-insure only group entities, mainly via authorised insurers on the IOM. Often, a captive insurer serves just one customer. Key vulnerabilities involve owner suitability and funding sources, with fraudulent claims also posing risks. Overall, the inherent and residual vulnerability for captive insurance is rated as Medium Low.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, B. NON-LIFE INSURANCE, B2 Commercial general insurance - d569715a6bde0604
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body: Commercial general insurance mainly covers businesses and groups, with most activity limited to the IOM and UK/British Isles. The sector is small and has lower risk of ML; both inherent and controlled vulnerabilities are rated Medium Low.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, B. NON-LIFE INSURANCE, B3 Insurance intermediation - bdbcb5ee064ac808
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
Intermediaries handling general insurance and pure protection products have low exposure to major risks, mostly serving local clients. These products are less prone to ML than some life insurance options. While premium refunds present minor vulnerabilities, these are addressed by AML measures; intermediary involvement in claim fraud remains possible but limited. Overall, both inherent and residual vulnerability in this sector is considered Low.

The assessment also undertook a detailed review of the AML controls in place for the Insurance sector. The assessment indicated that there continued to be no general AML control areas that require critical or urgent attention across the sector, although the sector assessment Highlights that insurers may continue to have potential gaps in prevention and detection of ML (transactions, screening, and changes in customer prole and behaviour), balancing manual intervention and reviews, with the use of technology in light of the pace of change in digital technologies.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, B. NON-LIFE INSURANCE, Recommended actions - 438ed9e534782407
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
Insurance is a mature and well-established financial services sector, contributing significantly to national income. The sector's strong track record in the IOM, experienced workforce, and comprehensive AML/CFT/CPF controls provide a solid foundation for managing ML risks. However, as global financial crime typologies evolve and new technologies emerge, the Insurance industry needs to remain alert and responsive to identify and mitigate risks.

Please see the Insurance sectoral report for a more detailed analysis of the sector for ML risks.

The Insurance Sector ML Risk Assessment identifies a small number of areas for improvement aligned to the strategic aims from the National Financial Crime Strategy 2024-2026. The actions are outlined in Chapter 13.

body:
As of 31 December 2025, there were 5 financial services licence-holders with Class 8 permissions. Of those 5 entities:

- 1 is a BDC;

- 1 undertakes payments services directly; and

- 3 are e-money issuers.

The Isle of Man Post Office also provides Class 8 activities, specifically BDC (Class 8(1)); MTS (Class 8(2)); and cheque cashing (Class 8(3)), which is limited to cashing cheques issued by the IOM Government in relation to benefit payments. IOMPO is exempted from having to hold a financial services licence; however, the FSA still retains powers over the Class 8 activity undertaken, including the power of inspection and being able to request and obtain information. The IOMPO is subject to the requirements of the AML/CFT Code in its entirety in relation to the aforementioned activities by virtue of being included within Schedule 4 of POCA. The IOMPO has not been included within this NRA.

All business in this sector is conducted face-to-face and mostly with residents of the IOM (98%) who are typically obtaining holiday currency. MONEY TRANSMISSION SERVICES: BUREAUX DE CHANGE

body:
Overall sector ML risk

- Threat: Medium High; Vulnerability: Medium; ML Risk Rating 2020: Medium; ML Risk Rating 2025: Medium

The overall assessment of payment services and electronic money activity in respect of ML risk is medium. While overall compliance with AML/CFT/CPF requirements appears strong (controls are rated as Medium High), the sector faces inherent risks due to its exposure to cross-border transactions, High-risk jurisdictions, and evolving payment technologies, resulting in a medium vulnerability rating. chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, MONEY TRANSMISSION SERVICES: AS PRINCIPAL AND E-MONEY, Background to the sector - fad56a2a6420b084
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
MONEY TRANSMISSION SERVICES: AS PRINCIPAL AND E-MONEY
body: The PSP/EMI sector is relatively nascent, with several entities only licensed within the last four years. Although the sector is small in terms of the numbers of firms and employees, it is growing rapidly, with many licence applications and enquiries. Recently, there has also been a significantly large increase in customer numbers within the sector due to the relocation of a firm within the sector to the IOM. The total number of customers in the sector is just under 2 million. It should be noted that many of these customers may hold a wallet but are not actively using the service. Further work is underway with the sector to consider how to segregate the customer numbers in this way to give a clear indication of active customers.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, MONEY TRANSMISSION SERVICES: AS PRINCIPAL AND E-MONEY, Threats - 798908a3187ac9af
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
MONEY TRANSMISSION SERVICES: AS PRINCIPAL AND E-MONEY
body:
As an IFC, the IOM's MTS sector primarily serves non-resident clients. This cross-border profile means that funds often originate outside the jurisdiction and related predicate offences typically occur overseas. The threat rating for the sector is Medium High; this is a product of the increasing threat landscape in the IOM (explained in earlier sections of this NRA) and the fact that this is a sector where the services of domestic or foreign firms could be used by persons/entities who wish to abuse the system to facilitate movements of illicit funds across borders.

It is, however, important to note that there are no recorded ML investigations or prosecutions featuring the sector. The FSA has not issued any civil penalties in respect of the licenceholders in this sector.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, MONEY TRANSMISSION SERVICES: AS PRINCIPAL AND E-MONEY, Vulnerabilities - 9247949ccc0c1ec4
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
MONEY TRANSMISSION SERVICES: AS PRINCIPAL AND E-MONEY
body:
Globally there has been rapid development and increased functionality of MTS products available on the market, particularly in relation to e-money. This has created challenges for countries and firms in ensuring these products are not misused for ML and other crimes.
Generally, several features of e-money and MTS - such as the simplicity and certainty of transactions, worldwide reach (in the case of e-money remitters), the cash character of transactions, and low-thresholds - could make them an attractive vehicle through which criminal and terrorist funds could enter the financial system and also undertake multiple transactions through the sector in order to layer funds with an illicit origin. This can be exacerbated with the speed at which a customer can register for and obtain an account, and the fact that the account can be established remotely by the customer and have a worldwide reach. It is therefore important that these firms have robust monitoring systems in place to help identify risks, akin to those used in banks. The firms must also hold client funds in segregated payment accounts with approved banks. However, at present financial flow data for the sector is not currently obtained by the FSA, which would be useful to further understand the activity in the sector and where funds are flowing to and from.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, MONEY TRANSMISSION SERVICES: AS PRINCIPAL AND E-MONEY, Vulnerabilities - 67153ac6d8f458c9
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
MONEY TRANSMISSION SERVICES: AS PRINCIPAL AND E-MONEY
body:
The sector may be used by both natural and nonnatural customers; it may also be used by those who are unable to directly access traditional banking services. The sector should take into account the rationale for and operation of the business relationship when customers apply for accounts. A mitigation in this area is that some firms within the sector require a credit card to fund the wallet.
Considering the activities taken by the MTS sector on the IOM, the licensed PSPs do not have an agent acting on their behalf, nor do agents of PSPs based in other jurisdictions operate in or from the IOM thereby potentially limiting the exposure in relation to those countries in which agents may be located.
The three EMIs are part of large groups which operate in the Latin American region, thereby potentially increasing the exposure of firms to risk of being vulnerable to ML, corruption, drug trafficking, and kidnapping. The groups are, however, very familiar with their customers and merchants, and therefore, relevant controls are integrated into these entities.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, MONEY TRANSMISSION SERVICES: AS PRINCIPAL AND E-MONEY, Vulnerabilities - 433dee3eb33f1187
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
MONEY TRANSMISSION SERVICES: AS PRINCIPAL AND E-MONEY
body: It is also important to note that the firms in the sector may use certain AML/CFT Code concessions in respect of lower-value transactions. This may increase the risk of MTS being vulnerable to ML, particularly where a product/ service comprises a number of smaller transactions. These concessions cannot be used in Higher-risk customer relationships and, where they are permitted, a number of conditions must be met. The use of concessions is something the FSA would examine during an inspection.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, MONEY TRANSMISSION SERVICES: AS PRINCIPAL AND E-MONEY, Key risks - fb2e7573d8c2a174
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
MONEY TRANSMISSION SERVICES: AS PRINCIPAL AND E-MONEY
body:
Perimeter risk: This is a relatively new business sector which attracts entrepreneurs with more of a technology background. Individuals may not be aware that the business is regulated and that a licence under the FSA08 is required. The FSA has identified cases of businesses undertaking or proposing to undertake PSP or EMI activities without the requisite licence, which have been addressed.
Technology risk: There is a risk, due to the relative infancy of the sector and the evolving technology, that new platforms and systems have not been properly tested and developed. Moreover, systems may not be designed to fully meet the AML/CFT/CPF control requirements in a jurisdiction.
Peer-to-peer payments risk: A Higher-risk activity offered by many PSPs is one whereby a customer may utilise their accounts for peer-to-peer transactions. Peer-to-peer transactions lend themselves to an enhanced ML risk because transfers can take place between multiple account-holders. This can happen very rapidly without funds ever moving through the segregated account held by the bank. The firm may not actually know who is ultimately undertaking the transaction. Frequently, transaction monitoring systems apply an element of trust to transactions within the system (particularly when the transactions are on their own platform) compared to payments coming in from an outside source, which are normally subject to a greater degree of scrutiny. Robust monitoring is needed in respect of peer-topeer transactions.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, MONEY TRANSMISSION SERVICES: AS PRINCIPAL AND E-MONEY, Key risks - 611c761019998e2c
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
MONEY TRANSMISSION SERVICES: AS PRINCIPAL AND E-MONEY
body: Virtual IBAN risk: Virtual International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs) allow customers to make payments in and out of an EMI's segregated account more directly than by utilising only cards or similar instruments. Because virtual IBANs do not hold balances in the same way as true IBANs, the risk of the bank's own transaction monitoring tools being unable to identify suspicious activity is heightened. It may result in difficulty in tracing the source and/or destination of funds, resulting in it being a method that could be used to facilitate financial crime. This can be a particular risk where a merchant is permitted to utilise a virtual IBAN. Due to these risks, there is a greater onus on the EMI's monitoring systems and controls to be sufficiently robust. The risks with virtual IBANs and those of peer-to-peer usage are similar.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, MONEY TRANSMISSION SERVICES: AS PRINCIPAL AND E-MONEY, Key risks - 067de3e551ddd5f1
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
MONEY TRANSMISSION SERVICES: AS PRINCIPAL AND E-MONEY
body:
Correspondent risk: Firms within the sector have found that obtaining pooled accounts (such as segregated accounts, client money accounts, and specified accounts) with banks has become increasingly difficult over the last several years. This has resulted in MTS licence applicants (and incumbents) seeking to establish segregated accounts with a limited number of institutions which are prepared to service this sector. These banks are mostly outside the IOM and typically have a Higher risk appetite. There is a risk should the bank holding the segregated accounts be frozen or fail due to regulatory failings or criminal prosecution. This would have a material impact on the IOM-based EMI itself, as it would be unable to redeem e-money issued.
Therefore, the vulnerability to ML for the sector has been assessed as Medium.
Figure 38: Top Ten Countries of PSP and EMI Customers (2024)
Consumers typically undertake lower-value and lower-volume transactions (typically less than USD $100 and fewer than 10 transactions per year). They will typically use their payment instruments for purchases on websites of merchants such as e-gaming service providers or purchases in a physical location via payment cards issued by the PSP/EMI. 73% of consumers are based in South America; the majority are rated as standard risk (60%), and there are a very small proportion of PEPs in the sector (0.02%).

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, PENSIONS, Overall Sector ML Risk - 490d2870a5407c51
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
- Threat: Low; Vulnerability: Medium

- ML Risk Rating 2020: Medium Low; ML Risk Rating 2020: Medium Low

Source: FSA

- Certain MTS Class 8 licenceholders (PSPs and EMIs) should provide quarterly financial flow information to the FSA. This was also identified in the TF NRA.

The overall assessment of ML risk for private Pensions is Medium Low. The overall risk level for this sector has stayed the same since 2020 NRA and reflects the low threat level assessment. It also reflects the fact that the features of typical pension products do not make it an attractive vehicle for ML. There are good AML controls for the sector which are rated as Medium High, however there are some legislative amendments required to the framework for the sector which has slightly increased the residual vulnerability (i.e. after considering mitigating controls) to Medium (from Medium Low in 2020).

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, PENSIONS, Background to the Sector - f04f049d0f5c5bd3
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
The private Pensions sector in the IOM is a wellestablished, well-regulated sector; if a private Pension is provided in or from the IOM it must be registered with the FSA as either an Authorised or Recognised scheme. In order to be authorised by the FSA the schemes must be established by way of irrevocable trust structures meeting the criteria set out within the Retirement Benefits Schemes Act 2000 ("RBSA"). Typically, the scheme is considered to be the customer of the Pension service provider.
The RBSA applies to all schemes operated in or from or offered to the residents of the IOM. Registered schemes are subdivided to cater for the needs of its members and will either be authorised as:

- Domestic schemes (primarily for habitually resident members in the IOM); or

- International schemes (for all other non-IOM resident individuals).
All schemes require the appointment of trustees who must be fit and proper to act in that capacity.
In addition to the trustee requirement, the RBSA imposes the requirement that each scheme (International or Domestic) must have an appointed a person in the IOM who is responsible for the management of the scheme (referred to in the RBSA as "the Administrator"). In order to act as administrator, it must be registered with the FSA and be a fit and proper person.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, PENSIONS, Background to the Sector - 346423ffd5296598
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
Administrators are registered as either 'Professional Schemes Administrators' (those providing pension scheme services by way of business) or 'In-House Schemes Administrators'. In-House Administrators only being registered where they act in respect of an individual domestic scheme (usually an occupational scheme). In-House Administrators do not act by way of business (and the last such registration was in 2012).
Schemes settled and operated outside of the IOM may be offered to local residents if they are recognised under the RBSA. There are only a limited number of Recognised Schemes (all of which are UK established occupational schemes).

body: Considering the threat of the sector, typically schemes are established as trusts which tend to see that funds difficult to access until certain criteria are met; for example, the member reaching a particular age; and therefore might be inaccessible for longer periods of time. Pensions do not generally offer the level of flexibility typically needed to be attractive for traditional ML purposes, however it is recognised that ML risks remain as the Pension scheme could be (partially) funded with proceeds of crime and/or be used to evade tax. There are no recorded ML investigations or prosecutions featuring the sector, nor has the FSA issued any civil penalties in respect of the licenceholders in this sector. chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, PENSIONS, Vulnerabilities - 1a00ffd2a42d921e
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body: The main ML vulnerabilities of IOM private Pension products tend to arise from personal schemes which may have complex underlying investment structures or taxation arrangements; these may be vulnerable to the disguise of the proceeds of fraud and/ or tax evasion. The use of a Pension scheme wouldn't typically be an attractive method by which to launder funds due to the typically long-term nature of these products. Cash would not typically be accepted for payment into a scheme; almost all contributions are through bank transfer. It should be noted that the sector generally has strong AML/CFT/CFP controls in place, albeit it has been identified the legislative framework does require some modernisation which is underway. Therefore, the vulnerability to ML for the sector has been assessed as Medium.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, SERVICES TO COLLECTIVE INVESTMENT SCHEMES, Background to the Sector - a56d64d0057a7f04
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
The provision of fund management and administration has long been a regulated activity on the IOM. Firms providing these services are licensed and supervised by the IOMFSA under the Financial Services Act 2008 (FSA08) (unless an exemption applies). A licence to carry on Class 3 activity permits firms to provide services to fund vehicles. It should be noted that, within the IOM, both the fund service provider and the IOM fund are independently subject to the provisions of the Isle of Man's AML/CFT Framework. This section of the NRA covers the following types of financial services activity which is licensable under the FSA08 :

- fund management/administration services; and

- the business of Isle of Man funds (collective investment schemes)
Licensed fund managers and administrators (and those with limited Class 3 permission) in the IOM provide services to a range of fund vehicles, both IOM funds (mostly non-retail), and overseas funds including valuation of assets and pricing of units; maintenance of the register of participants; issues, transfers and redemptions of units; accounting services and record keeping.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, SERVICES TO COLLECTIVE INVESTMENT SCHEMES, Background to the Sector - 4fe5a444b7b332cd
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
A significant portion, approximately 80% (by AUM), of the IOM's fund sector activity involves providing services to schemes domiciled outside the jurisdiction. These services are typically provided either directly to overseas schemes or to their managers and administrators. When an Isle of Man-based manager or administrator is appointed to an overseas scheme, it is generally indicative that the scheme operates within the professional or private investment space, and is not retail-facing.
Fund managers/administrators' customers are the funds themselves. Fund managers/administrators are responsible for assessing the ML risks associated with taking on funds as customers. This includes an understanding of not only the investor base but also considering what the fund is investing in, the fund structure, and the other functionaries providing services to the fund.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, SERVICES TO COLLECTIVE INVESTMENT SCHEMES, Background to the Sector - aecf11571ae291a9

body:
All funds established in the IOM under the Collective Investment Schemes Act 2008 are also "relevant persons" for the purpose of AML/CFT legislation; this means the AML/CFT Code also applies directly to IOM funds. In practice, the governing body of an IOM fund will delegate the majority (if not all) of AML/CFT matters to its functionaries (fund manager/administrator), but the governing body must understand and document what services the functionary is, and more importantly is not, providing in relation to the fund's obligations under the AML/CFT Code. This should be included as part of the functionary agreement between the fund and the Manager or Administrator.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, ACCOUNTING, TAX ADVISORS AND PAYROLL, Background to the Sector - 1819643c4bdd803a
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
The Accountancy services sector in the IOM consists of:

- External Accountants - who provide accountancy services to a third party,

- Tax Advisers - who give advice on a third party's tax affairs, and

- Payroll Agents - who are not the individual's employer but are involved with the payment of earnings to or for the benefit of, any individual.
Figure 45: Number of Accountancy Service Professionals (December 2025)
Source: FSA
For the purposes of this risk assessment as there are multiple crossovers between each category of registered person, the activities are generally assessed collectively, with any nuances being drawn out in the narrative below.
Those providing Accountancy services must register as a designated business with FSA under the DBROA and be subject to oversight in respect of compliance with the AML/CFT Code. The Accountancy services sector in the IOM ranges in size from sole practitioners to the offices of large international practices. The sector provides Accounting, Bookkeeping, Audit, Tax and Advisory services. Services, including advice on structures and the mitigation of tax liabilities, can be provided by Accountants and Tax Advisers but also by Legal Professionals and in-house experts in TCSPs. Where a Payroll Agent undertakes calculations relating to tax it should also be classed as a Tax Adviser.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, ACCOUNTING, TAX ADVISORS AND PAYROLL, Background to the Sector - 8eccbeb8e5a7ce55
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
External Accountants and Tax Advisers do not ordinarily handle customer funds, although they will have a good overview of the financial picture for their customer through the services provided, therefore it is imperative accountancy service providers remain vigilant in relation to customer activity recognising when something may be unusual or suspicious, reporting to the FIU, where appropriate.
Payroll Agents provide services for businesses including processing payroll calculations, collecting funds from an employer/ business, paying the net proceeds to the employee/contractor, ensuring accurate payroll tax and deductions, generating and distributing electronic payroll records and handling payroll compliance matters. There are no specific professional or technical qualifications required to work in the sector and no specific overall professional/industry body in the IOM. Payroll Agents play an important role in the transfer of funds, as these registered persons have an important role in the verification of the ultimate beneficiaries of any payroll distribution, which presents an opportunity for this sector to reduce exposure to financial crime in a critical part of the chain as it relates to the validation in the movement of funds.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, ACCOUNTING, TAX ADVISORS AND PAYROLL, Threats - a41465a9c39b329c
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
As an IFC, the IOM faces threats from both overseas and domestic criminal groups. The national threat landscape is explained elsewhere in this NRA. The use of the Accountancy Services sector by these criminal groups is possible and the IOM remains vigilant to the threats that organised criminal groups pose. There is the possible use of the Accountancy Services sector to provide (wittingly or unwittingly) seemingly legitimate services to criminal groups who seek to use the IOM to either hide the proceeds of criminal activity or to carry on illicit business.

Certain other activities performed by accountants are more susceptible to ML/TF including:

- Providing tax or other financial advice,

- Handling client assets,

- Formation of companies and trusts, and/or

- Company secretarial services.

It is important to note that there are no recent recorded ML investigations or prosecutions featuring the sector. However, the FSA has recently issued financial civil penalties in respect of some firms in this sector relating to identified areas of non-compliance with the AML/CFT Code. The assessed level of threat in this sector is Medium.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, ACCOUNTING, TAX ADVISORS AND PAYROLL, Vulnerabilities - 24c085877f9c9d94
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
Accountants and Tax Advisers can be used by potential money launderers in a number of ways, including:

- Providing an additional layer of professional legitimacy to criminal financial arrangements, especially where large sums may be involved and where accounts need to be audited locally.

- Use by organised crime groups to provide professional services that can be used to conceal or disguise criminal assets.

- Use by criminal groups as part of a suite of professional services (e.g. legal, accounting, company formation etc.) where the whole picture might not be visible to each adviser, this might be more applicable to a firm providing services internationally.

- By emerging sectors that require accountancy services (e.g., virtual assets, payment service providers) however the activity, and vulnerabilities of the sector may not be fully understood.

- By criminals being involved in the ownership of a firm. Payroll Agents can be used by potential money launderers in a number of ways, for example:

- Proceeds of crime paid to an employee or contractor by an employer, when the criminals are in fact both parties.

- The creation of 'ghost' employees by fraudsters using either real or fabricated personal details.

- Receipt of proceeds of crime, bribery or corruption.

- By criminals being involved in ownership of a firm.

body:
Overall Sector ML Risk

- Threat: Medium; Vulnerability: Medium Low; ML Risk Rating 2020: Medium; ML Risk Rating 2025: Medium Low

The FSA published a thematic review of the Accounting Profession (External Accountants, Tax Advisers and Payroll Agents) registered businesses in 2024 focusing on Customer Risk Assessments ("CRAs"). The thematic review has allowed the FSA to gather further data, assisting in risk assessing both the firms and sector itself, as well as building knowledge and findings to feed back into the AML/CFT Handbook and the AML/CFT/ CPF sector-specific guidance documents. The CRAs are vital to helping the firm understand and evidence the risks which their customers may pose to the business of the firm. CRAs allow firms to identify those customers with Higher-risk profiles, in order to apply appropriate procedures to prevent ML, as well as TF and PF. Detailed findings of the sector were included in the published report and firm-specific findings were provided in entity level reports. In addition, some firms in the sector were included in the Foreign PEP thematic review published in 2023 The findings of this review revealed some issues relating to CDD that resulted in enforcement action.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, ESTATE AGENTS, Recommended Actions - eda56dff0b7454e5
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
- Maintain the level of self-regulatory supervision being carried out by the Accountancy bodies including ongoing quality control checks by the FSA.

The overall assessment of the sector in respect of ML risk has decreased since the 2020 NRA and is assessed as Medium Low, driven by the fact the sector is small and highly domestic in nature and that the sector does not typically receive customer funds. There are also a number of other financial and nonfinancial professionals engaged in the property transactions (who are subject to the Island's AML/CFT/CPF Framework) and active supervision of the sector takes place.

In relation to the Estate Agency sector, there are some enhancements required to the legal framework, resulting in AML/CFT/CPF controls for the sector being rated as Medium.

This is a sector that does not handle large amounts of client money (rental funds may be handled by some Estate Agents but not sale proceeds). This, combined with the small sector and predominantly local customer base, therefore reduces vulnerability in respect of ML within the sector, resulting in a Medium Low vulnerability. The threat for the sector has been assessed as Medium.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, ESTATE AGENTS, Background to the Sector - 0981fd3819eec035
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
Estate Agents in the IOM are involved in the buying, selling, renting and property management of residential and commercial properties. The sector is small, consisting of mostly wellestablished firms with the majority of the work undertaken for IOM or UK customers. Purchase of property and land outside of the IOM is most often dealt with by the TCSP sector, via property agents in the UK and elsewhere.
The purchase and selling of land and property can be used to disguise the proceeds of crime and corruption, and this is a significant typology internationally. Real Estate is a relatively stable and safe investment which can be effective in generating returns on capital and it is therefore attractive to money launderers seeking to integrate or layer their assets.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, ESTATE AGENTS, Background to the Sector - bcb59adb682b5967
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
IOM Estate Agents are governed by the Estate Agent Act 1975, and it is the responsibility of the IOM's OFT to register each individual Estate Agent. Registration requires that an individual is a Fellow, Member or Associate of the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors ("RICS") or Fellow of the National Association of Estate Agents ("NAEA"). Furthermore, to establish an Estate Agency in the IOM a GBP£100,000 bond is required to be secured in addition to their professional institution obligations; currently such bonds are only available via one insurance company based on the IOM. The IOM is unique in its requirement for degree level professional qualifications and membership to practice since 1978. These additional professional obligations include redress schemes and professional conduct standards.
Estate Agents must also register as a designated business with the FSA under the DBROA. The activities of Estate Agents are designated under Schedule 4 to POCA 2008 as undertaking business in the regulated sector; as such they are required to comply with the AML/CFT Code and are supervised by the FSA in respect of compliance with AML/CFT/CPF requirements.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, ESTATE AGENTS, Background to the Sector - e2fd71b1ae6be6b6
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body: If a UK Estate Agent was to list an IOM property for sale this would fall outside the DNFBP regime and would rely on UK law. However, the involvement of other local professionals such as Advocates and other Financial Institutions in almost all cases would provide a level of AML assurance as they would have to comply with the IOM's AML/CFT/CPF Framework. Any ML offence would fall within the IOM's jurisdiction due to the location of the property. The OFT is responsible for ensuring that any non-IOM agents selling property within the IOM are notified of the requirements to register under the 1975 Act and DBROA as a designated business, or to undertake arrangements with a registered IOM agent.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, ESTATE AGENTS, Threats - 41dd967823e468c4
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
As an IFC, the IOM faces threats from overseas and domestic criminal groups. The use of the Real Estate sector by these criminal groups has been identified and Highlighted in recent international typologies, the IOM continues to remain vigilant to the threats that organised criminal groups pose. Recent international typologies have Highlighted the use of the IOM by organised criminal groups, some of which appear to involve the use of property to house illicit activities.

Real Estate offers both the opportunity to obtain premises from which criminals can operate, and also investment opportunities for the proceeds of criminal activity. These threats are present in the commercial and domestic markets and apply to sales and rentals. The threat of introducing criminal proceeds into the residential property sector is an internationally recognised typology that can be heightened by under or over-valuation and frequent sales/purchase of the same property. The assessed level of threat in the sector is Medium.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, ESTATE AGENTS, Vulnerabilities - 4f32d2d4ee146795
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
The Real Estate sector in the IOM consists of the purchase, sale and rental of commercial and residential property. The IOM has a stable Real Estate market, and the Government publishes and Annual Housing Market Review that details movement in prices and number of transactions.
The market is open to both domestic and overseas participants with no restrictions on ownership or rental thus the controls put in place by the sector are imperative to prevent the illicit use of property. This "open" market is potentially vulnerable to abuse from those seeking to integrate proceeds of criminal activity either domestically or internationally. Real Estate is a relatively stable and safe investment which can be effective in generating returns on capital and it is therefore attractive to money launderers seeking to integrate or layer their assets. Equally, lettings and property management can be used generate income or be used to provide premises for illicit activity. Letting also offers opportunities for a regular flow of payments to be made and received, which could be attractive to money launderers, particularly where cash is accepted.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, ESTATE AGENTS, Vulnerabilities - 8cbfce553b14bbac
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body: Most, if not all, sales are dealt with 'on the market' thus increasing transparency in terms of value and the parties involved. When acting for a seller of a property, IOM Estate Agents do not handle customer funds, however they do develop a more in-depth relationship with their customer in comparison to a bank or legal professional and may be aware of large amounts of cash being involved in a property sale or transaction. Estate Agents are therefore in a position to be able to identify unusual or suspicious behaviour and therefore file disclosures to the FIU, where appropriate. There is a risk however that Estate Agents may place an overreliance on the involvement of other supervised professionals (e.g. banks and legal professionals) as part of the transaction and assume that the responsibility for AML/CFT/CPF will be predominantly undertaken by the other parties who are in receipt of the funds. Informal "reliance" on CDD undertaken by other sectors is also a possibility. These identified vulnerabilities are mitigated by the fact that the majority of customers (circa 96%) are UK/IOM resident natural persons. Similarly, exposure to potentially Higher risk customer types, such as PEPs (0.3% of the customer base) are mitigated by the fact that 88% of those have UK/IOM nationality.
