In relation to the sale of Real Estate, as the AML/CFT Code stands currently, the Estate Agent's customer is the person selling the property. However, it is the expectation of the FSA, in line with international standards, for Estate Agents to identify and verify the identity of both the buyer as well as the seller in an arrangement. Therefore, the requirements of the AML/CFT Code such as risk assessment, customer due diligence (including source of funds), ongoing monitoring, record keeping etc. are expected to be applied to both parties. The AML/CFT Code will be updated in due course to reflect this position.

- Estate Agents generally act for IOM (76%) and UK (11%) resident customers which does reduce the risk of products and services being abused for ML. The vast majority of customers are also natural persons (88%).

- The incidence of non-face-to-face customer relationships remains very low (1.44%).

- Client money is not held by Estate Agents during sale or purchase.

- The use of cash in the sales/purchase sector is non-existent and infrequently used in the rental sector.

Software supply has grown into a material sector in its own right, with High cross-border B2B financial flows and vulnerabilities linked to opaque ownership structures and the use of virtual assets.
International cooperation is a key component of the GSC's supervisory approach. The GSC has established MoUs with foreign regulators, and a GSC staff member currently serves as co-lead of a FATF working group focused on casino-related risks.
Online gambling accounts for ~99% of deposits, with £762m deposited into online casinos in 2024. The sector currently supports 95 on-Island employees, but the economic value primarily arises from international online operations and B2B software supply. Licensed non-hosted software suppliers generated 62% of declared profit in 2024, surpassing online casinos (20%) and network services (18%).

body: The level of SARs received by the FIU remain low relative to the size of the sector and identified threats, though quality of the reports submitted is considered to be High. Whilst FIU reporting shows that online gambling was responsible for 50-67% of POCA disclosures over 2020-2023, 95% were received from a single reporting entity, with the majority of that 95% being dual-reported elsewhere. The entity in question held an Isle of Man Network Services Licence during this period and did not conduct player activity within the jurisdiction. The received reports largely relate to business to customer activity occurring externally to the Isle of Man, via internationally held gaming licences, with the decision to report being based solely on the physical location of staff and offices on the Isle of Man, not suspicious activity with an Isle of Man nexus or financial activity in the Isle of Man. Following updated legal advice, reporting in this manner has since ceased, with gaming representing only 30% of POCA SARs received in 2024. This figure is expected to reduce again for 2025.

This assessment of money laundering risk within the gambling sector Highlights a number of areas where further improvement is advisable. These findings are aligned with the strategic objectives outlined in the National Financial Crime Strategy for 2024-2026.

All the proposed actions are set out in detail in the Gambling Sectoral Report, and a number of key actions are included in the Recommended Actions in Chapter 13 below. By addressing these areas, the sector and the authorities can continue to strengthen the framework against financial crime and ensure a robust, resilient approach to managing risk.

Over the last five years the FSA has supervised no more than 3 HVGDs entities, with the last firm ceasing its registration in December 2023. Therefore, there are currently no registered HVGDs on the IOM. Proactively the FSA has collated information that indicates businesses on the IOM in sectors such as car dealers, jewellers and auctioneers would not accept large amounts of cash and would ask the customer to pay by card or bank transfer.

Based on this, and the fact there is an AML/CFT/CPF Framework already in place should a firm register with the FSA, there is limited ML risk identified in this sector at this time and the sector has been rated as Low.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, HIGH VALUE GOODS DEALERS ("HVGDS"), Background to the sector - ae254d9c92b8dc58
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
HVGDs are businesses that deal in goods and services of any description which involve total cash payments (one-off or linked transactions) which are equivalent in sterling to at least EUR€15,000. The term "total cash payment" is not defined in legislation, however the following instances should be considered:

- a single cash payment of EUR€15,000 or more;

- several cash payments totalling EUR€15,000 or more, including a series of payments and payments on account within a 90day period;

- cash payments totalling EUR€15,000 or more which appear to have been broken down into smaller amounts to potentially come below the threshold limit.

- cash paid by a customer totalling EUR€15,000 or more in any 90-day period;
Where the above occurs, the business is subject to the requirements of the AML/CFT Code and would also have to register with the FSA as a designated business under the DBROA.
The following businesses dealing in High value goods are present in the IOM:

- car and motor cycle dealerships,

- dealers in jewellery and precious metals,

- auctioneers and antique dealers, and

- art dealers.
Therefore, if these businesses were to accept total cash payments of at least EUR€15,000 (or equivalent sterling) they would be in-scope of the IOM's AML/CFT/CPF Framework.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, HIGH VALUE GOODS DEALERS ("HVGDS"), Vulnerabilities - 820aecb99a2e2892
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
High-value goods are appealing to criminals as they can be bought with criminal cash and can then be re-sold, either for profit or loss in exchange for clean funds. They can also be kept as a store of value, or, depending on the goods in question, used as status symbols. High-value payments for multiple lower value goods can also be used to launder criminal funds. These examples are well known global typologies.
Payments by cash or similar monetary instruments create a Higher risk for ML as there will be no clear audit trail and the origin of the funds is harder to trace. Transactions could also be purposefully split into linked transactions across the same, or different, entities within the sector to try to disguise the total amount of cash being spent.
The High-value goods themselves tend to be transportable, across international borders, internationally exchangeable and easy to trade anonymously. Gold is particularly attractive to money launderers because it has a High intrinsic value, is readily accepted across the world and can be melted down into many different forms which also makes it more transportable.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, LEGAL SERVICES, Background to the Sector - af6f7fef8ef64f50
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
The Legal sector in the IOM is made up of Advocates and Registered Legal Practitioners ("RLPs"). The Manx Bar is a fused profession meaning broadly that the roles of Solicitors and Barristers in England and Wales are combined; in order to practice law in the IOM, Legal Professionals have to pass the Manx Bar and complete a training period of up to two years with an IOM firm. Legal Professionals qualified to practice law in the IOM are advocates.
Given the very low numbers of RLPs operating in the IOM, this report focuses on the activities and vulnerabilities of Advocates. RLPs are briefly dealt with in a separate section within the NRA.
A sub-set of Advocates and RLPs must register with the FSA, under the DBROA and be subject to oversight in respect of compliance with the AML/CFT Code if certain activities are provided.

body:
Generally, the range of Legal services provided by Advocate firms includes: wills and probate work; criminal and civil litigation; family law; corporate and commercial work and conveyancing. Some Advocates may also undertake limited work in relation to trust and company formation and management. Unless this work is "incidental" to other legal work, they are required to obtain the relevant licence from the FSA. Some have separated out TCSP activities from the law firm into TCSP licenceholders.
Some firms predominantly focus on international business whereas others will primarily undertake domestic business. The nature of the services offered results in a number of customers engaging with the sector for one-off transactions; for example, the preparation and execution of a will is a finite instruction, as is a conveyancing transaction. However, such transactions may then lead to the establishment of a long-term relationship, whereby the firm will become very familiar with its customer and their arrangements. Approximately 80% of designated business activity undertaken by Advocates is domestic conveyancing, which involves handling client money, such money being the proceeds of a sale/purchase of Real Estate.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, LEGAL SERVICES, Threats - 959fc19621ac2b56
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
As an IFC, the IOM faces threats from overseas and domestic criminal groups. The national threat landscape is explained elsewhere in this NRA. The use of the Legal sector by these criminal groups is theoretically possible and the IOM remains vigilant to the threats that organised criminal groups pose. The possible use of the Legal sector to provide (wittingly or unwittingly) seemingly legitimate services to criminal groups who seek to use the IOM to either hide the proceeds of criminal activity or to carry on illicit business, for example via the purchase or sale of Real Estate, remains a concern. The formation, use and management of trusts or companies is examined in the TCSP Sectoral Risk Assessment.

It is important to note that there are no recent recorded ML investigations or prosecutions featuring the sector. Also, the FSA has not issued any civil penalties in respect of the firms in this sector. The assessed level of threat is Medium.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, LEGAL SERVICES, Vulnerabilities - 6c25357b526a054a
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body: Global typologies suggest that the Legal sector can be misused to provide a layer of "legitimacy" to transactions, especially in relation to the use of client accounts as it may enable criminals to either place money within the financial system and/or use the money as part of their layering activity, with fewer questions being asked by Banks and other financial institutions because of the perceived respectability and legitimacy added by the involvement of a Legal Professional. The strict client account rules imposed by the Isle of Man Law Society ("the Law Society") suggests that this is less of an issue on the IOM.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, LEGAL SERVICES, Vulnerabilities - 71188a22f7ffc46c
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
The use of Legal Professionals to facilitate the disguise of criminal proceeds in conveyancing transactions is mitigated in the IOM as the conveyancing process and the receipt and transfer of funds each go through a comprehensive process, which slows the transaction down, making it less attractive to criminals. In addition, all sales and purchases in the IOM must be registered. This mitigant could be further improved by consideration being given to giving the Land Registry powers/duties to monitor the Advocates' registering of sales/purchases, to Highlight the fact that a customer or related customers may be selling/purchasing multiple properties using multiple firms, as an Advocate would not have visibility on what another Advocate or firm are dealing with on behalf of that customer. In addition, it is important to note that where there are other financial institutions or designated business involved in a transaction those entities are also subject to the requirements of the AML/CFT Code and
supervised for the same.
The use of multiple legal structures that might be seen as "complex" are not unusual in the IOM, and are always subject to robust CDD and are subject to EDD if appropriate and rejected if the information provided is not clear. In addition, this is a niche area that some advocates specialise in. Nonetheless, it is important to highlight this as a potential vulnerability relevant to the sector.

body:
The identified vulnerabilities are further mitigated by the fact that the majority of customers (95%) are UK/IOM resident natural persons; this may reduce the potential risk of products and services being abused for ML as reliable CDD information is easier to source and update. Also, the use of introducers is decreasing within the sector.

The UK is the nearest comparable sectoral jurisdiction to the IOM, and London firms in particular provide a significant source of work for Advocates. The threats and vulnerabilities faced by UK Lawyers and Solicitors are therefore considered to be relevant to the IOM assessment, with the Highest inherent vulnerability being the extent and value of the work provided to High-net-worth clients, some of whom may also be PEPs. However, the IOM's exposure to potentially Higher risk customer types (including PEPs) is mitigated by the strong controls the IOM has in this area, and the fact that less than (circa 2% in 2024) of the IOM's Legal Professionals' customer base are PEPs. The use of non-face-to face transactions is low (circa 11% in 2024) and the use of cash might in theory be used to settle professional fees (for customers that do not use electronic banking), but cash acceptance is very rare.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, LEGAL SERVICES, Supervision - 2ff0ba5dffc1a672
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
Legal Professionals undertaking specified activities must register with the FSA under the DBROA. However, the FSA has delegated its oversight in respect of such person's AML/CFT/ CPF compliance to the Law Society, therefore the law firm may elect to be supervised by the FSA. Notwithstanding this, the option to be supervised by the FSA remains, and should a Legal Professional require enhanced supervision, or be subject to enforcement proceedings, oversight of such person would revert to the FSA. The Law Society and the FSA have a close working relationship and there is an active inspection programme. 78% of Legal Professionals are supervised by the Law Society and 22% are supervised by the FSA.
The Law Society has a compliance team which provides support and advice; oversees inspections and testing; and provides copies of all inspection reports to the FSA. The FSA will accompany the Law Society on a number of inspections each year for quality control purposes as per the delegation agreement in place. In addition, the FSA holds regular meetings with the compliance team of the Law Society to discuss the risk ratings of firms; inspection findings; and trends within the sector. The FSA retains its power to inspect those firms overseen by the Law Society as required. Where, during an inspection carried out by the Law Society, material contraventions of the relevant AML/CFT/CPF legislation are found, these are referred to the FSA for further consideration and action.

body:
The level of knowledge and awareness of ML risk is generally High amongst Advocates. Thus far the Law Society has conducted inspections of all of the Advocate firms undertaking designated business activity which it oversees. Compliance levels have been found to be generally strong, although the sector acknowledges that sourcing qualified and experienced staff can be a challenge in the current job market and an additional regulatory/compliance financial burden.
Legal Professional privilege does not negate the obligations placed on Advocates to comply with the IOM's AML/CFT/CPF legal framework or impede their ability to submit SARs to the FIU.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, LEGAL SERVICES, Recommended Actions - a35537f34c5fe2a4
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
Although the Legal Sector remains stable and the AML risk is and continues to be Medium, there are certain actions that should be taken to improve the sector's response the threats and vulnerabilities posed to the sector. These can be summarised as follows:

- It was noted by the members of the working group that the POCA should be reviewed and updated. Further, there is a potential need for the Legal sector sector-specific guidance to be enhanced to better explain what 'regulated business' means in respect of Legal Professionals.

- Maintain the level of self-regulatory supervision being carried out by the Law Society, including ongoing quality control checks by the FSA.

- Consideration being given to giving the Land Registry powers/ duties to monitor the Advocates registering of sales/purchases, to act as a further check and balance to Highlight if a client or related clients are selling/purchasing multiple properties using multiple firms, as an individual Advocate or even firm would not have visibility on what another Advocate or firm are dealing with on behalf of a specific client, but the Land Registry would see the full picture.

body:
There are 6 RLP firms in the IOM registered under the DBROA, half of this cohort have been subject to a supervisory inspection in recent years. RLPs provide Legal services but are not qualified to advise on areas of IOM Law and do not have a right of audience before the IOM's Courts. As RLPs cannot undertake conveyancing, they do not hold client money. They predominantly conduct work for HNWI's and overseas clients, but services are confined to lower risk activities.

A full risk assessment of this sector has not been conducted at this time, as there is not sufficient data to put the sector through the World Bank Model.

- Threat: Medium Low; Vulnerability: Medium; ML Risk Rating 2020: Medium Low; ML Risk Rating 2025: Medium Low

The overall assessment of the sector in respect of ML risk has remained the same since the 2020 NRA and is assessed as Medium Low. Common inherent risks faced by the sector in relation to ML include early repayments of loans using criminal proceeds, creating a facade of legitimate income, fast re-payment of a loan and quickly taking out another loan to launder the proceeds of crime. Consideration of these factors results in a Medium vulnerability rating to ML. The threat rating for the sector has been assessed as Medium Low.

Overall, within the sector, compliance with AML/CFT/CPF requirements is good and controls are rated as Medium. Although there are a significant number of registered Moneylenders in the IOM, the volume and level of transactions dealt with are low compared to many other sectors. The majority of customers are domestic with a sizeable proportion known to the lenders and met face-to-face.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, MONEYLENDING, Background to the Sector - 997186dbd23c469b
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
Moneylending is essentially the provision of credit to individuals or businesses with the expectation of repayment, often with interest. In the IOM the activity of moneylending specifically includes:

- The activity of Moneylending which is defined as: consumer credit; mortgage credit; factoring; and the financing of commercial transactions,

- A business which provides financial leasing arrangements in respect of products other than consumer products for and on behalf of customers, and

- A business which provides financial guarantees and commitments in respect of products other than consumer products for and on behalf of customers.

Moneylenders are covered by the Moneylenders Act 1991; anyone other than a Bank or other exempt organisation who runs a business of lending money in the IOM must be registered with the OFT as must anyone who collects money on behalf of a lender.

Those providing moneylending, financial leasing and financial guarantees must also register as a designated business with the FSA under the DBROA and be subject to oversight in respect of compliance with the AML/CFT Code.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, MONEYLENDING, Threats - f04d8c9142793ebe
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body: As an IFC, the IOM faces threats from both overseas and domestic criminal groups. The national threat landscape is explained elsewhere in this NRA. There is heightened exposure from foreign predicate offences, including fraud, bribery, corruption, and tax evasion with loan products vulnerable during the layering and integration stages. In the IOM, lending products may be misused to introduce illicit funds into the financial system via loan repayments funded from criminal proceeds. They could also be used to disguise beneficial ownership, particularly where corporate borrowers, nominee arrangements, or offshore structures are involved. Further, lending products could facilitate cross-border movement of value through loan disbursements, inter-company lending, or complex financing arrangements typical of IFC settings. It is important to note that there have been no recent recorded ML investigations or prosecutions featuring the sector. The assessed level of threat in this sector is Medium Low.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, MONEYLENDING, Vulnerabilities - 37ac7ba6f95dc342
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
Moneylending may present different vulnerabilities, the most common being where a loan is drawn down from the lender and then repaid with the proceeds of crime, possibly in cash, either very quickly after or in a short repayment period. This allows for the exchange of criminal proceeds with clean money from the loan provider and provides the criminal with documented evidence of a seemingly legitimate source of funds. However, where it is a cash repayment it can be more difficult to verify the source of the cash.

Early repayments carry a risk that the funds have emanated from a criminal lifestyle. This is likely to be more of a risk for smaller loans, in respect of larger loans (e.g. corporate lending) there would typically be more paperwork and documentation. Similarly, early repayment of loans followed by the taking out of another loan soon afterwards is also a recognised ML typology, as is the overpayment of loans and requesting reimbursement. The overall sector ML vulnerability has been assessed as Medium, which reflects some inherent vulnerabilities prevalent in the services identified above.

There are a number of mitigants to some of the aforementioned vulnerabilities when considering the customer base. Those operating in the Moneylending sector generally act for IOM (79%) or UK (20%) resident customers which may reduce the risk of products and services being abused for ML as reliable CDD information is more accessible with nearly 90% of business being conducted on a face-to-face basis. Overall numbers of PEPs are low (less than 1%) and 96% of PEPs present within the customer base are IOM resident. Considering risk ratings of customers, 0.36% are rated as Higher risk, 93% as lower and 6% as standard risk. The acceptance of cash was also considered, specifically due to the risk of repayment of cash, 89% of firms do not accept cash.

Since the previous NRA, the sector has been subject to targeted supervision from the FSA as part of a Moneylending thematic in 2024, which has taken place in parallel to any risk-based cycle of engagement relating to firms in the sector. The thematic review combined both information gathering through a sector specific questionnaire and inspections work, which allowed the FSA to gather further data, assisting in risk assessing both the firms and sector itself, as well as building knowledge and findings to feed back into the AML/CFT Handbook and the AML/CFT/CPF sector-specific guidance documents.

Source: FSA

This thematic focused on how firms had met their obligations in relation to CDD requirements, EDD requirements and also source of funds and wealth requirements. 20 Moneylenders were subject to inspections and the overall findings in relation to these areas of the Code were generally positive. Detailed findings of the sector were included in the published report and firmspecific findings were provided in entity level reports.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, NON-PROFIT ORGANISATIONS ("NPOS"), Background to the Sector - 6d2222d243f1fe08
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body: The IOM's Non-Profit sector consists of a range of organisations dedicated to charitable, religious, cultural, educational, and social purposes. There are a limited number of active entities and financial throughput is relatively modest. The sector is subject to appropriate oversight via the AGC in all cases and the FSA for a small number of Specified Non-Profit Organisations ("SNPOs") regarding AML, CFT and CPF. A recently published NPO TF NRA provides greater detail on the sector.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, NON-PROFIT ORGANISATIONS ("NPOS"), Size and Materiality - 48b12d76a55fc4c0
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
As of July 2024, there were 624 active NPOs in the IOM that met the FATF definition. The sector is relatively small, both by the number of organisations and the volume of funds handled. Most NPOs are registered charities overseen by the AGC and listed on the public Charity Register.
The majority of NPOs operate locally, with only a small fraction involved in international activities or Higher-risk jurisdictions. Most are small in terms of annual turnover, with 62% reporting less than GBP £25,000 per year.
The AG is the regulator for all registered charities in the IOM. (The scope of NPOs that fall within the FATF definition almost entirely coincides with the population of registered charities). Acknowledging the various risk factors within the NPO sector, the IOM Authorities have established a two-tier, risk-based oversight framework for NPOs. At a broad level, all NPOs registered as a charity are overseen by the AGC, ensuring transparency, financial accountability, and sound governance across the sector. The second-level oversight (above that provided by the AG) is conducted by the FSA with regard to SNPOs, which, following the determination in 2019, were identified as a Higher-risk category based on specific criteria, and thus subject to AML/CFT/CPF oversight.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, NON-PROFIT ORGANISATIONS ("NPOS"), Size and Materiality - d7aa5655c233a8ce
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
The DBROA requires businesses and professions carrying out activities that fall under the definition of a 'designated business' to register with the FSA; Schedule 1 includes SNPOs. SNPOs are also defined in Schedule 4 of the POCA. The SNPO population provides the FSA with data for the AML/CFT annual return. This covers a smaller number of areas than for regulated entities and includes training, showing the staff training topics undertaken in the year.
During the reporting period 2020 to 2024, there has been one AML inspection of an SNPO as part of the FSA's risk-based supervisory plan. In addition to this, each of the registered SNPOs has undergone an AML/CFT compliance business meeting with the FSA between 2023 and 2025.
The principal Act providing for the registration and regulation of charities is the Charities Registration and Regulation Act 2019 ("Charities Act"). It creates a public register and provides the AGC with powers to inquire into Charities and their management and administration, and to act for the protection of Charities. In order to be a Charity, the organisation needs to benefit the public. Charitable purposes are defined in Section 6 of the Charities Act.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, NON-PROFIT ORGANISATIONS ("NPOS"), Threats - 4d77e8ef816fe61e
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
The main ML threats faced by IOM NPOs include:

- Diversion of funds at the point of delivery, especially when operating in conflict or High-risk zones, where resources may be misappropriated for illicit purposes.

- Establishment of sham or front organisations, set up as fake charities to disguise illicit fundraising and ML activities.

Figure 1 shows the split by gross income, as measured by the requirements for annual accounts that have to be submitted to the AGC, for those with a domestic (IOM only) focus in raising and disbursing funds, and those that have some exposure to other countries, with the UK being the largest. This Highlights the small, domestic nature of the sector, and hence the low threat that the sector carries for money laundering.

Source: FSA

- Cash dependency and challenges accessing banking services, which can drive untraceable financial flows and create monitoring gaps.

While there are no recorded cases of NPOs in the IOM being prosecuted for ML, cases have occurred of fraud and misleading representation; such cases Highlight how weak oversight can facilitate misappropriation of funds. The threat rating for this sector is Low.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, NON-PROFIT ORGANISATIONS ("NPOS"), Vulnerabilities - c5217ac6b238dc66
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
Several vulnerabilities could exist within the sector:

- Weak governance and internal controls, especially among small or under-resourced NPOs, which may lack robust financial oversight, proper staff vetting, and detailed record-keeping.

- Reliance on cash due to Banking de-risking or lack of access to formal financial systems, increasing exposure to untraceable financial movements.

- P otential for misuse by insiders or intermediaries where oversight is insufficient.

- Complex international operations can make it difficult to monitor the end use of funds, particularly in High-risk jurisdictions.

Therefore, the overall sector ML vulnerability has been assessed as Medium.

body: The money laundering risk for the TCSP sector is assessed as Medium-High. The risk continues to be driven by the High threats facing the sector relating to a large international client base, widespread use of complex and multi-jurisdictional arrangements, exposure to foreign PEPs, and the provision of services to Higher-risk customers and jurisdictions. chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, TRUST AND CORPORATE SERVICES PROVIDERS ("TCSPS"), Background to the Sector - 93b724cd96b163e1
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
The TCSP sector is a significant part of the Isle of Man economy and is fully regulated by FSA (as a FI rather than a Designated Business); regulation is not limited to compliance only with AML/ CFT/CFP requirements but also extends to prudential matters and conduct of business.

TCSPs have a crucial role in attracting international business but are also important gatekeepers of the financial system. TCSPs provide the formation, administration, and management of legal persons and arrangements, including companies, trusts, and foundations, acting as vital gatekeepers to the Island's financial system. The FSA licenses only TCSPs which offer a full range of regulated services, including provision of directors and/or trustees, as opposed to purely acting as company formation agents. The sector has undergone consolidation in recent years, including increased private-equity ownership, and continues to operate with a Highly international footprint. Strong links with jurisdictions such as the UK, United States, South Africa, and Ireland contribute the sector's exposure to cross-border ML threats.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, TRUST AND CORPORATE SERVICES PROVIDERS ("TCSPS"), Size and Materiality - 5033f29b60973834
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body: As at 31 December 2025, 91 licensed firms operated within the TCSP sector, employing an estimated 2,000 staff members individuals and contributing 3% to national income. Assets under administration were estimated at £67 billion (2024). TCSPs provide services to approximately 17,000 companies (with around 80% incorporated locally) and over 10,700 trusts. Consistent with the Island's IFC profile, the majority of customers are non-resident, with concentrations linked to the UK and other overseas jurisdictions. The scale and international nature of the sector position it among the Higher-risk areas within the Island's financial services framework.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, TRUST AND CORPORATE SERVICES PROVIDERS ("TCSPS"), Threats - eab40742734a6933
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
The overall threat level facing the sector is assessed as High. TCSPs may be used to facilitate international layering and complex structuring linked to fraud, theft, tax evasion, bribery and corruption, and organised crime. Cross-sectoral threats are also relevant such as the growth of cross-border business servicing non-resident customers. There is also increasing exposure to technology-related risks (including emerging AI-enabled threats and developing alternative payment methods).

- increasing exposure to technology-related risks (including emerging AI-enabled threats)

SAR reporting by TCSPs remains consistent and of improving quality, with clear narratives and strong use of legislative references. Over 60% of SARs provide intelligence that is disseminated either domestically or internationally. The main predicate suspicions relate to tax offences, fraud, and corruption, mirroring the sector's international exposure profile. TCSPs remain one of the most referenced sectors in mutual legal assistance requests after banking.

The sector's overall ML vulnerability is assessed as medium-High Key inherent vulnerability drivers include:

- the scale and value of business undertaken

- provision of registered agent / office business as a limited service

- international and non-face-to-face delivery models

- the involvement of introducers (including those based in higher-risk jurisdictions)

- the prevalence of multi-jurisdictional and complex or seemingly complex structures

- complexity of international sanctions regimes

- customer profiles involving potentially higher risk customers such as foreign PEPs, CEPs and a concentration of non-natural persons

Generally in the sector, customers are assessed as posing a Higher inherent risk than in other sectors, which, to some extent, reflects the IOM business model. - Fully managed companies and trust boards These form the core of the sector's service offering with most relationships structured in this way. This service is generally considered to present lower inherent vulnerability, given the High degree of control and ongoing oversight by TCSPs.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, TRUST AND CORPORATE SERVICES PROVIDERS ("TCSPS"), AML/CFT/CPF Controls - c7c46650cbd2cc67
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
The sector benefits from a comprehensive legal and regulatory framework, with mostly High scores relating to effectiveness of supervision, use of administrative sanctions, and BO information availability. CDD and Beneficial Ownership requirements are well-embedded within the sector, and access to the Island's BO register has strengthened data accuracy and timeliness. Generally, progress has been observed in regard to TCSPs strengthening their controls.

The sector continues to face a number of challenges which are not uncommon to other sectors, including resource pressures for experienced compliance staff, which can impact the ability of firms to maintain robust oversight in relation to AML/CFT/CPF matters. There is also variability in the use of independent audits, resulting in differing levels of assurance across organisations. Ensuring alignment between the expectations of TCSPs and banks regarding customer information remains an area where further exploration is required. The sector must also manage emerging risks associated with technology advancements and evolving complexity of sanctions, which require ongoing adaptation and vigilance to safeguard against financial crime.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, SAFE CUSTODY, Threat - 38db59dc6b7eae0d
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
Over the last five years, the FSA has supervised no more than 5 entities that solely provide Safe Custody services. The 2020 ML/TF NRA assessed elements of Safe Custody within broader regulated sectors (primarily Banking and TCSP services). Risks Highlighted included potential misuse of Safe Custody boxes for placement or storage of physical assets linked to foreign predicate offences, consistent with the IOM's broader exposure to international ML threats. The threat rating for this sector is Low.

The risks in this sector remain similar to 2020, although there could be exposure to foreign criminality, and potential for concealment this is offset by the fact it is a very small sector with robust supervision and limited evidence of misuse therefore this sector has been rated as posing a low risk of ML, of which there is no change to the 2020 NRA risk rating.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, SAFE CUSTODY, Background to the Sector - c40be4cdc02d141f
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
In the IOM, "Safe Custody" is defined as a business that it is providing safe custody facilities for cash or liquid securities, deposit boxes or other secure storage facilities suitable for High-value physical items or assets, jewelry, precious metals, stones, bullion or documents of title. The IOM's Safe Custody sector is small and specialised, primarily comprising providers that secure storage and transportation for Highvalue physical assets (e.g. documents of title, precious metals, jewelry).

The service is typically offered by regulated financial institutions or licensed TCSPs who offer this under their existing license permissions where applicable. There may however be firms who offer this as a sole service, and such firms must register with the FSA as a designated business under the DBROA and would be subject to the requirements of the AML/ CFT Code.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, SAFE CUSTODY, Size and Materiality - 59281f7589b7c6cc
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
As of December 2025, there are 4 firms registered in this sector with approximately 1200 customers across these firms.

Considering the threats in the sector, the greatest ML threat arises not from domestic crime (which remains Low), but from foreign criminality involving High value portable assets, which may be stored in Safe Custody to obscure their origin. Crossborder movement of assets may use Safe Custody as a temporary placement or layering mechanism. There have not been any ML investigations in the period, nor has there been any supervisory action taken by the FSA in this sector.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, SAFE CUSTODY, Vulnerabilities - 7fedd7d7c9e7461b
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
Safe Custody could be used to store High-value goods (further information is provided in this NRA in relation to HVGDs) as part of an approach to obscure their origin, the following vulnerabilities should be considered by the sector:

- Nature of Assets - High value, easily portable assets could be stored to conceal beneficial ownership.

- Crossborder Client Base - International clients may present elevated ML risk from Higher corruption jurisdictions for example.

- Limited Transparency - Firms do not inspect box contents, reducing visibility unless compelled legally for example, by Competent Authorities.

- Temporary Storage During Layering - Offshore storage of documentation or bearer instruments is a known global typology.

The above factors are examples which highlight why it is imperative that firms in this sector closely monitor customer behavior and activity. Although these vulnerabilities have been identified the IOM benefits from strong mitigants such as:

- A comprehensive AML/CFT/CPF regulatory framework.

- Strong supervisory culture;

- In-person access reducing anonymity with 90% of customers met face to face;

- Low domestic crime; and coordinated intelligence structures.

Therefore, the overall sector ML vulnerability has been assessed as Medium.

headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
VIRTUAL ASSETS ("VA") AND VIRTUAL ASSET SERVICE PROVIDERS ("VASPS")
body:
- Threat: Medium High; Vulnerability: Medium; ML Risk Rating 2020: Medium High; ML Risk Rating 2025: Medium
As part of the 2026 NRA, a standalone NRA assessing the risk of both the exposure of VAs (as a product) and VASPs (as a sector) has been developed using the revised World Bank methodology specifically tailored to VA and VASPs. This incorporates improved data, new threat intelligence, and considers the enhanced supervisory methodology implemented by the FSA.
The overall ML risk for both the exposure to VAs and the VASP sector has been assessed as Medium, which has decreased from Medium High since the last NRA in 2020. PF and TF risks are assessed as very low. It is important to note that since the previous assessment there are fewer active VASPs in the Island. The threat environment has however become more complex in recent years resulting in a Medium High threat level. Supervisory enhancements, a deeper understanding of sectoral risk by Competent Authorities, introduction of the "Travel Rule" and increased industry knowledge and awareness have helped mitigate the overall risks. Additional improvements in law enforcement capability, data collection, and blockchain analytics capacity are underway, helping to strengthen the Island's response to evolving VA risks.

VIRTUAL ASSETS ("VA") AND VIRTUAL ASSET SERVICE PROVIDERS ("VASPS")
body: The risk is mostly driven by international threat exposure including cyber enabled fraud such as investment/romance scams and money laundering linked to illicit gambling or the purchase (in both international and domestic cases) of illicit goods including drugs using VAs. The sector's international, and often non face-to-face, operating model, combined with the complexity and speed of transactions, creates opportunities for misuse by individuals seeking to conceal the proceeds of crime. Also, most Isle of Man VASPs use brokerage or OTC models, which do carry some Higher inherent risks than centralised exchange platforms.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, VIRTUAL ASSETS ("VA") AND VIRTUAL ASSET SERVICE PROVIDERS ("VASPS"), Background to the Sector - 81eae8b5e9938cff
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
VIRTUAL ASSETS ("VA") AND VIRTUAL ASSET SERVICE PROVIDERS ("VASPS")
body:
Undertaking VASP activity in the IOM has been classed as a designated business since 2018. VASPs must therefore register with the FSA under the DBROA. The activities of VASPs are included within Schedule 4 to POCA 2008 as business in the regulated sector; as such they are required to comply with the AML/CFT Code and are supervised by the FSA in respect of compliance with AML/CFT/CPF requirements. The definitions of both "VA" and "VASP" mirror those included in the FATF standards.

Supervision of VASPs in the IOM aligns closely with FATF Standards and includes a robust registration process, fit and proper checks, the application of comprehensive AML/CFT/CPF standards, and compliance with the "Travel Rule" Code. The main services offered by VASPs in the IOM include custody and administration of VAs, exchange of VAs for other VAs and exchange of VAs for fiat and receive or transmit orders for VAs.

The are no global exchanges registered in the IOM. The registered firms operate a broker/dealer or over the counter (OTC) type model, using proprietary capital to execute bilateral trades with customers, and liquidity providers, focusing on the exchange of VAs to fiat, and vice versa. Services offered also include facilitating the acceptance of VAs and a means of payment for goods and services. One VASP reported to offer loans in fiat currency backed by Bitcoin as collateral.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, VIRTUAL ASSETS ("VA") AND VIRTUAL ASSET SERVICE PROVIDERS ("VASPS"), Materiality and Size - 1436279108a47343
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
VIRTUAL ASSETS ("VA") AND VIRTUAL ASSET SERVICE PROVIDERS ("VASPS")
body: The IOM's VASP sector is relatively small in size but plays an important role within the Island's digital and finance services landscape. As at December 2025 there were 19 VASPs registered under the DBRO Act, of which 4 are currently active. These entities primarily offer brokerage or OTC services, and none operate as global exchanges. The sector serves roughly 46,000 customers, of whom around 83% are non-resident and predominantly UK-based, reflecting the Island's broader international profile. Other countries where customers are resident include Australia, Italy and France. This international footprint heightens exposure to foreign predicate crime and cross-border laundering risks.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, VIRTUAL ASSETS ("VA") AND VIRTUAL ASSET SERVICE PROVIDERS ("VASPS"), Threats - 9aa641a20833dbe6
headers: 12. ML Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
VIRTUAL ASSETS ("VA") AND VIRTUAL ASSET SERVICE PROVIDERS ("VASPS")
body:
The overall ML threat to the use of VAs and the VASP sector is assessed as Medium High, reflecting the emerging risks driven by international and cyber-enabled criminality. Law enforcement data indicates a concentration of threats in areas such as cyber-enabled fraud including romance and investment scams, ransomware, payment for illicit products/services via VAs and the use of e.g. Bitcoin and stablecoins for layering, and exploitation of un-hosted wallets. These patterns broadly mirror typologies observed in other jurisdictions and Highlighted by FATF, INTERPOL, and blockchain analytics providers.

Most SARs filed by VASPs under POCA relate to international fraud typologies, with strong links to the UK. The number of VASP-submitted SARs has remained consistent over the period 2020-2025 with 80 received in 2025 (7.91% of the overall SARs submitted that year). Domestic offending exists but remains limited, mainly linked to drugs. Investigations cases involving VA and VASPs are primarily linked to organised crime groups and cyber-enabled fraud and are characterised by rapid international flows.

Indirect exposure to other sectors largely concerns online gambling. Operators using permitted VA models (convert-to-fiat prior to play) typically observe lower inherent exposure, with stablecoins forming the primary asset type. Banking, insurance and DNFBPs have very limited exposure, TCSPs maintain client relationships with VASPs and continue to play a role in corporate structuring.

body:
The recommendations identified below Highlight areas where delivering improvements will help to address threats and residual vulnerabilities identified during the ML NRA process. The list does not include all of the recommendations which have been made in other parts of the IOM NRA which have been published, for example the TF and LPA NRAs. However, where recommendations have been made in those reports which have a significant bearing on AML measures and are referred in this report, a reference has been made.
Where recommendations have been made in respect of the AML framework for FIs and DNFBPs (see Chapter 12) and are repeated across a number of sectors, these are summarised below. Sector specific recommendations are included.
Recommended actions across all parts of the NRA are being captured as part of a programme to develop a national action plan (NAP).
Strategic aim: Public sector and industry work together to achieve a common goal of meeting international standards Review new AML/CFT/CPF governance arrangements by April 2026 to ensure their completeness and effectiveness. Introduce outstanding MOUs and Codes of Practice (in particular, in relation to effective information-sharing among border law enforcement agencies).

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 14. How this NRA Should be Used - 401aaa4e3239b28a
headers: 14. How this NRA Should be Used
body:
In keeping with the objectives of the NRA, relevant persons on the IOM must comply with the IOM AML/CFT Code in having regard to relevant risk factors as part of their assessment of any ML risk exposure.

Paragraph 5(3) (b) of the AML/CFT Code 2019 sets out that; "The business risk assessment must have regard to all relevant risk factors, including [….] any relevant findings of the most recent National Risk Assessment relating to the Island". This ensures that relevant persons must, as part of their risk framework, consider and assess the most recent ML trends and vulnerabilities as they relate to the IOM and the sector in which they operate.

In January 2024 the FSA published a thematic review of BRAs for the TCSP sector. The review considers paragraph 5(3)(b) of the Code which mandates the areas for consideration in a BRA. A report and accompanying webinar were published covering areas of good practice and where improvements can be made, this can be utilised by all sectors to assist developing a robust BRA. In addition to the Codes requiring consideration of the NRA in supervised entities' risk assessments, chapter 6.3 of the AML/ CFT Handbook directs a relevant person to provide or arrange education and training regarding the BRA. Senior management should consider whether the NRA identifies matters which need to be brought to the attention of their colleagues and implement changes accordingly. ■

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 15. Updating the ML NRA - d90fa0453c320b01
body:
One of the key inputs to the Island's NRAs is the risk data provided to the regulators from supervised entities via STRIX AML. Where published NRAs and industry sector reports include aggregated industry data, each firm should consider how their own data compares with the published data. This will assist them to better understand their risk profile compared to the national metrics, threats and vulnerabilities.
Businesses in the regulated sector are obliged by the FSA, GSC and SNPO Codes to undertake and update the BRA, which 'assists relevant persons to understand where, when, how and to what extent they are exposed to ML/TF risk and which areas of their business they should prioritise in combatting ML/TF.' The Code states that a BRA must have regard to any relevant findings of the most recent NRA relating to the Island. Therefore, Industry must be able to show how they have considered and mitigated the relevant risks identified in this NRA. Given a number of NRAs are being published over the course of several months, it is acceptable to consider each NRA as it is published, but update the overall BRA at its next formal review date. Consideration should also be given to the CRA and TRA and if these require updating.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), 16. Appendices, Progression of Actions from the 2020 NRA Through the 2021 and 2024 Financial Crime Strategies - Key Themes - 838676bf5225a716
headers: Progression of Actions from the 2020 NRA Through the 2021 and 2024 Financial Crime Strategies - Key Themes
body:
The progression from the 2020 National Risk Assessment (NRA) through the 2021-23 and 2024-26 Financial Crime Strategies reflects steady progress from identifying deficiencies to building capability, and ultimately towards evidencing maturity and effectiveness. The 2020 NRA largely diagnoses gaps across governance, data quality, supervisory consistency, and sector specific vulnerabilities, while noting the need for stronger legislative frameworks, deeper intelligence analysis, and greater scrutiny of complex ownership structures. It establishes the foundations for a more coordinated national response, a refreshed strategic direction and in particular improved utilisation of existing powers.
The 2021-23 Strategy translates identified deficiencies into structured actions. The focus is on strengthening legislative tools, deepening risk-based supervision, expanding data collection and analysis, and enhancing enforcement capability. Engagement with industry was evolving into more formalised partnerships with participation in international bodies becoming more deliberate and consistent. This Strategy works to embed processes, improve skills, and establish clear mechanisms for collaboration across agencies and sectors.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), Appendix II: Mutual Evaluation Report 2016 (IO1) and Recommended Actions - 7f33c7c8ceca11cb
headers: Appendix II: Mutual Evaluation Report 2016 (IO1) and Recommended Actions
body:
The 2016 Fifth Round Mutual Evaluation of the Isle of Man rated 'National AML/CFT Policies and Coordination' (IO1) as 'substantial'. The Recommended Actions identified in the MER specific to IO1 have been fully addressed.
The Island was required to report on progress three times since the last MER regarding implementation of any remaining technical deficiencies in the FATF Recommendations. Moneyval published their 4th Enhanced Follow-Up Report (FUR) and Technical Compliance Re-Rating in November 2022. The Isle of Man is Compliant or Largely Compliant with 39 of the 40 Recommendation and Partially Compliant with Recommendation 23 - DNFBP's Other Measures.
The deficiencies noted for Recommendation 23 were (i) no specific requirement in the AML/CFT Code or Gambling Code in relation to having an independent audit function; and (ii) no specific requirement in the AML/CFT Code for groups to have group-wide programmes against ML/TF.
The Isle of Man has taken steps to address these deficiencies as noted by the FUR, however to date R23 has not been re-rated. Further consideration is being given to the remaining areas identified as requiring attention.
Recommended Action Progress
As identified in the NRA, the authorities should take steps to collect statistics on outgoing and incoming flows of funds in the financial sector. The IOM should then conduct a reassessment of those areas which would have benefitted from these statistics, mainly cross-border ML and TF threats.

Banking financial flow data has been available since 2018. This data and other detailed industry data collected by the regulators since 2022 has provided the authorities with a greater understanding of the exposure of the Island to potential and actual cross-border ML, PF, and TF threats.
Industry data collected by the regulators since 2017, has provided the authorities with a clear picture of the nationality and the place of residence of beneficial owners, which is used to inform the NRA. Detailed information collected for a Risk Assessment concerning legal persons and arrangements is further adding to that understanding and will further inform risk mitigation measures.
The authorities should seek to understand where the beneficial owners of assets managed or held by regulated entities in the IOM are from and consider this information in the next iteration of the NRA.
Recommended Action Progress

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), Appendix II: Mutual Evaluation Report 2016 (IO1) and Recommended Actions - c1a653b7f3499243
headers: Appendix II: Mutual Evaluation Report 2016 (IO1) and Recommended Actions
body:
The Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism Code 2019 included an updated "Introduced Business" paragraph which mandated that, when a customer is introduced by one entity (the introducer) to another (such as a bank), and elements of customer due diligence are provided by the introducer, the bank must assess the risk associated with the introducer as part of the broader Customer Risk Assessment. This assessment should also consider internal mitigation factors, such as whether the customer has been met by staff of the receiving entity, and the way in which CDD was obtained by the introducer.
By increasing staffing resources at the borders, a greater understanding of the threat of cash entering and leaving the Island is being formed, which in turn informs law enforcement agencies of the risks and where to focus resources. The industry data now available to the FSA provides a more detailed understanding of DNFBs, including the Real Estate sector and the Legal sector, and informs the understanding of the risk profile of these sectors.
The IOM should undertake a more detailed assessment of the risk resulting from the use by banks of CDD information provided by TCSPs that have collected this information in turn from a professional intermediary. The authorities should also consider reassessing the risk posed by lawyers, the Real Estate sector, and the threat posed by cash entering and exiting the IOM.

A Risk Assessment of simplified measures relating to the regulatory framework from a ML/TF/PF perspective has been undertaken. This risk assessment is an internal document; however, further information at a High level can be found under Chapter 6 of this NRA.
The authorities have made significant efforts to ensure alignment between the objectives and activities of the FIU and LEAs and AML/CFT policies and identified risks. All authorities contribute to the Financial Crime Strategy; all authorities are represented at political, strategic, and operational level, and activities are monitored and reported upon. As part of a revised governance framework, a Multi-Agency Cooperation Working Group was established.
Going forward, it should be ensured that the objectives and activities of the FIU and LEAs are consistent with AML/CFT policies and identified ML/TF risks.

The authorities published a formal PF policy in 2018 and have proactively provided outreach to industry in relation to PF, including webinars, factsheets, and presentations. The Isle of Man is currently conducting a multi-agency PF risk assessment. Measures to strengthen cooperation have been introduced, including, but not limited to, new arrangements at the borders and a revised national governance structure for AML/CFT. In addition, a Sanctions Operational Group has been formed to strengthen cooperation mechanisms between agencies on sanctions matters.
The authorities should introduce (or strengthen existing ones, as the case may be) cooperation mechanisms in those areas which are identified as missing in this report, including a formal PF policy.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), Appendix IV: Countries That Pose or May Pose a Higher Risk and Countries to which the IOM has a Higher Exposure - d000aa160094605e
headers: Appendix IV: Countries That Pose or May Pose a Higher Risk and Countries to which the IOM has a Higher Exposure
body:
The Isle of Man identifies countries by the risk they pose:

- 'List A' is a list specifying jurisdictions which the FATF has made a call on its members and other jurisdictions to apply countermeasures to protect the international financial system from the ongoing and substantial risks of ML/TF emanating from the jurisdiction. List A currently comprises 3 jurisdictions.

- ''List B' is a list specifying jurisdictions with strategic AML/CFT deficiencies or those considered may pose a higher risk of ML/ TF. List B is made up of two lists:

- List Bi - consists of countries that FATF has identified as having strategic AML/ CFT deficiencies for which they have developed an action plan with the FATF. It also identifies jurisdictions that have not made sufficient progress on their action plans agreed with the FATF

- List Bii - this section specifies additional jurisdictions that have also been identified as those that may pose a higher risk of ML or TF by the IOM Government. The list is prepared, in accordance with an established methodology, using data gathered from various commercial intelligence sources that cover ML, TF, crime, transparency and bribery/corruption risk.

The June 2025 (3 July 2025) published lists were used for this document with the exception of payment flows, which used the November 2024 list (effective as at 31 December 2024).

headers: Appendix IV: Countries That Pose or May Pose a Higher Risk and Countries to which the IOM has a Higher Exposure
body:
List B(i) ongoing
- Jurisdiction: Argentina; Risk profile: ● Some external OCGs from neighbouring jurisdictions use Argentina's financial system to launder the funds gained from drug trafficking and other predicate offences. (Section 3, p. 7) ● LPAs present a weakness in Argentina's AML regime, as BO information is not always supplied accurately or adequately to law enforcement upon request, and the identity checks required on trustees of foreign-established trusts do not meet FATF requirements. (Section 1(k), p. 6)
- Jurisdiction: Brazil; Risk profile: ● As the most populous country and largest economy in South America, and with a long, porous border and coastline, Brazil is inherently exposed to financial crime. An informal economy and a regulated sector that is frequently subject to abuse put Brazil at significant risk of being utilised for ML. (Section 2, p. 5)
- Jurisdiction: France; Risk profile: ● France's primary ML threats originate from fraud relating to tax, social security, and customs duties; other predicate offences affecting the country include human trafficking and corruption by domestic and foreign PEPs. (Section 3, p. 5) ● France's most recent MER commended the country on its robust legal framework for tackling ML which translates into an effective enforcement regime. Supervision of DNFBPs and due diligence regulations regarding PEPs were identified as areas for improvement (Sections 5-6, p. 6)

headers: Appendix IV: Countries That Pose or May Pose a Higher Risk and Countries to which the IOM has a Higher Exposure
body:
- Jurisdiction: Gibraltar; Risk profile: ● Gibraltar's risk of ML derives from its border with Spain, where OCGs engaging in the trafficking of drugs and tobacco may wish to launder their funds through a jurisdiction with certain vulnerable sectors, (§ 2, p. 7) including e-money and TCSPs. (Section 3, p. 7)
- Jurisdiction: Guernsey; Risk profile: ● Guernsey's ML risk primarily derives from its use as a transit hub for illicit funds originating from larger jurisdictions and sometimes being directed through multiple IFCs including the Bailiwick. (Section 2, p. 9)
- Jurisdiction: Hong Kong, China; Risk profile: ● HKC is a major continental and global financial centre for a number of financial sectors, including securities, insurance, and wealth management (Section 2, p. 5)-a status which puts it at significant threat to the laundering of the proceeds of (primarily external) crime. (Section 3, p. 5) ● Smaller FIs and DNFBPs operating exclusively in HKC have an insufficient understanding of ML risks, as do certain minor supervisory bodies. The FATF expressed concern that Dealers in Precious Metals and Stones and certain financial leasing firms are not subject to any AML regulations. (Section 1(e), p. 4)

headers: Appendix IV: Countries That Pose or May Pose a Higher Risk and Countries to which the IOM has a Higher Exposure
body:
- Jurisdiction: India; Risk profile: ● India faces a high risk of ML, in large part due to its status as a global centre for fraud factories, the revenue from which is either laundered locally or externally before being reintegrated into the Indian economy. (Section 2, p. 4) ● Law enforcement also lacks the resources to effectively detect and prevent human trafficking and drug smuggling, two other common predicate offences for ML. (Section 1, p. 3) ● Customer background checks for criminality are inadequate among DNFBPs, particularly for Dealers in Precious Metals and Stones. (Section 1, p. 4)
- Jurisdiction: Ireland; Risk profile: ● Domestic organised crime organisations, including former paramilitary groups, constitute Ireland's main ML threat; their activities include drug smuggling, human trafficking, and fraud operations. (Section 3, p. 5) A large number of PSPs-a sector warranting enhanced supervision due to its risk nature-use Ireland a base for their EU activities. (Section 4, p. 5)
- Jurisdiction: Japan; Risk profile: ● Organised crime groups are active in Japan and launder the proceeds from a variety of predicate offences, including fraud and drug trafficking. There is also a high rate of illegal money transfers from foreign actors. (Section 2, p. 6)

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), Appendix IV: Countries That Pose or May Pose a Higher Risk and Countries to which the IOM has a Higher Exposure, NON-HIGHER RISK JURISDICTIONS: - de7efbc5961f3b99
headers: Appendix IV: Countries That Pose or May Pose a Higher Risk and Countries to which the IOM has a Higher Exposure
body:
- Jurisdiction: Jersey; Risk profile: ● Jersey has a sizeable wealth management sector with an international clientele, which leaves it exposed to ML by foreign criminals. The variety of financial services offered by Jersey requires stringent regulation, (Section 2, p. 8) and the FATF were satisfied with the cooperation between agencies to enforce this regulation. (Section 1(a), p. 5) ● Requirements for CDD checks by firms were noted as a weakness in Jersey's AML regime as they relied too heavily on self-declarations by potential clients, and such checks had only recently been introduced for DNFBPs and VASPs at the time of Jersey's MER in 2024. (Section 1(h), p. 7)
- Jurisdiction: Kenya; Risk profile: ● The FATF assessed Kenya as having high exposure to ML and the transit of drugs and illegal wildlife, (Section 2, p. 10) ● Customs officials did not detect as many undeclared cash transmissions as would be expected from a jurisdiction with Kenya's regional financial significance. (Section 1(g), p. 9) ● DNFBPs and other non-bank FIs are not adequately supervised or regulated for AML compliance, and inspections fail to consider the effectiveness of FIs' compliance systems. (Section 1(i), p. 9) VASPs are not regulated by Kenyan authorities, and the jurisdiction has not carried out an NRA to gauge the ML threat posed by VAs. (Section 1(m), p. 9)

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), Appendix IV: Countries That Pose or May Pose a Higher Risk and Countries to which the IOM has a Higher Exposure, NON-HIGHER RISK JURISDICTIONS: - 55e6f6df3ef33471
headers: Appendix IV: Countries That Pose or May Pose a Higher Risk and Countries to which the IOM has a Higher Exposure
body:
- Jurisdiction: Luxembourg; Risk profile: ● 23% of Luxembourg's GDP derives from the finance/insurance sector, it has the largest investment fund market in Europe, and it is a continental centre for the hosting of payment and e-money institutions. (Section 2, p. 5) This international-facing nature of Luxembourg's finance sector leaves it exposed to the threat of ML for the proceeds of foreign predicate offences. (Section 3, p. 6) ● DNFBPs, particularly real estate agents and Dealers in Precious Metals and Stones, lack a detailed understanding of their AML obligations, reflected in the low number of suspicious transactions reports filed by the sector. (Section 1(9), p. 4)
- Jurisdiction: Malta; Risk profile: ● Remote gaming is a significant contributor to the Maltese economy. This is an industry with a high vulnerability to ML due to its non-face-to-face nature and the frequent use of prepaid cards for transactions. Malta's banking and TCSP sectors primarily service non-residents, and OCGs are active in the country, all factors which raise Malta's threat exposure. (Sections 2-4, p. 9) ● Outside of banks and casinos, FIs were rarely able to demonstrate to the FATF their understanding of ML typologies, casting a negative light on the integrity of Malta's Suspicious Transaction Reporting procedure. (Section 1, p. 7)

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), Appendix IV: Countries That Pose or May Pose a Higher Risk and Countries to which the IOM has a Higher Exposure, NON-HIGHER RISK JURISDICTIONS: - 04fc7ecac7a7e42b
headers: Appendix IV: Countries That Pose or May Pose a Higher Risk and Countries to which the IOM has a Higher Exposure
body: - Jurisdiction: Mexico; Risk profile: ● Drug smuggling and human trafficking, among other predicate offences, generate a very high volume of revenue in Mexico; (Section 2, p. 5) when combined with a large cash-based, informal economy (Section 4, p. 5) and a significant flow of cash across the border with the US, this puts Mexican banks at high risk of ML. (Section 3, p. 5) ● Understanding of complex ML threats is limited among Mexican DNFBPs, and the wider financial sector fails to fully recognise corruption as a predicate offence for ML. (Section 1, p. 3) ● The CDD conducted by FIs on the beneficial owners of potential customers is inadequate and rarely scrutinises the declarations made by customers themselves, and FIs typically do not know the controlling personnel of their customers beyond the surface level of legal ownership. (Section 1, p. 4)

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), Appendix IV: Countries That Pose or May Pose a Higher Risk and Countries to which the IOM has a Higher Exposure, NON-HIGHER RISK JURISDICTIONS: - f41d72da7f9551b3
headers: Appendix IV: Countries That Pose or May Pose a Higher Risk and Countries to which the IOM has a Higher Exposure
body: - Jurisdiction: Singapore; Risk profile: ● 77% of funds managed by Singaporean firms originate externally, mostly from the Asia-Pacific region. This is a region with a high volume of organised crime activity, thus Singapore is vulnerable to the laundering of the proceeds of illicit activity. (Section 3, p. 5) ● The FATF praised Singapore in its most recent MER for its sophisticated AML regime and powerful law enforcement network but noted some gaps in detailed understanding among supervisory authorities of the jurisdiction's transnational ML threat; this gap in understanding was also observed in DNFBPs. (Section 1, pp. 3-4) ● Singapore's NRA did not analyse the risk level for LPAs beyond acknowledging that they could be used to obscure the origins of illicit funds, and DNFBPs struggle to meet requirements for ascertaining BO. (Section 1, p. 4)

headers: Appendix IV: Countries That Pose or May Pose a Higher Risk and Countries to which the IOM has a Higher Exposure
body:
- Jurisdiction: South Africa; Risk profile: ● With a high volume of domestic proceeds-generating crime, and as the regional hub for finance in sub-Saharan Africa, South Africa has an inherent vulnerability to financial crime. (Section 2, p. 5) These factors, combined with widespread corruption in law enforcement, (Section 3, p. 5) put the jurisdiction's financial system at significant threat of ML. ● Though the institutions responsible for combatting financial crime in South Africa understand the risks and threats of ML, (Section 1(a), p. 3) their powers to combat it have been undermined by a prolonged period of state corruption, from which the country was slowly recovering at the time of the FATF's most recent assessment in 2021. (Section 1(b), p. 3) ● South Africa has a substantial informal economy and struggles to detect and confiscate undeclared cross-border cash moved into the country. (Section 1(f), p. 4) ● TCSPs are regularly exploited due to inadequate transparency requirements for registering BO. (Section 3, p. 5)
- Jurisdiction: United Arab Emirates; Risk profile: ● While the UAE exercises its wide confiscation powers against the proceeds of domestic crime, the jurisdiction could not demonstrate that an adequate quantity of assets generated from foreign predicate offences are seized. The cross-border movement of cash and precious metals is not effectively monitored. ((Section 1(e), p. 4)

headers: Appendix IV: Countries That Pose or May Pose a Higher Risk and Countries to which the IOM has a Higher Exposure
body: - Jurisdiction: United Kingdom; Risk profile: ● The United Kingdom is exposed to a high risk of money laundering as a result of its openness to international business and a sizeable professional services sector. 2% of UK firms surveyed in 2024 reported experiencing known or suspected ML in the preceding 12 months. (Section 3.1, pp. 20-21) ● The UK's 2025 ML/TF NRA highlighted the jurisdiction's exposure to both traditional, cash-based ML (Section 3.5, p. 21) and the risks posed by emerging financial technologies, such as online payment service providers, cryptoassets, and the use of AI to evade fraud detection software. (Section 3.4, p. 20) ● The UK's previous NRA, published in 2020, identified the jurisdiction's ML/TF risk to be particularly significant in the following sectors: banking and financial services; real estate; legal and accountancy services; trust and company service providers; and cryptoassets. (Section 2.9, pp. 12-13)

headers: Appendix IV: Countries That Pose or May Pose a Higher Risk and Countries to which the IOM has a Higher Exposure
body: - Jurisdiction: United States; Risk profile: ● As the world's largest economy, and with the dollar as the predominant currency of international finance, (p. 3) the United States is exposed to a number of high-level ML threats, and its risk landscape for ML has evolved significantly due to technological and geopolitical developments. (p. 96) ● The US' 2024 NRA attributes much of its ML risk to foreign actors, including Mexican drug trafficking organisations, Chinese organised crime groups, and cybercrime groups linked to Russia and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea. (p. 3) ● Among the ML vulnerabilities identified in the US' NRA are: a.the bulk smuggling by OCGs of cash into and out of the US, particularly across the border with Mexico, to evade reporting requirements for high-value transactions; (pp. 43-44) b.the exploitation of exemptions to recently implemented legislation on the reporting of beneficial ownership information; (pp. 54-55) c.noted delays in banks resolving identified AML deficiencies or filing SARs. (p. 66)
