body:
Module 1 Quality of AML Policy & Strategy
The IOM Government has a robust AML framework and upholds international standards, with increased resources and a restructured approach since the last NRA which is being embedded. A National Financial Crime Strategy (2024-2026), approved in Tynwald, is in place as are targeted preventive measures. Cross-Government collaboration supports a unified approach under 'Our Island Plan'. A forthcoming National Action Plan (2026) will detail actions for authorities. The Financial Crime Strategic Board (FCSB) steers policy and resource allocation, aligning activities with the National Strategy and enhancing risk management through thematic groups. The AML/CFT Policy Office oversees international engagement and analysis of effectiveness. Regulated entities must update risk assessments, integrating NRA findings and jurisdictional guidance. Legislative measures to align the AML framework with FCSB objectives have seen delays and, while a number are progressing, some will require prioritisation following the 2026 General Election.
Module 2 Effectiveness of ML Crime Definition 1.0 Excellent

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), Appendix VI: National Anti-Money Laundering Controls - 3d0802dfa694868b
headers: Appendix VI: National Anti-Money Laundering Controls
body:
Money laundering (ML) is criminalised under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2008 (POCA), with a definition in section 158(11) that aligns with international standards. Tax crimes and self-laundering are included; a conviction for the predicate offence is not required. There are no specific sentencing guidelines within the Manx courts, the judiciary refer to the UK sentencing guidelines for ML. Penalties for ML range from fines to up to fourteen years' imprisonment. Non-compliance with AML regulations can result in up to two years' imprisonment, unlimited fines, or both. All parties involved, including those who fail to disclose, can be prosecuted.
Module 3 Comprehensiveness of Asset Forfeiture Laws 0.7 High

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), Appendix VI: National Anti-Money Laundering Controls - 68429c0328476a77
headers: Appendix VI: National Anti-Money Laundering Controls
body:
The IOM has comprehensive confiscation measures for investigating, tracing, and seizing property suspected of being crime proceeds. Existing asset forfeiture legislation in POCA (and other Acts) covers the proceeds and instrumentalities of money laundering and its predicate offences, including profits derived from criminality and property of corresponding value. Foreign non-conviction-based confiscation orders can also be enforced, regardless of proceedings abroad. The AGC can apply for High Court property freezing orders to secure assets for recovery and Customs and Immigration can seize cash and BNIs linked to money laundering, predicate offences, or false declarations. Confiscated assets have included cryptocurrency and properties, with proceeds placed into a seized asset fund managed by the FIU Board. Legislative updates are being considered to better reflect the changing landscape regarding technological advancements and the AGC is developing systems for more effective seized asset management, including written procedures and tracking of Restraint Orders to monitor total values.
Module 4 Quality of FIU Intelligence Gathering and Processing 0.7 High

The FIU created under the 2016 FIU Act, has a staff of 25 and operates independently, reporting directly to an FIU Board. It is a member of the Egmont Group since 2000. Its Strategic Objectives & Annual Plan 2023/24 outline recent restructuring. Every FIU team member receives specialised training in AML and financial crime prevention, supported by both external and internal programs. Despite these initiatives, staff retention has remained challenging. The Themis online platform streamlines reporting for regulated entities and facilitates communication. Standardised feedback for MLROs and updated guidance aim to improve the quality of disclosures, though more feedback on intelligence use is needed. International feedback, particularly via the Egmont network, is improving. The FIU collaborates with the FSA and can access financial flow data to inform strategic projects; it also hosts a co-located PIMLIT Case Development Unit (CDU). Further cooperation with tax is being explored to help educate and inform and to identify any gaps that can be addressed. The FIU is currently working to improve its operational case committee process; further development is needed for strategic analysis, intelligence handling, and database management policies.
Module 5 Capacity & Resources for Financial Crime Investigation (including Asset Forfeiture) 0.7 High

body: Significant investment has enhanced financial crime enforcement, including the creation of the Proactive International Money Laundering Investigation Team (PIMLIT) in 2022, to handle complex, cross-border cases with a dedicated team of 31. This includes analysts, a prosecuting lawyer, and industry specialists. Investigations have increased, with 10 active international money laundering cases involving large proceeds, and three major multi-agency operations in 2024-25 resulting in the seizure of around £300 million and substantial digital and physical evidence. PIMLIT has developed cryptocurrency tracing capabilities, leading to its first civil recovery of $1.2 million USD in crypto. Most ongoing operations involve cryptocurrencies such as USD Tether and Ethereum. Successful domestic prosecutions are mainly linked to drug trafficking, associated ML and OCG offending, with the Serious & Organised Crime Unit leading high-level cases.

The International Cooperation and Asset Recovery Unit (ICART) deals with international asset matters. All domestic civil asset recovery has been merged into prosecutions into a newly formed Financial Crime Asset Recovery Unit (FCARU). ICART recovered $41,189.17 and £989,033.41 in 2024 and is adopting advanced tools and training for VAs. Notably, ICART enforced 12 search and seizure warrants, issued the Island's first production order for detained cash investigation, and supported a US conviction for fraud and tax evasion totalling $4.8M. Challenges remain in international cooperation, especially with large or cryptocurrency-related cases, but new processes are being implemented to improve the use of incoming Letters of Request for asset identification and intelligence.
Module 6 Independence and Integrity of Financial Crime Investigators (including Asset Forfeiture) 0.9 Close to Excellent
The IOM upholds strong standards of integrity in law enforcement, evidenced by the prosecution of high-profile individuals and staff, including police officers and civilian staff, for offences such as bribery and theft. No cases of corruption related to ML offences have been identified. The Bribery Act 2013 is the relevant legislation, supported by the ABC Strategy 2022-2027. Concerns can be reported via the Themis system. While not rated by Transparency International, the IOM generally compares to the UK

The Prosecutions Division advises the IOMC and public authorities on potential criminal charges, with prosecutors making decisions on behalf of the AG. A rota system ensures year-round out-of-hours coverage for charging decisions. Responsibilities are split between a general team and a dedicated Financial Crime Asset Recovery Unit (FCARU), to improve specialisation, which automatically handles PIMLIT and ECU matters (with guidelines for other agency referrals). A senior legal officer has been seconded to the police to support PIMLIT and ECU. Financial crime is a core focus. The FCARU works closely with ICART to identify where parallel civil investigations may be appropriate. While ML prosecutions show success in convictions and confiscations, these primarily relate to drug trafficking; international ML convictions are still developing. The Prosecution team can seek support from King's Counsel (KC) in the UK for complex cases. The 2020 NRA noted a lack of specialised ML prosecution training; this has since been addressed. There have been several cases where a variety of assets have been seized and effectively managed. Formalisation of tools and procedures for managing restrained and seized assets outside of financial products, whether under the control of the AGC or the Police need to be reviewed and any identified improvements implemented.
Module 8 Independence and Integrity of Financial Crime Prosecutors (including Asset Forfeiture) 0.9 Close to Excellent

body:
All criminal prosecutions, including economic crimes, are managed by the AGC, with the AG and Solicitor General appointed and removable only by the monarch. Complaints against law officers can be escalated to the Tynwald Commissioner for Administration (Ombudsman) if unresolved internally. The Financial Crime Asset Recovery Unit, supported by the AG, determines high level money laundering prosecutions. Processes incorporate checks and balances, including Crown Officer reviews and the possibility of judicial review, as exemplified in Bell vs HM Solicitor General & Others (May 2024). The code for Prosecutors under the Criminal Procedures and Investigations Act 2016 guides impartial and evidence-based decisions. Clear separation exists between the judiciary, AGC, police, and executive, with standards enforced by Advocate Practice Rules and the Advocates Disciplinary Tribunal. Past high-profile prosecutions, such as that of a former Attorney General for perjury and acts against public justice and a former prosecuting advocate for a speeding charge, demonstrate prosecutorial independence.

headers: Appendix VI: National Anti-Money Laundering Controls
body: The IOM operates as a separate legal jurisdiction from the UK, with a legal system based on English common law and Acts of Tynwald. Manx Courts are guided by English precedents unless local law applies. The judiciary comprises Deemsters (judges), with the First Deemster as President of the High Court, plus Summary Court High Bailiff/Deputy High Bailiff, part-time judges, and lay magistrates. Serious criminal cases are dealt with by the Court of General Gaol Delivery, while appeals go to the Staff of Government Division and, ultimately, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London. Additional Deemsters or judicial officers may be appointed as needed, and Judges from England and Wales, senior UK Barristers, and local senior advocates serve as Panel Deemsters for complex cases.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), Appendix VI: National Anti-Money Laundering Controls - 46d0cf1c5da23684

body:
Financial crime cases are heard by specialist judges, and urgent court orders may be granted by any High Court Judge or Panel Deemster. Recent legal reforms allow judge-only trials for complex fraud cases, aiming to boost court capacity. The IOM Law Society regulates the legal profession, with advocates fulfilling both solicitor and barrister roles. Training has improved through collaboration with the Judicial College of England and Wales, and digital capabilities are increasing. However, manual processes, limited space, and recruitment challenges persist, especially for large or high-profile trials. Planned updates to the Justice Reform Act and resource allocation for major money laundering trials are intended to address these limitations.
Module 10 Independence and Integrity of Judges 1.0 Excellent
Judicial appointments are made transparently and independently, with all judges appointed by the King based on panel recommendations. Judges are not politically appointed and must retire at 75, ensuring impartiality and integrity. ML trials and related offences offences proceed without interference, political or social pressure, corruption, intimidation, or abuse of office. All proceedings are recorded, judgments are published with reasons, and complaints follow a set process; appeals can ultimately be heard by the UK Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.

body:
Most passenger and freight traffic into the IOM passes through a single airport and ferry terminal, simplifying enforcement. While there are a few small airstrips, the coastline is susceptible to illegal entry by small vessels. Airlines require ID checks for flights where baggage is checked in and for flights to the Republic of Ireland, but ID checks are not required for sailings within the CTA. Agencies closely monitor foreign parcels at the Post Office in coordination with UK counterparts. The non-cash-based economy limits large-scale cash generation, with most smuggled cash tied to drug trafficking from UK-based OCGs; authorities have documented attempts to import and remove such cash. Controls on cash and similar instruments are generally robust, with improved cooperation between customs, police, and port security reflected in cash declarations and ML arrests at ports. Criminals are increasingly using luxury goods to move value out of the IOM as enforcement tightens. Locally issued notes moved into the UK are eventually returned to the IOM, however tracking this flow remains a challenge, which other Crown Dependencies who also issue their own notes, have identified. Ongoing measures include enhancing C&I training and strengthening intelligence-sharing with partner agencies to support targeted operations.
Module 15 Effectiveness of International Cooperation 0.7 High

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), Appendix VI: National Anti-Money Laundering Controls - 4e03822fcf0dd589
headers: Appendix VI: National Anti-Money Laundering Controls
body: The IOM possesses a robust legal framework for mutual legal assistance (MLA) in money laundering, related offences, and terrorist financing, including civil recovery. International cooperation is assured by legislation and is not generally contingent on reciprocity or treaties. Dual criminality is required for certain coercive measures (such as restraint and confiscation) but IOM case law confirms that this is not dependent upon the categorisation or wording of the offence that is required. In Sejeroe-Olsen v HMAG [2019] MLR 233 the Staff of Government Division stated that it was not necessary for an offence in the IOM to be on "all fours" with the offences in the requesting jurisdiction, rather that "what is required… is whether the essence of the conduct would constitute an offence here, and not, with respect, proven conduct (i.e. guilt)." The AGC centrally coordinates MLA requests, using a prioritisation system for urgent matters such as asset restraint. ICART provides timely and effective MLA, actively participating in international networks and supporting asset recovery, extradition, and information sharing. The IOM maintains a central beneficial ownership register in line with global standards, with its authorities exchanging information internationally through established channels such as the Egmont Group.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), Appendix VI: National Anti-Money Laundering Controls - 7a7f0f3462effe5d

body:
An upgraded case management system has recently been introduced. ICART has faced key person risk due to reliance on a few specialists; expertise within the team has benefitted from specialist training provided by the City of London Police Economic Crime Academy and other international experts. Extension of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2008 to include external orders enforcement to foreign civil forfeiture orders which was identified as a gap in the previous NRA has been addressed (Part 2A Article 55).
Module 16 Availability of Independent Audit 0.8 Very High
There have been no changes to audit laws under the Companies Act 1982 and 2006 since the last NRA. Independent audits follow UK & Ireland International Standards, with oversight by the UK FRC for markettraded companies. Most non-public companies under the 2006 Act are not required to have audits, while those under the 1931 Act must be audited unless exempted based on size and staffing criteria. FSA and GSC-regulated entities must submit annual audited accounts, except for certain DNFBPs, and license holders or those handling client money need independent auditor assurance. Regulated entities generally file audited returns within four months, with exceptions for some foreign firms. Insurers and professional administrators of Retirement Benefit Schemes also have specific audit and reporting requirements.
Module 17 Level of Financial Integrity 0.7 High

The IOM enjoys strong membership in professional bodies, with high CPD engagement and a strong emphasis on ethics. Criminal and civil proceedings involving professionals are reported in the press, social media, and trade journals, with regulatory actions published by authorities and the FSA posting enforcement notices and penalties on its website. Judgments are made publicly accessible on the IOM Courts of Justice website, which offers comprehensive search capabilities. The Registrar
General, acting as Registrar of Companies, publishes dissolved company lists. The tax system requires detailed financial disclosures on income and assets from individuals and legal entities, and authorities have robust enforcement powers. Civil penalties apply to non-compliance for both direct and indirect taxes. Investigators use financial records for tracing in money laundering cases, and regulated entities typically cooperate well.
Module 18 Tax Enforcement 0.8 Very High

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), Appendix VI: National Anti-Money Laundering Controls - bce1e6c28a9372f8
headers: Appendix VI: National Anti-Money Laundering Controls
body: Direct and indirect taxes come under the authority of the Treasury. Responsibility for IOM income tax and National Insurance lies with the Assessor of Income Tax, the head of the Income Tax Division (ITD). For international direct taxation purposes, the Assessor is the competent authority. Four Deputy Assessors have full delegated powers. Responsibility for indirect tax administration, compliance and enforcement is delegated to the Customs and Immigration Division; the head of the Division is 'the Collector'. Staff in both Divisions must sign the Official Secrets Act, follow Civil Service Regulations, and complete yearly security training. New employees are vetted, only qualified officers handle high-risk cases, and regular audits occur. Conflicts of interest must be declared, and all staff adhere to the Bribery Act 2013 and the Government Whistleblowing Policy.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), Appendix VI: National Anti-Money Laundering Controls - 523173b8c3ce60b0
headers: Appendix VI: National Anti-Money Laundering Controls
body: Direct Tax: ITD operates under strict confidentiality and statutory rules as pursuant to section 106 of the Income Tax Act 1970 every person having any official duty under the Income Tax Acts has a duty of confidentiality in relation to all income tax documents and information. That said, the Income Tax Act (sections 106A - 106F) also provides for the sharing of such confidential information with other authorities, including law enforcement and the regulators, where it is appropriate to do so. All casework is graded by risk, with high-risk cases reserved for experienced officers. The Division has strong legal powers to deter non-compliance, charging civil penalties for late or missing returns, escalating to public legal proceedings if necessary. Serious and complex cases are handled by an investigation team and anonymised appeal summaries published with the Commissioners' consent. Tax compliance is generally good.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), Appendix VI: National Anti-Money Laundering Controls - 614e0c81851f2090
headers: Appendix VI: National Anti-Money Laundering Controls
body:
Indirect Tax: The Collector oversees a team responsible for indirect tax administration, compliance, and enforcement. C&I undergoes regular inspection by the UK National Audit Office (NAO) to assess compliance with the Customs and Excise Agreement. HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) in the UK provides training under the Revenue Sharing Agreement and C&I also coordinates with HMRC regarding policy matters. The Indirect Tax audit team is responsible for setting its own targets; it alone determines which traders require audits based on the level of risk identified by the Division. The Customs and Excise Management Act 1986 (sections 174B and 174C) enables information to be shared in relation to all the assigned matters the Division is responsible for, and also the power to be able to obtain information from authorities relating to the functions and assigned matters of the Division ("assigned matters" is defined in section 184(1)). Most indirect tax court cases involve deliberate VAT fraud. In 2020, one couple was jailed for evading £4.65 million in VAT. In 2022, a conviction was secured for £190,000 in VAT fraud. In 2023, an individual received a prison sentence of over three years for evading £1.1 million in VAT and in 2024, eight businesses were fined more than £10,000 each for failing to pay income tax and National Insurance.
Module 19 Formalisation of the Economy 0.9 Close to Excellent

body:
The IOM has a formal, services-based economy with limited informal activity. Informal contributions to GDP are low, partly due to very high employment rates and support schemes such as Jobseeker's Allowance. There is extensive public data available regarding the island's economy and demography. It is assessed that the GDP share relating to the informal economy amounts to less than 10%. The Department for Enterprise's 2022 report highlights a move toward digital payments, with cash use declining further. Residents must participate in the financial system to access utilities and government services, with strict regulations and VAT registration required for most business activities. Laws are well enforced by authorities. Recent increases in drug and cash seizures, as well as rising immigration crime and cases of labour exploitation, suggest a potential for growth in the shadow economy which will need to be monitored.
Module 20 Availability of Reliable Identification Infrastructurey 0.7 High

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), Appendix VI: National Anti-Money Laundering Controls - 110d23e28f275604

body:
The IOM Government issues various photographic identification documents, including passports and driving licences; there is no requirement to carry identity cards. The Island acts as an issuing authority for British Passports, with the IOM variant being processed locally and printed securely in the UK by HM Passport Office. New applicants undergo ID checks and an interview. Driving licences are issued by IOM Post, acting as a licencing agent for the DOI. The Island keeps an Electoral Register. Within the Common Travel Area, there are no formal border controls between the IOM the UK, Channel Islands, and ROI and therefore no mandatory ID checks; this can allow some to avoid identification. Enhanced data collection and sharing between police, customs, and immigration is being developed. Concerns have been raised about the robustness of the IOM driving licence as ID. While procedures and checks are in place, its primary purpose is not as a national ID card, although it is used by banks along with proof of address. Closer working between the DoI Highway Services, the police, immigration and potentially other departments/agencies need to be explored. Electronic billing and ID methods pose new risks, but there have been no known fraud cases. Staff at businesses are trained to identify fraudulent documents, and extra precautions are taken for non face-to-face transactions.

Government and industry rely on internationally recognised credit and identification services, with FIs and DNFBPs having significant expertise in sourcing external data for non-resident customers. Industry uses robust customer, transaction and staff screening processes using a combination of in-house, group, or purchased tools such as World Check, Riskscreen, LexisNexis and other international databases to screen customers for PEPs, sanctions, and adverse media, all of which are globally accessible. Most residents' addresses and phone numbers can be found via IsleofMan.com, and reliable information is accessible from sources like credit bureaus, electoral rolls, and Companies House. Court judgements.
Regulatory notices are also available online including published information regarding disqualified Directors. Banks and businesses use independent sources to verify details about individuals and entities in other jurisdictions. The AML/CFT Handbook offers guidance regarding the use of electronic sources and approved providers. Isle of Man companies generally aren't required to file accounts with the registry, so accounts are usually obtained directly. While there's no local credit bureau, agencies like Experian are widely used, and use of comprehensive transaction monitoring systems is standard.

headers: Appendix VI: National Anti-Money Laundering Controls
body:
The Beneficial Ownership Act 2017 places IOM corporate and legal entities under the same legislation regarding registrable beneficial ownership (RBO). It created a central database for the recording of RBO of legal persons. The central database went live in July 2017. The BOA requires each legal entity to which the Act applies to appoint a Nominated Officer who is a natural person ordinarily resident in the IOM. Where the legal entity is in receipt of corporate services comprising Class 4 regulated activity provided by a person licensed by the FSA, that person may undertake the responsibilities of the Nominated Officer, and in practice, this will typically be a TCSP. Overall, TCSPs are the Nominated Officer for 54.8% of all companies to which the Act applies (see Figure 55).
Subject to initial authorisation by Companies Registry, the Beneficial Ownership Database is accessible electronically. Only designated individuals (currently 146 in total) within the competent authorities have access to the database. An audit log is in place. The competent authorities can extract on an individual or receive a bulk download.
Where information is not held on the central Beneficial Ownership Database owned by Companies Registry, it is held by ITD or the TCSP (or another regulated entity that has the entity as its customer, such as a bank).
Source: Companies Registry and Income Tax Divisioni

Mitigation measures are strong in many areas and include:

- The central BOA database is supported by verification mechanisms and both civil and criminal penalties for non-compliance, with reporting required at incorporation, upon changes, and annually.

Source: Companies Registtry

- Companies Registry validates all non-TCSP RBO submissions and 25% of TCSP submissions, raising queries with Nominated Officers when inconsistencies arise, placing responsibility on them to act.

- Obliged entities must notify the Registry within one week of discovering incorrect entries; failure to do so is an offence, and the FSA oversees compliance and imposes penalties, including fixed civil fines since 2024.

- Multiple agencies have access to RBO information; the IOM Companies Registry provides online access, and since January 2025, obliged entities can request information for AML/CFT/CPF purposes.

- Not all legal persons and arrangements are centrally recorded on the IOM database; TCSPs retain information for foreign entities and trusts, and they supply it to authorities when required.

- A significant proportion of companies, especially those administered by TCSPs, lack central RBO records, often due to discretionary trusts in their structure.

- Bearer shares are banned and Directors have fiduciary duties, but nominee shareholder arrangements remain a minor risk outside regulated sectors.

- Controls and resources at Companies Registry have improved since 2020, with effective domestic cooperation and robust international information exchange supporting transparency.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), Appendix VII: Methodology - 9a728ebc325fdb9e
body:
The National Financial Crime Strategy states its "Strategic Objective 2" to be: to "use a risk-based approach to identify risk, coordinate appropriate actions and apply resources to ensure identified risk is addressed and mitigated." WB methodology was used for the 2015 and 2020 ML/TF NRAs. It has been used to provide consistency with previously published NRAs. The WB approach is consistent with FATF guidance published in 2025.
In the WB methodology for risk assessment, the tool treats ML risk as a product of two main components: threat and vulnerability. The consequences are integrated into those two components through weights, preconditions, and network structure, and are not assessed separately. This approach is adopted at both national and sectoral levels for the IOM.

Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), Appendix VII: Methodology - 7683e6b383862c20
body:
Where available, this Risk Assessment uses data from the years 2020 to 2024 inclusive. These four years represent the period since publication of the last NRA. Some data, due to its sensitivity, is not included in this document.
The WB ML assessment tool follows five steps, which this report follows in Chapters 8, 9, 10, 11, and 12.

- Step 1: Identify ML Threats

- Step 2: Assess National ML Threat Level

- Step 3: Sectoral ML Risk Analysis

- Step 4: Assessment of National Vulnerability

- Step 5: Calculation of National ML Risk
Each step is supported by WB Excel spreadsheets. Step 3 is underpinned by four detailed sectoral reports on Banking, Insurance, Gambling, and Trust and Corporate Service Providers, and a sectoral report on Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers that considers ML (and TF and PF risks). These reports have been published. Step 4 is underpinned by a detailed, unpublished workbook which provides the summary narrative for this document.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), Appendix VII: Methodology, QUALITATIVE WORK - d3b4aae026404371
body:
Three workshops were held with participation from across all the agencies, Government, regulators and law enforcement. The workshops considered cross-border and national threats and national vulnerabilities, and agreed key points and, where applicable, ratings for the WB model. The expert judgement of those in attendance, plus several follow-up meetings, were included. In addition, various externally published documents have been referenced, including a number of NRAs from other countries. A summary of the work undertaken by the authorities on national threat and vulnerability is included in this ML NRA.
The regulators led sectoral engagement to inform the WB national vulnerabilities modules. These workshops, most of which were also attended by representatives from the FIU and the AML/CFT Policy Office, involved around 100 meetings (including those with the TCSP sector to inform the LPA Risk Assessment). Several sectors, notably Banking, Insurance, and TCSPs, were met with several times and provided significant levels of expert knowledge to the process. A full list of the engagement that took place is available.

chunk_id: Money Laundering National Risk Assessment (March 2026), Appendix VII: Methodology, QUALITATIVE WORK - e8ed5fbc3910c46d
body:
Sectoral assessments used the financial centres part of the WB model where applicable and analysed the products and services provided by that sector. While there was sufficient data and information on most sectors to use the model, this was not the case for a small number where, for example, there was only one firm, or in the case of HVGDs, none are currently registered. The NRA has taken this into account.
For the purposes of the model, each sector is assigned a rating for threat and a 'weighting' which reflects factors specific to the Isle of Man. The vulnerability score is a direct product of the engagement between regulators and the relevant sectoral representatives.
